THE INVENTOR'S WIFE.
It's easy to talk- O'f—the patience of Job. Humph Job had nothin' to try him; If he'd been married to 'Bijah Brown, folks wouldn't
_ have dared come nigh him. Trials indeed! Now rll tell you what—if you want to be sick of your life, Jest come and change places with me a spell—for I'm an

inventor's wife. And sech inventions! I'm never sure, when I Jake up my coffee-pot, That 'dijah hain't been " improvin' " it, and it mayn't go off like a shot. Why, didn't he make 1119 a cradle once, that would keep itself a-rockin' ? And didn't it pitch the baby out, and wasn't his head bruised shockin' ? And there was his "patent peeler," too—a wonderful _
thing, I'll say' • Etat it had one fault—it never stopped till the apple was peeled away. AB for locks, and clocks, and mowin' machines, and
, reapers, and all such trash, Why 'Bijah's invented heaps of 'em, but they don't bring in no cash. Law ! that don't worry him—not at all; lie's the aggra-
vatinest man— He'll set in his little workshop there, and whistle and
think and plan, Inventin' a Jew's harp to go by steam, or a new-fangled powder-horn, While the children's goin' barefoot to school, and the
weeds is chokin' Our corn. When 'Wish and me kep' company, he warn' t like this,
you know; Our folks all thought he was dreadful smart; but that

was years ago. He was handsome as any pictur' then, and he had such a glib, bright way— I never thought that a time would come when I'd rue my weddin' day; But when I've been forced to chop the wood, and tend
....... _ _ _ to the farm besides, And look at 'Bijah a-settin' there, I've jest dropped down
and cried. We lost the hull of our turnip crop while he was in-
ventin' a gun; But I counted it one of my marcies when it bu'st before it was done. So be turned it into a "burglar alarm." It ought to
give thieves a fright ; 'Twould scare an honest man out of his wits, ef he sot it off at night.

Sometimes I wonder ef 'Bijah's crazy, he does sech cufous things; Hey I told you about his bedstead yet? 'Twas full of wheels and springs; It hod a key to wind it up, and a clock face at the head, All you did was to turn them hands, and, at any hour you said, That bed got up and Shook itself, and bounced you on
the floor, And then shet up, just like a box, so you couldn't sleep
any more. Wa'al, 'Bijah ho fixed it all complete, and he sot it at
•. _ , half-past five. But he ha In't more'n got into it, when—dear me! sakes alive ! Them wheels began to whiz and whir! 1 heard a fearful

snap. And there was that bedstead, with 'llijah inside, shet up, jest like a trap ! I screamed, of course; but 'twan't no use. Then I worked thet hull long night, A-tryin' to open the pesky thing. At last I got in a fright: I couldn't hr•ar his voice inside, and I thought he might be dyin'. So I took a crowbar and smashed it in. There was rßijali peacefully lyite, Inventin' a way to git out agin. That was all very well to say. But I don't believe he'd havc found it out if I'd left him in all day.
how, senre I've told you my story, do you wonder I'm tired of my life? Or think it strange I often wish I warn't an inventor's wife? —AI.
E. T. CORHHTT.

div.p: Varitties.

"Can a clergyman marry himself ?" asks a Yankee paper. All we can say is that if he does he gets a very Poor wife. "Don't trouble to see me to the door," said a fair caller to her host. "Trouble? Indeed, it is no trouble. It is quite a pleasure." "Throw up your situation ?" "Certainly, lam about to marry." "1)0 you propose to live on love ?" " on my love's father." Dullard: "Do you know women love to see themselves in print? Brightly: "They ought to be encouraged, my boy; a precious sight cheaper than silk." Courage that grows from constitution often forsakes the man when he has occasion for it; courage which arises from a sense of duty acts in a uniform manner. "Please, ma'am, can you help a poor man who is out of work ?" "I dare say I Can find something for you to de." "Thanks. If you could give me some washing to do, I'll take it, home to my wile." A clergyman, who owed his situation to a titled patron rather than to his abilities, in visiting his parish- ioners for the purpose of cateelosing them, asked one old Presbyterian—" Who made Paul a preacher ?" "It wasna the Marquis," replied the old man, with a grim Bmilp and a shake of the head. There was a Sir Judkin Fitzgerald, who, being Sheriff tif Tipperary, had, it was said, during the Rebellion of 1796, practised great cruelties. Among other things, he was reported to have dipped the cat-o'-nine tails in brine before a flogging. By way of excuse to Keller, lie boasted that, by his firmness, he had "preserved the country." "..No," said Jerry, "hut you pickled it." . -. • .

, A diminutive- drummer in a local brass band in Scot- land wan in the habit, when out parading with his com- rades, of walking bv sound and not by sight, owing to his drum being so high that he was unable to see over it. The band, on Saturday afternoons, paraded usually in one direction, but the other day the leader thought he would change the route a little, and turned down a by- street. The drummer, unaware of this movement, kept on his accustomed way, drumming as hard as ever he could. By and by, after finishing hie part, and not,hear- ins!, the others, he stopped, and pushing his drum to one side, he looked to see what was the matter. His astonish- ment may be imagined at finding that he was alone. "Rae !" he cried to some bystanders, "has ony o' ye Seen a band hereabout?" THE GUILE OF THE GREEKS.—As traders, the Hellenes know no masters, and in the "tricks" which have been associated with commerce since the days of the classical satirists the Levantine has little to learn. There is a vulgar proverb, well known in the Mediterranean coun- tries, to the effect that one Armenian can outwit two Jews, and one Greek two Armenians; and the French term for a rogue and an Athenian being the same, this exceeding sharpness of the " Grec" is substantially recognised. The "Greek guile" consists mainly in great industry, energy, and acuteness in preferring to "do" rather than in being "done," and in reaping the rewards which the listless, lazy races around them envy, but have neither the ability nor the nerve to grasp. They are not very truthful, but that is not a marked fea- talre in the Christian character in the East. They are also vain, envious, and jealous; but these unpleasant features are not peculiar to them. But they are lull of enterprise. A Bulgarian peasant's family is rooted te the soil. A Greek peasant, on the contrary, encourages his children to leave their native farm and seek their fortune abroad.—The Countries of the World. tHE LONDON BANNERS' CLEARING HOUSH.—The scien- tific system on which our commerce is based cannot be better illustrated than by a description of the Bankers' Clearing Howe. By its means some twenty million pounds sterling are paid and received by business men every day without a single coin ever changing hands. The gold remains in the vaults at the Bank of England. The payments are made by means of cheques and bills, and these are taken by the payees to their various bankers, the amounts being placed to their credit in time to meet cheques drawn against them on the same day. Thus, it a merchant receives a cheque for £lO,OOO, 'he tan pay it into his bank, and can immediately draw ten crossed cheques for £l,OOO each or a hundred crossed cheques for £lOO each, with the knowledge that his banker will honour them, and that the payments will be balanced by the amounts received. And each receiver of a £lOO cheque may, in his turn, hand it to his banker and draw ten cheques of £lO each against it. Yet in the whole course of these transactions no money changes 'bands. How, then, is the matter arranged? There are 'twenty-seven City banks belonging to the Clearing House, and these act as agents for innumerable West- end and provincial bankers who are not members of the institution. The representatives of all the clearing banks meet at the Bankers' Clearing House, and the cheques held by one bank against another are exchanged, the balances being settled by a draft on the Bank of Eng- land. The Bank of England simply debits the account of one bank and credits another, so that the actual pass- ing of coin becomes unnecessary. The clearing of cheques on country bankers takes place in the morning, commencing at twelve o'clock. Sometimes as many as 80,000 country cheques are cleared, each one of which, it may be interesting to state, has to be entered eight times in the course of its passage through the banks and the Clearing House.—Cosseirs Saturday Journal.

THE SCHOOLMASTER AND HIS VISITOR. The Schoolmaster sat in his class-room, the evening prayer had been said; His thoughts were in front of a problem, his hands at the back of his head. He had many dark problems before him, and to make his decisions quite fair, He was turning them round in his noddle, and working them out on the square. There were numberless letters laid open, from parents, and guardians, and aunts, Full of grumbles and growls without number, and worries, and wishes, and wants. Mistress Smith was alarmed for her Tornmy, she thought they had whipped him too strong, He was always a good boy at home, she was sure he would never do wrong. She had a great horror of whipping— it crushed out the manhood and pride; She had nothing to say against leather, unless it was tanning the hide: She thought that the soul was embittered by stinging the body with pain; She believed in the sugar of kindness,

- but not in the sugar of cane. Mistress Brown desired Willie a whipping, he grew such a masterful lad; He did not get on with his studies, and so disobedient and bad; He quarrelled and swore with his brothers,
and so many lies he would tell, She was sure that the school was to blame,

and she wished they would wallop him well. She was one that believed a sound beating would do the boy good and no hurt, For even the best Brussels carpets were beaten to fetch out the dirt; By beating, bar-iron was toughened, and grain was divided from st, aw, And marble was shaped into beauty, and boys were subjected to law. Mistress Jones was concerned for her Jimmy, afraid he was, going insane; They must really not work him so hard, . . .

she thought it would crack his poor brain; He was killing himself with his studies, the examination to pass. And he sat till the bottom of night, to keep at the top of his:class. Mister Robinson thought them too easy with idleback Dick, and he said That they were to poke him up smartly, and leather it into his head; If he didn't progress a bit faster he shouldn't allow him to stay; They must put on the screw and the rawhide, or else he should take him away. Mistress Dibb disapproved of her Bobby sitting near to those children of Medd's, She thought they were not overclean, they always were scratching their heads. And old Mistress Simpson was writing, to look after her boy at play, And not let him climb up the swing-pole, and wear all his trousers away. Another was making complaints that his boy coming home often lingers, Moreover he blackened his hands by cleaning his slate with his fingers, And this one was learning to swear, for he used a. had word to his mother; And that one was spoiling his boots by standing one foot on the other. „. And so the schoolmaster kept reading these grumbles and growls without end, And many a time he was puzzled what sort of an answer to send. Some culprits were there, too, before him, awaiting the punishment due, Pretending to feel very sorry. and trying to look very blue. They had scribbled the wall of the class-room, and made it appear such a fright, That he sometimes felt sorry he ever had taught them to draw or to write. And they read penny-dreadfuls, with stories of murder and blood-thirsty deed; He was almost afraid he had cursed them, in teaching the rascals to read. And while he was thinking and thinking, he heard a great noise on the stair,• So he rose from his seat in a hurry, and peeped down to see who was there, When he saw a stout, jolly old fellow, a farmer at once you would guess him, Who came up all-smiling and nodding, and bluffly began to address him— " Good-day te ya, Mister Skealmaisther, the evening is desperate fine: Ah thowt ah wad gist vs a call aboot that young sonnie o' mine. Ah couldn't persuade him to come, sea all left him beliont ma at yam, But somehoo it's waintly possesst ma to mak' a skealmaisther o' Sam. He's A kind ov a slackback you knaw, ah never could get him te worrk, He searcelins wad addle his sawt wiv a ploo, or a shovel, or forrk. Aleve tried him agean and agean, , bud alt tinnd that he's flea use at yam, Sea me an' ma MISALIS agreed te mak' a slrealmaistlier o' Sam. If all sends him to wark, why, he'll chunther, an' o'io ma the ntrfullest leaak.s. He'd a deal rayt her hg uppod sofy wi novels an' them soon o' beaaks, Sea ah thowt a skealmaisther wad suit him. • a lowse soort o' job d'ye see, Just to keep a few banes oot o' mischief, as easy, as easy can be. Ov coorse you've to larn 'ern te coont, an' te figger a bit, an' te read, An' te sharpen 'ern up if they're numskulls, wiv a lalidabber ower their heed, Bud WS as oasy as easy you knaw, an' all think it wad just suit oor Sam, An' ma missus she's just o' ma mind, for she says that's he nea use at yarn. It was nobbut this morning ah sent him to gan and to harm some land. He was beaming asleep uppod foaf, wiv a ruhbishly beaak in his hand; Ah gay' him a bunch wi' me feaat an' rattled him yarming of/ yam. Sea all think that MAI send him to you, you !nun mak' a skealmaisther o' Sam. He's a stiff and a runty young fellow, ah think that he'll grow up a wopper: He'd wallop the best lad you've got, an' ah think lie would wallop him proper; But still he's a slackback you knaw, . an' seeing he's ne3 use at yam, Ah think ail shall send him to you, you mun mak' a skealmaisther o' Sam."

The schoolmaster answered him slowly— " A slackback is useless I tear. I'm sure he won't make a schoolmaster, it's no use your bringing him here. He would find out the work WAS much harder than ploughing or pulling a rake. You think it's as easy as easy, and ttvit's where you make the mistake. Has Sam a kind heart in hislansorn? a wish human souls to exalt? Can he say a firm word without harshness, and know when to look o'er a fault? Has he got au unquenchable thirst to irnpr)v., and to polish his mind? Dees he know when to punish a culprit, and when to seem deaf and look blind? Can he build in the minds of his pupils a love for the good and the true? Can he guide them in what to believe, and to know, and to he, and to do? Do his eyes flash with earnest emotion of knowledge, of zeal, and of skill? Has tIIS got a great heartful of patience? a firm and unbendable will? Can he bear to be fretted and worried a score or two times in a day? Be angered without showing anger, and still have a kind word to say? Can he work seven days in a week in an atmosphere bitter as gall? • - Short pay and long credit at that, and overtime no pay at all'? Can he come to his work in the morning with spirits inventive and bright? And never look jaded all day, though limp as a dishcloth at night? Can he rouse the dark vision of dulness, and curb an untamable will? Restrain a too-forward conceit, and shyness with confidence fill? Can he rivet a wandering eye, and soften a boisterous tread'? Can he do twenty things at a time. and see through the back of his head?" And thus, as the master kept talking, the farmer was lifting his hair, And backing and backing his footsteps, until he had backed down the stair; And the.n he gave way to his feelings, as soon as he got to to the foot,— "Good night te va, Alisther Skealmaistlier, I think you have gone off yer nut." —GEO. The Messrs. Truman, we understand, are purchasing largely in Shire horses for parties interested in the South American Republic. As the Messrs. Truman have already this year made large purchases for their estab- lishment in the States, it can easily be understood on wl•at a large scale their operations are conducted. The Beaver steamer Lake Superior, which sailed rrorn Liverpool on July 20th with 240 horses, the largest number ever shipped from the Mersey for breeding pur- poses, passed Quebec within eight days and arrived at Montreal in eight days twenty-one hours, all the horses, with the exceptim of two, being landed alive and in splendid condition. A new departure, greatly to be commended, is made by the Royal Agricultural Society in offering prizes, in connection with next year's show, for hops, jam, and fruit, preserved, bottled, and desiccated. Prizes are also to be offered for cider and perry, presumably under the impression that an increased consumption of these beverages might be promoted, and thus increase the demand for fruit. . .

GRAIN STOCKS—The diminution in arrivals and the increase of consumption during the past month has further reduced the grain stocks at Liverpool by about 58,000 quarters. The return of the stocks just taken shows 480,558 quarters wheat, 125,509 maize, 25,242 barley, 29,993 oats, 9,746 beans, and 5,119 peas; with 2.869 loads of oatmeal and 90,960 sacks of flour. Ihe stocks on the 31st of July last year comprised 1,024,413 quarters wheat, 135,294 maize, 10,882 barley, 2,525 oats, 12.529 beans, and 20,000 peas; with 5,960 loads of oat- meal and 122,113 sacks ot flour. SHEEP WASITING.—Mr. Isaac Holden, M.P., writes as follows on the subject of sheep washing :—" Washing wool on the sheep's back, as well as scouring it, as it is called, after being clipped, before sending it to the mar- ket, is absurd, injurious to the wool, and wasteful. The wool becomes felted in the proOss in both cases. The practice generally in France, in La Plata, and in South Australia, is to clip the sheep without washing, and to pack the wool in the grease. It keeps better, is softer, and is washed more easily and more perfectly when it arrives in the grease or yolk at the weight-house of the comber or manufacturer with at least one-half of the soap."

We regret to learn that the third annual report of the Small Farms and Labourers' Land Company is not a favourable one. At first the company appeared to be prospering, and a dividend of 5 percent. was paid to share- holders at the end of the first year. Unfortunately, signs of prosperity for the occupiers of the land have from the first been wanting, and it appears that during the past year many of them have been unable to pay their rents, while others have had reductions granted. Still, the directors believe the system to be working well, as the tenants, it is said, are cultivating their holdings pro- perly, and are carrying cut improvements. We fear there is but a poor chance in these hard times for small farmers, who rely chiefly on corn-growing for a living, especially if they occupy land as poor as most of that on the Lamborne estate is.

WATERY FOODS.--Brewers' grains, succulent grass and roots, are credited with producing a large flow of poor milk as compared with such drier aliment as hay, straw, and meal, notwithstanding that whilst consuming the latter the cows have ready access to an abundant supply of water. If this be so, what are the physiological con- ditions which explain it? Professor Wanklyn in his book says that by drinking large quantities of water cows dilute the urine, but not the milk. It would ap- pear, therefore, that the yield cannot be largely in- creased by the direct administration of water, even if it can by the consumption of watery foods. The quality, however, can be reduced by feeding cows on watery foods, simply because such foods contain tittle nutri- ment, and the animal cannot consume sufficient bulk daily of the solid constituents necessary to repair the frame, and produce abundant rich milk at the same time. If the appetite did not fail, and the stomach be- come too full, the case might be different. But you can- not put a quart of beer into a pint pot. CLOVPR FOR Pies.—A well-known transatlantic writer on pigs, says: "Cure some clover for the hogs to eat next winter. Cut it when in full blossom, and put it where it can be had, so that the hogs can be foddered with it twice a day. My hogs will almost winter on it. They will eat it as hay, or better, if cut and wetted with a little bran, or meal put on it. A corn farmer may laugh at my notion, but I will beat him in pigs in the spring and in profits in the fall." This suggestion is worthy of a trial. especially as it seems reasonable. At the recent convention Of Wisconsin dairymen, Mr. Stephen F•aville gave a most instructive address about clover, which he considers the "dairyman's sheet anchor." Among the other points insisted on, was the wisdom of putting hogs on clover pasture in summer. He surprised the convention by asserting that more pounds of pork can be made from one acre of clover than from art acre of corn. The proof he subinitted in support of this statement was as follows: 50 bushels of shelled Indian corn would be fully an average yield per acre, and 121 b. of pork for one bushel of Indian corn would be fully up to the average. That would give 6001 b. for the acre of corn. "An acre of good clover," he says, "will pasture eight hogs from the time clover starts in spring till fall. A fair growing hog, weighing 1001 b., on being turned out in the spring will gain another 1001 b, by fall, without any other feed than clover. That would be 8001 b for the clover, as against 6001 b. for the Indian corn. What an advantage on the side of the clover, and can it be disputed ? "

PREPARING FOR A WET HARVEST. It would be well for farmers in the south, east, and other parts of England—who are not in the habit of taking the precautions usual in Scotland and some of the northern English counties against the spoiling of cut crops by rain—to consider whether they will not alter their practice in the event of the present wet weather continuing. Throughout the greater portion of the principal corn-growing counties of England harvesting is carried on Upon the assumption that the prevailing weather will be dry, and in the majority of seasons this assumption is justified by experience. Even wheat and oats, when cut by a self-delivery reaping machine, are left in the swath for some hours, and sometimes for days, before being tied and set up in shocks, or stooas as they are often termed; and when the shocks are made they are not protected against rain. In the case of barley, it is still more common t 3 leave it in the swath, and the greater portion of it in many parts of England is not tied in sheaves at all, but Is carted loose. Beans are nearly always tied, but are not protected; while peas and seeci vetches are left in little heaps as they are "made up," and are even more exposed to damage from wet than corn in the unturned swath is. Now, there is a good deal of saving or labour in this happy-go-lucky system, exaept that it is becoming generally the impres- sion that it pays to tie barley; and, one year with another, perhaps the methods referred to are those most suitable to the districts in which they are common. But the question is whether, in the event of harvest having to be commenced without any prospect of settled fine weather, a change should not be made for one season, at I any rate. While throwing out a few suggestions as to easy methods of protecting cut corn while it is in the fields, we invite our readers to "compare notes" in our columns upon this peculiarly seaso.able subject. We having nothing new to suggest, but only desire to , recommend the adoption of Precautions commonly ' taltea in rainy districts or countries. With respect to the cereals, when a binder is not used, it will be a safe- guard to tie closely after the reaping machine, and to stook as soon as a small quantity is tied. Of course, if this is done oats must not be cut as green as they some- times are, lest they should heat and mould. So far we have only- got to the extent of avoiding the custom of leaving the corn upon the ground in the swath or in sheaf not set up. Bnt if the weather seems likely to be wet it will be well to protect the stooks. The simplest method of doing that is to place six or eight sheaves in I a circle, with the butt ends diverging, so as to allow the air to circulate among them, and at the same time to bring the heads compactly together, in which position an inverted sheaf, opened and spread out, can be placed over them. The rain can then only get at the ears of the upright sheaves after penetrating the butt end of the covering sheaf, and a heavy rainfall is required to do' that. As to the ears of the inverted sheaf, spread out singly or nearly so, as they are, and hanging downwards, they quickly dry after a wetting. This plan, which costs but little, is available for wheat, barley (all to be tied up), oats, and beans. We are by no means certain, indeed, that it costa anything in the Ion; run, because
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUG

the stooks are much 'less liable to be blown down 1 when made in this fashian than when set up in the ordinary way, and in windy seasons a, good deal of work in setting up sheaves is necessary when corn is long• in the fields. As to peas and seed vetches, the plan—or an adaptation of it—more common in certain foreign countries than in any part of the United Kingdom—may be recommended. It consists of setting up hurdles in rows across the field, and hang- ing the peas and vetches upon them to dry. When so placed, they will quickly dry after rain, and seldom take any harm. The best way, though it requiries more hurdles, is to set them up in pairs in the shape of an in- verted V, for when so set they are firmer, and will hold the material placed upon them more securely and more out-spread. If readers experienced in the harvesting of crops in rainy districts can improve upon our suggestion we shall be glad to give publicity to their plans. The terrible weather which has pursued the unlucky hus- bandman for seven or eight weeks is surely:forewarning enough, and it will be well for farmers in all parts of the kingdom to be forearmed, too, by having placed-at their disposal the best plans for harvesting77corn in wet weather. Since the preceding remarks were written a beautiful change in the weather has been experienced. If the sunshine has "come to stay," the more trouble- some of the methods of saving crops, such as the use of hurdles, are not likely tope adopted; but unless there should be very assuring signs of settled weather, some of the precautions suggested may with advantage be adopted.—Agricultural Gazette.

PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. Br Ilisou Barn. =IL—HOUSEKEEPING. During the many years of my married life, I have held firmly to the theory that if women would reduce their income and expenditure to paper in the form of a debit and credit account, they would soon be a long way ahead in the savings bank. Whenever I have submitted this proposition with more than usual gusto to Mrs. Bette, she has invariably answered "Fiddlesticks" with far more emphasis than argument; and when I have-quietly pointed out that although fiddlesticks may be very useful things in their way, they have no bearing upon the subject at issue, she tells me that if I think I can manage the house better than she can, I had better do it, that's all.

Now, although I don't (for reasons to be set before you) feel quite so sanguine upon the infallibility of domestic bookkeeping as I once did, I am as much as ever convinced that women, as a rule, don't cultivate ratiocination.

When Mrs. Bette reminded me that it was a long time since the family went to the sc.aside, I naturally asked what family she alluded to; after informing me that she didn't like people to he aggravating, she said I knew very well that she meant our family. The said family was present at the time, and as I cast my eyes despairingly upon its units, I was humbled. lam afraid that I am not so proud of them sometimes as fought to be; and when visions of five olive branches wrestling in the railway train amidst a waggon load of spades, buckets, and et-cteras flit across my mind's eye, the freezing sensation down my, spinal column sought to convince me that pride is sure at sometime or other to have a fall. I mentally skimmed over the reflections with a rapidity horn of several seaside experiences, and finally pleaded indisposition, and if ycu are a peter fanplias yourself, you will, no doubt, under- stand it thoroughly. If not, I should advise yon to get a little experience by taking the workhouse children away for a day's holiday, under your sole charge. Mrs. Bette pertly told inc that if I had been capable of looking after myself, she would have taken the children and gone without me. Fancy the position; my character was fairly at stake, so I said, "Try me for a week or set" and that is how I happen to know such a lot about housekeeping. The first thing .a housekeeper who holds the opinion stated has to do IS to rule off a sheet of foolscap with two cash columns, and the next thing is to take stock. If the housekeeper is a male, he ought to engage some- body to waken him in a morning if he doesn't want to meet people coming home to dinner when he is going to business; but I only mention this by the way. After I had paid the butchers, bakers, grocers, and other bills for the previous week—which I had put down on my sheet like a martyr—my liabilities began to assume dangerous proportions, and the sundries had very soon to be carried forward. The milkmen wanted to charge me for the morning he had called when the blinds were still down, and because I asked him if he thought I was as easily swindled as women, he chose to take the cream off my breakfasts by refusing to call again. Of course I can make my own breakfasts and teas. You soon get to know by experience whether it takes one teaspoonful or seven teaspoonfuls to make a brewing; but it is really astonishing what a lot of pots accumulate in the course of a few days when you haven't time to wash them up. When I had used every 'cup and saucer, pint pot, and basin in the house, I started off to use them a second time, and in picking out the cleanest I upset such a pile of crockery that it took me about half an hour to pick up the pieces.. It clearly wouldn't do to set such a precedent for pot breaking, for it had almoat become a science of destruction at our house before I participated in it, so there was no other reasonable course left but to take one of each of the only two pairs of cups and saucers left whole, and to set off on a matching expeditmn. I won't trouble you with detailing low much I was swindlea out of in this transaction. It trikes me now as being rather funny that the possibility of the newness of my purchase being detected never once crossed my mind. one thing crossed my mied very forcibly, and that was that when I had entered the cost of that set on my sheet, it began to lose any resemblance it might once have had to a balance sheet. Whew! what sundries there are in a week's household account. When I had added the expenditure side three times, the amount came out as appalling as the winding up statement, of any bankrupt. Then I began to look over the items carefully, and to strike out those that I thought didn't rightly belong to the housekeeping account, such as these—Ts one pint of brandy used as a narcotic; to prepaid rep'fi telegram to Airs B. "Where do you keep the soap ?" To two ounces of best navy cut, and so on. But this didn't lessen the account much. If I could have managed to increase the credit side of the account at the same ratio, all would have been well; but the words, "By one week's salary," and the amount, remained unaltered, and at last became an eyesore. In strict confidence I tell you, that I looked round the house to see if anybody watched me, although I knew there was no one to watch, and stealthily committed my first and last household account to the flames. I lay the whole of the blame of failure upon those everlasting sundries. I don't think I have once urged the advisability of domestic bookkeeping since. The amount of physical labour done by a housekeeper varies according to the temperament of the individual, more especially if the individual is living alone. For instance, one housekeeper will make a bed every day, while another housekeeper will sleep in every bed in the house successively without any making. I believe the Latter mode is followed mostly by male housekeepers. It is really surprising what non-laborious utility can be got out of three beds by sleeping the first night on the right side of number one bed, second night on the left slap, third night in the middle, and so on with the other two. You cannot be fairly charged with doing anything unreasonable in this, because your only motive in doing it is to keep the beds aired, of coune. A masculine housekeeper should study the principles of combustion before taking the seale of °Mae, as other- wise he is apt to waste a good deal of powerful elocution when lighting the fire; but I And that such knowledge doesn't astist you much in carting the ashes out, which is to be lamented. When the pile of ashes is—say just beginning to come over the fender, the only thin., for it is to take off your coat and evacuate them 'by the crudest possible form of hand labour. If the people in the adjoining houses don't laugh at you (in your journeys up and down the yard) as much as you could wish, you will still have the satisfaction of getting the fire to burn.

If there is one thing calcuated to irritate the male housekeeper more than any other, it is to hear a bass voice thundering up the bedroom stairs at one o'clock in morning, "Do Non want to be robbed?" - • .

I appeal to any sensible man whether or not this is a reasonable question to ask at such an hour, and in such a manner. What with getting out of bed bead first, the noise, and the bright light of a bull's-eye lantern streaming upon you, it is impossible to tell for awhile whether it is a volcanic eruption, a fire, or simply a gasometer burst. When the adventure happened to me, after locking the door with the constarle outside, I thought that the whole affair resembled a wake as much as anything. The best way to avoid such a disturbance is to lock the doors before you go to bed. Taking everything into consideration, I don't think male housekeepera are likely to be a success, particularly if the judge is to be a woman. After eight days of what appeared to me to be a struggle against fate, I awaited —how anxiously I am not prepared to admit—for the approbation due to my unflagging diligence and self- abnegation. It won't take long to describe it. After the usual greetings had been exchanged between us, Mrs. Bette remarked, "Why, Hugh, the nouse is like a pigstye!" If lam ever expected to step up again in`o the rank of housekeeper, somebody will be disappointed.
Mrs. Riley: " Are ycz on calling terms wid our neigh- bour ?" Mrs. Murphy: Av coorse I am, Mrs. Riley. She called me a thafe, and I called her another."

div.head: CHAPTER V.
div.p: CHAPTER V.
THE ATELIER DESNOYERS.

About twelve years after the events recorded in the last chapters a mixed company of students were present in the Atelier Desnoyers; 'in Paris, some foreigners being permitted to work as visitors. The lame majority of the students belonged to the better classes of society, others to the lower middle class, whilst a few had sprung from a still lower rank. The realistic -movement in keeping with Republican notions involves the upsetting of many long-cherished ideas in that France where there are at present so many men endowed with genuine artistic talent and activity, and ardently doing their work. Eleven o'clock had struck. The model wile had been consulted about his position three hours be- fore—having chosen a pose recommended as involving the least fatigue—was already beginning to tire,. He was longing to be able to move his feet from the chalk marks which had been drawn to enable him to find their exact places. It was a lofty room, thirty feet square, lighted by one big window. The walls were painted roughly in indistinct red, a colour which might have passed for a dark terra-cotta, sincared and dabbled with various other tints, where the students had wiped their brushes and the superfluous colour off their palettes. Behind the model WRS a curtain of grey tapestry, a good deal the worse for wear, and round the (leis on which he sat was a widening semicircle of steels, some so high that the stmlents- had to lean -against them. An inventory could have been taken in a minute or two of the rest of the furniture. There was a high iron stove, and an earthen- ware pan and pipkin for washing brushes, with a basin of steaming water on the stove to keep the atmosphere from becoming 'too dry. A book containing the names and addresses of the pupils, a code ot rules which hung on the -walls— with racks for portfolios—a few plaster castes, a lay figure, and a skeleton completed the rest of the furniture. _ _ _

Tongues wagged as the students worked—some of them in charcoal, some in black and white chalk, some in colour. But the voices never rose beyond the murmur which decorum allowed, for the patron of this Atelier thought, with other sages, that silence was golden. Jokes were cut in a low tone by men who treated even the skeleton en bon eamarade, but the chances were that a neighbour might find the joke embetant. A mixture of all classes was here, a. 4 well as a mixture of nationalities, and each pupil was left as much as possible to the dio. tation of nature, being allowed to follow ,his own particular fancy. , Half-past eleven struck again from the ugly old clock on the painted wall. There was an interval of ten minutes, not only for the necessary rest afforded to the model, but for the appearance of the master.

Sudden silence reigned when he entered the room. 4 "Le. patron y est ! , said a , youth, addressing a fellow-pupil, who sat by his side, and in an instant there was the silence of expectation and anxiety. The patron seldom praised anyone, but he had sent out even the sons of simple peasants from among the young artists " who thronged his ateliers— , many of them his own friends and proteges—to carry the celebrity of his teaching into the world. He knew at a glance when to detect good promising 1 raw material, and to throw it aside again if it did I not prove workable. He was a clear-eyed, short, but energetic-looking man, with dark hair tinged with grey, and a voice which-some said was like a steam saw, speaking in rapid staccato words, few as possible, but like bullets going straight to the mark. ' "That sort of work is puerile," he said, 'as he passed a Paris exquisite, who had dressed himself ' for the occasion in a picturesque holland blouse, 1 and who had been spending his time in stippling a 1 certain portion of his sketch. The patron eared , nothing that the angry blood rose at once to the face of the sufficiently, conceited student. It was his duty to discourage all art which aimed at being pretty rather than thorough, showy rather than cor- rect. Broader handling, with a proper idea of the relative value of light and shade, was to be discerned in the work of the next pupil, a man of the people, who worked at a trade for four days in the week, in order that he might defray his expenses at the atelier for the other two or three. The master simply said to him, 44 You ought to do better work than that." To the third, a rich young Jew, who, .owing to in- fluence , and money, had got a picture into the Salon, and his head turned into the bargain he took ad-,, ' vantage to say, seeing that he Isms muddling over some difficulty requiring dexterous manipulation; _ I. " Ask Gaston to shew you how that is done." I Now Gaston was a pronounced Conimunist, who 1 sat at his elbow dressed in clothes from which the other shrank, for fear they should prove infectious; Gaston had never had a picture in the Salon—a mis- fortune for which the patron comforted him by tell- ing him that the Salon, besides a fair amount of good paintings, always contained it lot of rubbish. To another—a sallow-skinned Armenian—he said, " Good, that is making progress !" The poor fellow needed encouragement, and the "patron," was accustomed to say, "There are only two nations--Lfools and intelligent people." The keen--eyed artist eared nothing for treading on the , toes of the conceited. There was no studied antithesis, no sparkling epigram in his speech, no stock figures of rhetoric. But he spoke his thoughts without stint, little heeding when he had his pro- fessional spectacles on, whether We made an uncom- fortable sensation or not. He had all that feeling 1 of responsibility which befits a "patron "of his stand- ing in a country where the fine arts are made a de- partment of government. lie spared no one, not even those who had tho enthusiasm of genius; and as he paused before the all painting of a lad who had dashed in his sketch with almost fever heats using as few pigments as possible his manner was not encouraging; though' he halted longer than usual. There was-determina- tion and ease in the sketch, but the elements of drawing had been disregarded. " How often have I told you, Campion," he said, as the lad raised a pallid face, the features of which were finely chiselled, somewhat impatiently, as he waited for the master's verdict. "How often have I told you that you must crawl before you can walk, and feel your feet before you can run!' , "You have kept me trammelled long enough—it is time I should "ti to sell my, paintings." begin " Probleu !" said the master, with a shrug, as he answered the direct appeal of the dark blue eyes, "how many years have you, men garcon,?" "Nineteen," muttered the lad under his breath, "but, monsieur, I cannot see my sister starve." "Is there only mademoiselle your sister ?" was the question which he vouchsafed in return. Yet the professional spectacles were a 'little dimmed as the patron took them off to wipe them. For this youth, sometimes an idler, sometimes a worker, just as the fit took him, wasnot one of those light-hearted young rascals, enfants de Paris, who fenced. with jests, and were ever ready to parry them with sharp counter remarks. The boy looked ill-fed, and the master knowing something of his history, '1 11ra.9 aware that here was neither a Socialist full of 1 grievances nor a farceur ready to toss about ideas on a social pitchfork. "Distrust the opinion of the unprofessional public —distrust the temptation to scale the Capitol. the 1 , back way where only the geese will clamour at 1 you," he said a little sadly as he passed to the next ! worker. A close observer. might have seen that the Same shadow of sadness deepened on his fa:be as he , lingered a little longer than usual by Campion's companion. Pierre Ddbois had been nick-named the "lloppcl-ganger" of Raymond Campion, who always 1 protected him from the jests of the other students. There was something touching in the dog-like devotion which Dubois shewed to his protector. Pierre was a Breton, whose father had been a working house-painter, and who had come to Paris with the idea that he, too, might paint pictures. The elder Dubois had died early, and left his son an orphan. Had it not been for the generosity 61 the patron it is likely enough that this young min would quickly have followed.. him. As it was the unfortunate Pierre was being educated under diffi- cultic& His mother, who still lived, had let hilt* drop from her arms in an access of sudden fright when she had been tempted to gape at a mounte- bank in one of the crowds of Paris. The boy was then nearly two years old, and had fallen with violence on the stones. He was irretrievably injured. The back which had never properly developed was rounded ' at the shoulders. The .head had the appearance of being slightly tilted backwards as if it were supported upon the shoulders without any neck; and the pathetic expression of the face, with large, solemn dark eyes, reminded one of the appealing look of some suffering dumb animal. , But Pierre had ability, and indomitable persever- ance, Ile worked, rather leaning against than sitting ' upou the tall staidl which was placed next W

Campion's, at Fite back of the semicircle. He was not tall enough to sit,his•legs being bowed and shrunken. but ho never complained of fatigue, and preferred thi tall stool at the back of the room, close to the dingy:looking walls, to any place where he might be exposed to keener observation. The jokes made at his expense had been heartless, if hot savage. That touch of barbarism, characteristic of one side of Parisian nature, which delights in dissecting human feeling, and making a mock at human agony, even in its most ugly and repulsive details, attracted the idler students to the infirmities of Pierre Dubois. He had been often driven to bay in the absence -of the .patron, had more than once meditated suicide,and wonld probably have furnished a fresh sensation for the Morgue, had not Raymond Campion selected him for his friend. Campion was not calculating,or accustomed to analyse his motives. He and Dubois had been at the same school as boys,. the expenses of both being in great measure defrayed by the kindness of Desnoyers. It . had perhaps,- never occurred to Raymond that his motives were not altogether unmixed when he absented himself from a. prize-giving on one occasion at that school, that he might sit by the bedside of Pier!) and nurse him with skill and attention. missed the applause, which would have been az- music to his ears if he had presented himself in person to take his prize; but it was better still to hear of the flattering encomiums which he had earned by his act of self.denial from the master and parents of the other boys. Even then Pierre had fagged for him and helped him to get his prize, just as now he often put a finishing touch or rendered the outlines of Ray- mond's pictures still nore effective. How much the patron suspected of this as he looked with a touch of melancholy at the hunchbalck's draw- ing it would have been difficult to say, and he knew as well as the other students that "Damon and Pythias" (as the two were familiarly called) had placed themselves in this position to save the crippled lad from jeers. There was soul and purpose in the hunchback's face, as there was a measure of poetic genius in Campion's. But Pierre Dubois could do what Campion could not. He could grapple with a difficulty, and plod till he had conquered it. Childish he was in his canine fidelity to the lad who had befriended him, but not so childish in some respects as Raymond, one side of whose nature had,never been properly developed. Desnoyers nodded his head, and said something to himself, as he looked at the careful study in black and white chalk,et which Dubois had been diligently engaged. The hunchback shrugged,and laid 'down his pencil. The patron never praised him, but he looked his encouragement, which was better than praise. "Yet I shall never make anything of it. I shall always be second-rate," thought the young artist, whose personalinfirmity inclined him to take a low estimate of his own performances. His heart would have leapt with joy if he could have guessed how Desnoyers was thinking that his sketch in black and white,with the depth and breadth of its shadows and the delicacy of its handling, was worth a hundred of the more ambitious and careless sketches dashed off by Raymond in his egotism and his haste.
CHAPTER VI. PERE DESNOYERS.

A few minutes afterwards the patron left the studio. Having performed his duty in sharply criticising the students, he now made his adieux with true French politeness. He had assured one or two disappointed young fellows, whom he could not conscientiously recommend to continue their studies, of the greatness of his regret that he %tank' no longer have the honour and pleasure Of reckoning them amongst his pupils. He tried to impress on them that they had still his "distinguished eensideration," and ended bY bowing to everyone in "ensemble," with a general 4' Bonjour, messieurs !" His exit was a relief to these of a talkative disposition. For the first time during the day there was r general wagging of tongues, at the expense of sr unfortunate dog which seemed to be the worse for the. paint it had imbibed during the hours when its master had been occupied with work. "It will soon agree with its constitution",—itis not the first time—Alions, cito yen, id faut so2grir," and the lad to whom the animal belonged administered a cruel kick which made Pierre Dubois wince, and look the othenway in sympathy. He had learnt from sore experience the uselessness of trying to interfere when other animals were persecuted like himself. The sufferings of the Paris horses and of the harmless 'I%N are condoned by popular opinion and considered amusing rather than otherwise. Very possibly the student who joined with others in laughing at the expense of his miserable dog had himself been the victim of some of the cruel practical jokes said to be prattised on young,, artists at the ateliers of the Beaux-Arts. Raymond Campion had as yet never been subjected to them. No Wiles, even when he was a little boy, had been able to withstand the flashes of light from the usually smouldering fire in the eyes of the English sister, who had come to meet him as he left his school; and none of the boys had tried to take liberties with her brother. He had been a "little brother" then; and had seen nothing humiliating in the fact that a girl should prove helpful both to him- self and Pierre. But as soon as Raymond was fifteen circumstances had altered. He had suddenly made growth, as English boys generally do, just as when the wood begins to harden and the sap to flow more freely in the branches of the young trees. Had there been anyone at hand to guide his de- velopment in a healthy direction the Whole circum- stances of his life might have been altered. As it was, he contented ,himself with awaking to the fact that 4ie must shew his manhood by resenting the interference of a jeune fidle. He was irritated now as he glanced outside the studio and saw a familiar girlish figure, neatly but plainly dressed, pacing up and down.- "I am not coming, home yet," he said, hastily joining her, and then returning to his com- panions. She winced a little as she looked up to him with one of her bright smiles, and prepared to return without him. For was there.not a new coiner at the studio that day, and was there not an exaction of blackmail on all Such 'new comers—harmless enough in itself—known as bienvenue. Was not the new student expected to celebrate his coming by Inviting others to partake of a great bowl of punch, or rather Sauterne-cup, in which they drank to his good luck, and to the long reign of liberty, equality, and fraternity ? . Well, it would not be much of the Sauterne that would fan to Raymond's share,. and if he did smoke a cigarette there was no harm in that, "One must 'not keep lads foe tight," said the patron's voice, breaking in on her reverie. He, too, had been watching the slender figure pacing up and down; Ursula was one of his special favourites. And the old master might be excused for lookin;., her. Not that she was exactly beautiful, but there was something in her different from the other female•etudente whom he taught in another studio close by. "C'est un type" artists had said of her, looking at her critically. But she had always refused a sitting to them. She was not narrow and insular as mest English girls were said to be. The :angles had been rubbed off by long living on the Con- tinent, and by long study of art, not only in Paris, but at Dusseldorf, Munich, Rome, and Madrid. She and her brother scarcely knew how it was that Ray- mond had drifted to the Atelier Desnoyers, drawn there as if. ,by a Magnet in preference to the more public Ecole des Beaux Arta. Probably it was be- cause the patron had been kind to Ursula as well as himself, and had charged the orphans nothing for his instruction:

Monsieur Gustave Desnoyers was as little a flirt as it was possible for a gallant Frenchman of his age to be. The amount of his gallantry was fairly indicated by the appellation, which ptuck • to him, of Pere DesnoyerS: Fatherly as he was, with his strong artistic instincts, it would have been impossible for him to help his glance resting with approbation on the large, powerful, sympathetic .eves which were suddenly raised to his, with golden lights in them, like those which dance on the surface of a stream of brown water,deepeninginto grey depths where it is shaded by weeds, as the grey bands round these hazel orbs were shaded by the lashes. It was not so much the variety of colour which attracted hiin in the eyes, for such a blending of curious tints is to be seen in the majority of eyes, which we too hastily classify into black, brown, or blue, till a little artistic study convinces us of our delusion. It was rather the goodness, the brightness, the innocence, the idea of purity winch the look conveyed to a man accus- tomed by his professional instinct to catch the inner sentiment in a landscape and the true soul in a face. He knew how the innocence of such a look was apt to be deceptive in women, but not in this case,where the girl, left alone without a mother, had passed un- contaminated through the foulest atmospheres with a more than mesmeric faculty for taming lions worse thaU the one which threatened Una. There was a fairness and graciousness about her, in spite of her youth and intelligence—an aid iseptic quality, not only for counteracting evil, but for ren- d.erin,,r, her scarcely aware of its existence. Bo thought the Ql4l s hc 1111,3Cre4 by her, ztL isealied a

sigh of disapprobation, as he remembered that 5118 was no longer among his pupils. " Ah, I knew I had failed, as usual—l have not got it in me—it is of ,no use for me to lament about it," she had said, with an attempt at laughter, almost more sorry for his disappointment than for her own failure,when year after year she had made no progress : Desnoyers answered nothing—there wag little for him „to answer. Great pains had been,, taken with her sketches. There were no glort" defects, no discordant notes in them—the relative values had been all rememberedthere was nothing to blame her for, yet she would never make an artist. "it is canvas wasted," she gained courage t° say one day with an air of emphatic decision. "Don't you think I know it? Don't you thiuk„ after all your teaching I can see what is o'ol and what is not, and I see it as well as you 4'do I say to 'myself, as the peasant said to Rousseau,: 'Why don't you paint the tree—the tree is there au the time?' Don't ,you think I want to paint the fisherman Whom you have given me to paint so well costumed, and that I want to remember the sea behind him? I want to paint it. I See it in 1131,, imagination. But my father was mistaken. I do 110' inherit his tastes." It was on the tip of Desnoyers' tongue to say— • "God forbid, my child, you should inherit anything from such a father." But he restrained himself. It had been one of Ursula's ways. Di escaping fro° the claws of the lion, to muse on a fond delusion re: specting her father. Instead the master answered, if YO4 have failed, the fault is mine.' "No—oh no," she responded enthusiastically; look upon you not only as a Lehrmeister, as ta Germans say, but a Mehrmeister." The patron was silent, and she continued— "It is not your fault or mine either; think, it is absurd for a girl to waste time who has no distinct talent for it. Now, as an ax flower-maker I could get some money, and teaching as you have given me for form and would come in beautifully—and, you know, l make a living." There was an opportunity for paying a comp] Desnoyers was ashamed of himself for prof' it. "You ought to do nothing but grow and like the flowers, instead of making them." He had roused her then. "Oh," she said, "if you think I can sit s bask in the sunshine, and wait to get mello the slow processes of nature, you are mistaken. I do not want to add to the number of those p, tory,twaddling pictures,wbose owner a have no —no tour de force. I wish; with all my heart, was something else which I could do." (i'o be continued.)

BaShi-Bazouks, under a captain and four Bente:o- -w/4a, to surprise Debeb. Adem Aga, with 100 'Bashi- . ttbze, followed to cover the rear. At Eloa the lan captain was informed that Debeb had 470 in consequence of which he waited for Adem Aga, woe on the march had enlisted two hundred As- [ -t_ rtins. This, however, caused some delay, so that _ganeiti was only reached on the Bth of August. -ebeh, who had been informed of the Italian move- was found to have made every preparation to de- ..'erld the place. Nevertheless, the Italian captain, after •,lArrounding the village, gallantly entered it with a oeuteriant and 100 Bashi-Batouks and drove out the • 4bYssinians from a small fort which they then occupied; ;:tOtit the Assaortins, who had already been guilty of feathery in sending information to Debeb during the laarch of the Italian force, deserted during the fighting, Itold joining the enemy attacked the Italians. The de- :flee of the fort thus 'became impossible. The captain lieutenant were wounded in several places; and the asshi-Bazouks left the position in disorder. The treachery the Assaortins and the preponderance of the force gained by the enemy produced h 'panic ameng. ;443 Bashi-Razouks who were waiting outside the Nail- 4'age• Three Italian lieutenants and a few soldiers anerately resisted the enemy's onslaught without "elding an inch of ground. It appears that all the talian officers, with the exception of one, perhaps, fell 1,11 the fighting. About 400 of our Bashi-Razouks• were 11nd at Uad. The Italian officers fought heroically. • Ira' losses are 350 men. Many of the Bashi-Bazouks who ~"ave returned are wounded. They brought back their 'leg with them. It is believed that Adem Aga waf• ~,_ ed. In addition to 20 Assaortins already held as ..."eatages, the Italian commander has arrested:2o more ,Ten of the same tribe." All the other lkiii rewers have token formal cognisance of the two Italian 'Oates el the 25th ult.

RETIREMENT OF COIINT VONMIGITKE. Ilsrmns, Mormax.—Count Von Moltke has definitely 'withdrawn from official life, resigning his' post as Chief 1/44,,f the Staff of the German Army. General Count Wal- ersee has been nominated successor in this office to the ?rlerable stmtsgist. In a gracious and affectionate ..t.tter to Count Von Moltke the Emperor has nominated tft President of the Committee for Imperial Defence.

. A general who had brought Austria to her knees in Ll'ell days and France to the ground Imes many weeks Fllifait, says a contemporary, `have rested on his laurels when the peace earn; in 1:871. Moltke set 1% work and reorganised his office. Porten years he Itlis hard at work at the General Ft:01,4111cl' under his 'land became a school of generalshin nerhaps it itr.nuld be more correct to say a milita,., university. We by side with his studies of strategy and 'organisa- , ton and the plans which he kept .prepared and up to llate for any probable wars in Which Germany light be engaged, he was constantly. selecting the 4t officers in the whole army and training them to ,lle leaders of troops, The military histories pro- 'mated under his supervision are quarries of strategic adorn from which all the studious soldiers of iarope have for twenty yeurs drawn the materials 1.4 their theoretical structures. !Moltke himself ,1141 published no theory of war, itli that he has f‘eknowledged in the theoretical department being an ellllay written for the. Mitetair grockenblatt in 1865 Ikl the effects of breech-loading rifles upon the conduct lil.f battles. But Moltke's doctrine, though not pub- ,,,lethed in an'.' treatise, lives snd worksin the Prussian `leneral Staff. All the brilliant writers who have ;ransformed and remodelled the art of -ever during the ltl!lit twenty years are his pupils. Von' Verdy, Blume. :011 der Gobs, and Hohenlehe have all, sat at his feet. `xecordinglv, if it is well-known that thg Prussian army between 1857 and 1866 made enormous strides in e'ery respect. if it is the wonder el the, military world that this army after its brilliant feats of 1866 made the llillendid advances which were witresself in 1870, it is lilially certain, if less widely known: that the improve-, Illents made between 1871 and 1888 are still more 910rOUgh and sweeping. For all this constant devotion It would be a mistake to give one man. the exclusive credit. It is the tradition of the.Flohenzollerns and of thS Prussian service. But Moltke has 'been the teacher of all the younger men. THE DISMEIVIBERMENT - OF 'FRANCE.

QUESTIONS.

Mr. W. H. Sigma, replying to Sir It. Lethbridge, said he was aware that under the new rules ot pnocedure only questions of a financial or emoomical clia'raoter could be discussed on the Indian Budget. As regards general questions on Indian administration arid india, g riev- ances, it was open to hon, members to discuss them, as other questions were discussed, on Tuesdays and 'Thurs- days throughout the session. In reply to Mr. E. Robertson, Mr. W. H. Saurts said it was perfectly true that in the House er Lords uR Bator - day it was agreed by a majority to insert in the Mort. main and Charitable, Uses Bill a clause exempting Stehle College, Oxford, frairn the provisions of the Mortinain Act. The amendment was moved without any previous ! arrangement with the Government, and the Government had to consider whether they would allow the bill to be lost Or agree with the'Lords' amendments. The Victoria University, in Manchester, had been exempted, and iii -these circumstances the Government thought tlieinseires -fully justified in agreeing, to the hill in the form in whichi itliecl been amended by the Lords. Mr. Rotlearsost asked svhether the Victoria University wasan institution regulated by Act of Parliament, but before the question could .be answered, Black Rod was announced, and he summoned the House to the Lords to hear the Royal Assent given by commission to certain bills. THE MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT. Mr. :Jamison moved the adjournment of the HOLM. ME. E. Roirserscm protested against the extraordinary Legislative manumvres by which the law of England was changed on a very important subject, and Reble College exempted from the operation ef the Mortmain Act with. out any notice being given to the House, and without consideration by the House. He gave notice that on the first opportunity he would move to bring in a bill to disineorporate that instititution.-----Mr. G. Hownti like- wise entered a protest, on the mine subject—Mr. J. ROBERTS thought thp Government had been guilty nt most discreditable conduct in relation to Kahle College. —Mr. BROADHURST charged the Government with sharp practice in connection with Heble College. The Souceron-GENRRAL held that there was no ground for the accusation of Allem practice, and there was, moreover, no ground for saying that the Government had made no answer to Mr. Robertson, for the First Lord of the Treasury had fully answered the questions which the member for Dundee had addressed to him.

_ Mr. ASQUITH was of opinion that the charge of sharp practice was justified by all the circumstances. Mr. JACKSON repudiated the charge of sharp practice, and denied thatthe Attornev-General had departed from his engagements or violated his promises. The Mort. main 13ill was urgent in the sense that the Government were anxious to issue without delay the new and revised edition of the statutes, and that could not be done until this bill passed. Sir W. HART DYKE, answering the appeal of Colonel Hughes, admitted that the present position of the Lon- don School Board constituencies was unsatisfactory, and that they were quite unmanageable as regards numbers. He regretted that adverse circumstances had prevented the Government dealing with the matter. The Govesn- meat would carefully consider the matter, with a view to legislation, during the recess. The Rouse adjourned at 3 p.m., until November 6th, members as usual filing singly past the Speaker and wishing him good-bye.
, THE EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, AUGUST 18,1888.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Important discoveries of gold have been taste at Trawdynydd on the Plas-Captain Ferro. Messrs. Owen, ot Featiniog, are opening out a mine of remarkable rich- ness. A lump of quartz, 60Ib. in weight, has been un- earthed, which, on analysis, was found to contain 40 ounces of gold to the ton.

IMPROVEMENT IN THE CLYDE SHIPBOILDINO is understood that Messrs. Thompson, of Clyde Bank, have secured the contract for a new large gunboat foe the Japanese Government. The vessel is to be fitted with all the latest improvements. There is a prospect of the Clyde shipyards being busy throughout the winter. GOLD-MINING IN WeLas.—ANOTITEit Drscovsier.—Gold has been struck in the Clonga Gold Mine, near Dotelly, 120 ft. deep, immediately 'beneath the spot where some years ago £25,000 worth of gold was obtained. The Earl of Winchelses., chairman of the Morgan Mining Com- pany, has taken a residence near the mine for the sum- mer months.

Early on Saturday morning, a young man named James Hodgkinson was found shot in the head, and lying unconscious in a pool of blood in the shop of Mr. R. Smedley, ieweller, South-parade, Matlock Bath. A revolver with one chamber discharged lay close by. Be is recovering, but the bullet, which entered the mouth, cannot be traced. The affiair is a mystery. On Tuesday, 'while the tasaenger steamer, Queen of the Bay, was leaving Cardiff for Bristol, she struck on the anchor of a dredger, lying in the entrance channel, knocking a hole in her bottom, and causing her to foun- der. There were over LOCI passengers on board, and a good deal of •consternation prevailed; but the- were eventAmlly got off in beats without loss of life or injury.

An ILL-Tann) FAIWILY:A "child,' namlcl Ethel Brown, daughter of a 'Stalybridge town councillor. met with a singular death on Sunday. She had been into a neigh- bour's house with an elder sister, and on returning crossed a large yard. in which was a vessel containing about six inches of water. While playing the child fell In head first, and was drowned before assistance arrived. brother of the deceased was fatally scalded a short time ago by falling backwards into a pan containing a small quantity of belling water. At Strattord' Petty Sessions; On Saturday, Wm. Barber was charged, on reinand;-with causing the death of Mrs. Prengli, by administering a noxious drug.—Mr. Angus I,ewis appeared for the Treasury. and said the case was one of great complication,. end that, though there was little direCteridenee; there was the history of a secret note, and 'the' Cowardly flight of prisoner, who left Mrs. Brenda° Wtruggie.With death. After evidence had been givemsapplementing' that adduced at the inquest, the accused was Itirther remanded for a week.

Parlimentary 'return was published on Saturday giving thelotal cost, of the police in the metropolis and in boroughs in Great Britain with over 100,000 inhabi- tants. The •crist- in the metropolitan police district is £1,527,05; in the City 'of London, £109,208; Liverpool, £134,076; £100,480: Birmingham, £49,387; Manchester;£77.773 ; Leeds, £37.117; Sheffield, £31,274; Edinburgh, 142,765; Bristol. £31,738; Bradford, I £21,369; 'Nottingham:. £12,317; Salford, £30,840; Kin?, .ton-on-Hull. SECESSION TO RIME. - The Irish Catholic of Saturday says: A report has reached us from a ',most reliable source which indicates asnlmost certain the conversion to Catholicity of a much- respected female member of the Royal Family of Great Britain. We should hesitate to give publicity to this intelligence were it not that its origin gives us every reasonto rely. on, its authenticity, ar.d it is now only necessary" to say that should it happily prove well founded; the near relationship which exists between tho distinguished lady in question and the monarch of Eng- land will render her conversion one of the most me- morable which has occurred within the last half-century.

SIXTY MILES AN HOLM ON TIM SWITCHI3ACK.—Over 610,000 persons have had a threepenny rush on the Switchback Railway at Glasgow Exhibition up to date. representing a total revenue exceeding £7,600. Very few of the entbibition visitors seem to have the caution of the Cockney gentleman who lately surveyed the switch- bank' through a pair of gold•rimmed cyegla.s.ses. "What may bo the speed of your machines at their most accele- I•ratedrpoint?" he asked one of the attendants. "Sixty ' miles an hour, sir!" replied the attendant Off came the gOld-riznmed eyeglasses at once, and, turning to his wife, the justly alarmed gentlemen said: "Sixty miles an hour; ray dear! I'm sorry, but I cannot recommend it—can not recommend it!"

STOPPAGE OF .A STEEL WORKS: 1,000 HINDS IDLE. Land ore, near Swansea, has been thrown into a state of consternation by the sudden and unexpected stop- page of • the New Landore Steel Works, belonging to Messrs.-Siemens and Company, Limited. On Saturday, most of the workmen were, at two hours' notice, paid off, (midmost of the furnaces were put out on Sunday. The restrlt is that over 1,000 men, to whom upwards of £1.300 were paid weekly, are now out of employment The cause of the stoppage is unknown. A meeting of directors will, it is said, be held in ,London to discuss matters. Mr. Frederick Siemens, nephew of the late-Sir W. Siemens, visited the works last week, and it is be- lieved• that this visit has been the cause of closing. At present things appear in a state of uncertainty, but it is reported that both works are likely to remain idle for about•six months. •

COII7,MHON TN TUE CHANNEL : A STEAMER SeNR.— A collieir,n occurred on Sunday morning, about five o'clodr, thirty miles off the Start, between the barque Abbey TOWII, ot Liverpool. on a voyage from London to amstralitat,with cement, and the steamer Bosphorus, of Newcastle,, from Alexandria for London with grain. There was.a thick fog at the time, and the two vessels ran into each other before it was possible to prevent a collision, the result being that the Bosphorus had a large noie knocked into her and sank soon afterwards. 'Fier crew of :27 And a lady passenger succeeded in escaping from the Bosphorus to the Abbey Town, and the latter vessel made. for Plymouth, she also having her bows Smashed ini,and she oalv escaped from foundering by her collision bulkheads. The lady passenger lost £2OO m money and all her wearing apparel. • - -

DILEUNG BURGLARY IN LIVRILYOOL.—At an early hour an Sundaranerning it was discovered that a very daring burglary textbeen committed at the Holt Hotel, Ken- sington.tiverpool, the property of Mr. Walter Bromley. The eervantoon•coming downstairs about a quarter-past seven, found'the place in confusion, drawers being open, bills ,and papers strewn about, cigar boxes on the door, and the safe door open. On examination it was found that £33 had been taken from the safe, and, not content with this, the hapudent burglars took 2s. 6d. out of the barmy:ea coat pocket, 4/4. which had been left in the drawer, and a , pair of new boots belonging to the manager. Three battles of spirits and two boxes of cigars are also missing: while in the lavatory an empty chasatimgne bottle and two glasses were found. A win- dow and a door at. the back were wide open, the burglars evidently not bothering themselves about closing them,

Lira or ass ENGLISH PRISON.—Some strange dis- closures as to the treatment of prisoners were made at an inquest held at Chelmsford Prison on Saturday on the body cif Thomas Ingate, who, on May 7. was senteneed to four •months' hard labour for assaulting a police-constable at •Weet• Ilam. Major Lane (governor of the prison) said ithat Ingate had been in prison five times previously. In those periods he had once re- ceived extra punishmect for laughing while on the wheel, on another occaaion he had been put on bread and • water for three days•for defacing a meat tin, on a third occasion he had been giveri.extra eard labour for loiter- ing while on the wheel, and on a fourth occasion he had been given an additional .lortnight on the wheel for looking round in chapel.---4m reply to the Coroner (Mr. C. C. Lewis), Major Lane said that the latter punish- ment was the heaviest he had the power to inflict.—The Coroner said he thought •in such cases as this it would be well to err on the side cff -mercy. He suggested that the punishment should be modified in future.—Medical evidence was given to the effect that Ingate's death was caused by jaundice, and a verdict was returned accord- ingly. THE GREAT Lou RAYT'S WOYAGE A SUCCESS:— The great log raft from Joggins, Nova Scotia. went through Hell Gate at New 'York at high tide about noon on Saturday, and passed down the East River to its des- tination in tow of seven tugs. From the bank the raft looked like a gigantic whale, or big ship bottom upwards. There was apparently a great deal more of it below the surface than above, and from its shiplike shape and the submergence, apparently, of the ends it did not look nearly as long as it was reported to be. It was really 592 feet long, 55 wide, and drew 23 -feet of water. It was built of 24,000 logs, averaging 13 inches in diameter and 33 feet in length, and containing 5,000,000 feet of timber. The raft is cigar-shaped. The logs are bound together by wire ropes and chains. Two big tugs towed it down from the Bay of Fundy, where it has been under construction since November, when Mr. Leary's other and unfortunate venture was launched. To transport such a =vase of timber by the usual method would re- quire 45 lumber schooners and cost 30,000 dollars. The two tugs for towing it only charged 4,500 dollars. It is estimated that the owners will realise 75,000 to 100,000 dollars from their venture.

Moe EXCITING SCENES AT DOUGLAS.—Os Satur- day, the Manx Line steamer was announced to start from Douglas at 8 a.m., but long before that hour hundreds of people thronged to the pier, and struggled and fought to get on board. At twenty minutes to eight o'clock she was crammed and had to sail, the crowd on the pier venting their disappointment in no measured terms. No information could be had as to whether the people on the pier could get to Liverpool by the New Manx Line, and meanwhile the Old Manx Company's steamers, Morm's Isle and Ben•my-Chree, took large numbers of the Manx Line passengers on board and sailed to Liverpool. The same company also put the Duke of Connaught on the station, although she had just come in with 400 trippers from Fleetwood. The Duke of Con. naught sailed at nine o'clock with about 600 people. During this the Miuix Line had officially made arrange- ments to cope with the traffic, and chartered the Barrow Company's steamer Manxman, and that vessel sailed at ten o'clock with the remainder of the passengers—about 809. Complaints were very loud at the prospect of hav- ing to wait for the afternoon steamer to get to Liverpool, and the Manx Line have lost hundreds of passengers througt. reot having another steamer in readiness.

The return of Mr. Cross will not affect the position of parties in the Douse of Commons. PARLIAMENTARY SITTINGS .AND DIVISIONS.

Monday was the 121st day on which the House of Com- mons sat for the transaction of business this session. The Lords have met on 89 clays. The Commons have in the course of the session divided 276 times, which, allowing a quarter of an hour for each division, has taken up just 69 hours, or the whole of about seven working days.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND MR. PARNELL. Mr. Chamberlain writes to The limes, in reply to Mr. Parnell's letter of the 4th of August, stating that a great pressure of work had prevented him from replying earlier. Mr. Chamberlain finds "a great difficulty in ascertaining what is the issue between us, or on what. point Mr. Parnell differs from any statement of mine with reference to the communications which took place between Mr. O'Shea and myself in 1884 and 1885. Pre- viously to the appearance of this letter I had understood that he denied that Mr. O'Shea had any authority to re- present his views, and that he repudiated all responsi- bility for the scheme for a. National Council or Central Board submitted to me by that gentleman. Now, however, I gather that what Mr. Parnell intended to repudiate was all cognisance or approval of vehat he calls my plan. The letters from Mr. Parnell to which I have referred in confirmation of my statement show that Mr. O'Shea was the confidential exponent of Mr. Parnell's views at the time and also prove Mr. Parnell's authorship of this scheme, but these points are not disputed in Mr. Par- nell's letter to you. The correspondence at the same time corrobonstes Mr. Parnell's statement that he did uot put forward this proposal as a substitute for an Irish Parliament. The whole question WKS discussed with my colleagues at the time, and the scheme was finally rejected by the Government. When the new Government was formed I endeavoured to learn whether Mr. Parnell still adhered to his proposal, and about the middle of July Mr. O'Shea informed me that in view of the altered state of affairs, and having regard to a recent speech of Lord Carnarvon's, Mr. Parnell con- sidered it doubtful whether it would be worth while to encumber the Irish question with any larger extension of the local government to Ireland than to England. I to not think, therefore, that on this point there is now any conflict of testimony between Mr. Parnell and my- self."

We (The Times) have no doubt whatever that Scotch judges and juries will administer indifferent justice and honestly co-operate in the discovery of the truth, nor Jo we care very much for any tactical advantages which Mr. Parnell may think he has obtained. The main point to which public attention will be directed is the extraordinary delay in Mr. Par- aell's resort to his legal remedy, and, when the reason is asked, what answer can be made either before a jury or elsewhere? If Mr. Parnell had brought his action in the Scotch Courts fifteen or sixteen months ago—and he had then sub- substantially the same grounds of complaint that he has now--it might have been matter for surprise that an Irish politician should choose to proceed against a London journal in Scotland, but no one could have charged him with evading the issue.
