div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

The inquest on Patrick Byrne, of Ballybeg, County Wicklow, who was killed last week in a poaching affray on Lord Clifden's property, concluded at a lath hour on Monday. The jury returned a verdict that" Byrne came by his death from a gunshot wound, inflicted by Michael Walsh, of Kilcross, gamekeeper to Colonel Tighe, and that Walsh was guilty of manslaughter." A rider was added blaming the keeper for provoking the poachers. Walsh still lives, but is belived to be dying of his wounds.

div.head: AIR. REDMOND AND THE PHCENIX PARE MURDERS.
div.p: AIR. REDMOND AND THE PHCENIX PARE MURDERS.

Mr. John Redmond telegraphs to the Star newspaper from Wexford :—•• Just seen Glass's letter in Satur- day's Times. Have no recollection of calling at telegraph office, Manchester, day after Phoenix Park murders. It is possible, but more likely inquiries were made by some of my friends. The fact, however, remains that neither from there, nor the detective office, nor from any other source, did I learn of the murder of Burke until long after the meeting."
THE SUICIDE OF DR. RIDLEY.
The inquest as to the death of Dr. Ridley was resumed

Captain Featheritonhaug,h, recalled, deposed that Dr. Ridley was entered on the visiting book of the prison ny the gate keeper a. unknown. lie was not in a lachry- mose condition. When he heard that Mr. O'Brien's clothes had been brought into the prison he was annoyed that he should have been betrayed by the staff. George Bartley. chief warder of Tullamore Prison. de- posed that Mr. Mandeville on release weighed within 21bs. of his weight on committal. Captain Featherstonhaugh, in further examination, said he was in no way influenced in enforcing the prison discipline by Dr. Parr. Mr. Lane was confined to his cell because he would not exercise with the ordinary prisoners. He was never asked to exercise with pick- pockets, as witness had undertaken that he would not be asked to associate with prisoners convicted of larceny.

When the inquiry wns resumed. Dr. Moorhead deposed that he examined Mr. William O'Brien on December 7th. He presented every delicate appearance. Witness knew that he suff—ed from delicacy of the tunas. He had an interview' n Dr. Ridley, and strongly recommended Mr. O'Brien's removal to the hospital. Dr. Ridley said he could not, do so, and witness said that Dr. Ridley could command his services as magistrate or doctor, to get him removed.

At the Ridley inquest at Fermoy, on Wednesday, Dr. Barr was cross-examined. Afterwards, Dr. Ronayne, a medical officer of the Board of Trade and health officer of Youghal, was called. He said his report on the con- dition of the Tullamore prisoners was a faithful one, and not untrue or unfounded, as stated by Dr. Barr. The witness was cross-examined as to his having written some of his report before seeing Mr. O'Brien, and he ad- mitted that ho made certain statements from information received.

The inquest was continued on Thursday. Mr. An- drews, now Governor of Downpatrick Prison, but for- merly of Tullamore Gaol, said that when Drs. Ridley and Moorhead met in the prison they did not speak to each other, Dr. Ronayne was cross-examined as to the draft reports he drew up before visiting Tullamore Gaol, and he said he wrote them from information, but he intended them to be corrected by examination. The evi- dence was brought to a close, and the inquiry Was ad- journed till Friday morning, when the counsel will ad- dress the caroner.and jury. ACCIDENT TO A. MANX STEAMER.- srx 'PERSONS INJURED.

! During Sunday nighta fierce gale raged off Fleetwood and the Lancashire coast, The wind blew from the west with the force of a hurricane, and at times rain fell in torrents. Some slight damage has been done to build- ings in the district. From Fleetwood comes news of a serious accident on'board the fine ship Duke of Con- naught, which, along with the other steamers of that. port, have been so busily engaged during the past week ' in taking passengers over to the Isle of Man and Ireland. ' About four o'clook in the morning, the steamer Duke of Connaught left Fleetwood for Douglas. with about 800 excursionists. who had arrived by special train from the Halifax district When she was about ten miles out the mast. fell. /treating the utmost consternation on board and seriously injuring several of the passengers. 'The captain at, once put back to Fleetwood, and as soon as she reached .the Quay the Meat doctors were summoned. Dr.'llarnsay was the first to arrive, and Dr. Orr and Dr. 75us5tt followsd, and -a medical gentleman , belonging to lialifaxoviMhappened to be on board the steamer. also 'rendered aid to the injured passengers. Many were strffering from fright, and it was astonishing that only about half-a-dozen had received serious injuries. One gentleman, belonging to Halifax, had several of his ribs broken, and the doctors found on examination thatthe ends of the ribs had penetrated one ot hi lungs. The Duke Of Connaught afterwards left for Douglas. where -she arrired without further mishap at eleven o'clock. After the passengers had disembarked, the broken mast WAS sawn off close to the deck, and hoisted on to the 'Victoria Pier. The steamer returned to Fleetwood from Douglas the same night, arriving about midnight, but brought little more than a third of the .passengers who crossed with her in the morning. Very rough weather was experienced in croeising to Douglas, and many were in an unfit state and ethers afraid tcpreturti at night, though the storm had moderated.
THE FATAL TUMP FROM A LONDON BRIDGE.

An inquest vraa 'held at Deptford, on Monday, on the body of Larry Donovan, who met. his death by jumping into the Thames from 'Hungerford Bridge. Evidence that the deceased had declared his intention Of making the jump, and of the finding of the body was given, and the jury returned a verdict -that deceased was killed by jumping into the Thames. On Tuesday week .(the day of his death) an appeal appeared in theSportinglye for funds to enable Donovan to redeem a massive gOld. medal presented to him by Mr. Richard K. Fes, proptietor of the New IT:orlr Police Gazelle. and to ray his •passage to America. His non- recognition in England had preyed on the mind of the deceased, and for months past he had given way to drinking, and at. last he had become so reduced as to have to seek SIWAPT in .common lodging-houses, and in one of these on the Saturday previous to b4s death he was ill-used. On Monday night, or rather Tuesday morning, •he was taken •iiy some sporting .men to one of the German clubsin-the neighbourhood el Leices- ter-square, and on leaving there he went in company with his friends to one Of the early morning :houses which open at 4 am, in Covent Garden. Here,,as was his wont, Larry began to talk of his jumping feats, and after.a lot of chaff and badinage, a bet of £2 to nothing was laid him that he wodid not jump from Charing Cross Bridge. This Donovan .readily accepted, and in company with the layer of the odds, proceeded to the bridge, and having only taken his coat off, jumped in. No heat was provided in case of accident, and the moment he left the bridge his .companions, becoming frightened, left him to his fate. The only reason to he assigned for his death was that in jumping he did not go down straight, but struck the water with his ribs.

His joints were badly swollen, , and he was bent with agony. He was advised to apply prepartion of which so much is heard. Ile did so. In two days the change was marvellous. His cure was en- tirely due to St. Jacobs Oil, of which he used one bottle. Although sixty years of age, he now walks as I well as ever. The case of a young woman was mentioned. She was in a helpless condition from rheumatism for three years. The same wonderful remedy cured her. The case of Mr. Tliomas Bagshaw, 34, Caro- line-sr., was investigated. He was confined to the house for twenty-one weeks with rheumatism. The day after using this magical cure he was able to resume work. Mr. Thompson stated to the reporter that the above are only a few of the many cases that are continually corn- ing under his notice, where St. Jacobs Oil had cured peo- ple, where all other remedies had signally failed. So great had become the demand for this deservedly popu- lar remedy, that instead of procuring his supplies from the wholesale house, the same as he did his other medi- cines, he procured St. Jacobs Oil direct from the proprie- tors, The Charles A. Vogeler Company, of 45, Barring- don-road, London, in sixty dozen lots or seven hundred and twenty bottles at each order, and that owing to its deserved popularity, the 'demand increases every month."
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday warning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. Greening, Jolley, T. Jones, Isher- wood, J. Houghton, Ratcliffe, Clarke, Eckersley, Harrison. Grange, Wright, W. Houghton; ,T. C. Sutton (clerk), S.Sutton (assistant clerk), and C. H. Ward (workhouse master).
SCHOOL FEES.
The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 73 cases, 67 of winch were old and 6 new cases.—On the motion of Mr. GBXENING the minuteswere adopted.
HAINHILL ASYLIIN.

The CHAIRMAN reported that a neputation from the Board had visited Rainhill Asylum to see the patients be- longing to the Warrington Union there. They found the patients to be very comfortable, and everything seemed to be done in the best possible manner for the unfortu- nate inmates. The deputation were very courteously received, and a disposition was shown to afford them every facility for seeing the patients and inspecting the management of the institution.

div.head: BOUNDARPFS.QUESTION.
div.p: THE BOUNDARPFS.QUESTION.

The CLIAIR3fAN referred to the announcement in the newspapers that the Boundary Commissioners had re- ported in favour of the severance of the townships of Grappenhall, Thelwall, and the extra municipal portion of Latchford from the Warrington Union. They would remember, he said, that the Board a short time ago deter- mined to increase the accommodation at the workhouse, and they might be interested in knowing whether thesever- ance of those townships would in any way affect the de- termination to increase the size of the house. The re- commendations of the Commissioners would be sent to the County Councils to be established next year, and the probability was that the Councils would adopt the re- commendations of the Commissioners. It behoved that Board, therefore, to see how they stoed in the matter. The rateable value of the Union would be reduced by more than £16,000, while it would be relieved of pauper cases only to an infinitesimal extent, because they had few pauper cases from the district that was to be taken away. The people who were poor lived in Warringtor, and drifted into that workhouse when sick or poorly. The Board would be in a worse condition, as the rate- able value of the townships referred to would be taken from them, while there would still be the same necessity for an enlargement of the workhouse.—The CLERK said that men who had worked at Grappenhall and Thelwall for many years, and at length became unable to work, came to Warrington and stayed all night at a lodging house ; attention might be called to their condition, and the relieving officer had to deal with them asWarrington poor. If Thelwall and Grappenhall were taken from the Warrington Union cases such as these would still inevit- ably become chargeable to the Warrington Union. (Hear, hear.) That had been experienced very much of late, for until provision had been made by Mr. Walker, the Ship Canal contractor, men had come in, not only from the Runcorn Union, but also from the Altrincham Union. For some miles along the canal they had, when hurt, or in some way needing help, come to Warrington, where the . workhouse and medical attendance was available. In some cases these men had been told that their proper place was Dutton Workhouse, but they re- fused to go. With regard to the extension of the work- house and hospital he could only advise them that it would not make the least difference in the expense in- volved if those townships were separated from the rest- of the Union. The same demand would be made upon them for the same help, except as the Chairman had said, to an infinitesimal degree. How a relieving officer was to pass a case from Thelwall to Dutton workhouse, and how immediate medical treatment was to be had there, if it were needed, he did not know.—The WORK- HOUSE latesrau, in reply to a question, said there was only Ow inmate of the workhouse from Grappenhall and one from Thelwall. There were 23 from the whole of Latchford including that position which was to remain in the Warrington Union.—Mr. Itarczwee said it ap- peared that Runcorn Union would get the benefit of the rates of Grappenhall and Thelwall, while the Warrington Union would have to keep the poor. (Hear, hear.) He asked if anything could be done to prevent the Commis- sioners recommendations being carried out. The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the rateable value of the Runcorn Union would also be considerably increased by the Ship Canal going through the townships to be added to it.—The CLERK in replying to Mr. Ratcliffe's question, said he had received a copy of the memorial presented by the Town Council of Warrington to the President of the Local Government Board applying that Warrington might be made into a separate county but that could not not be done owing to the limit of population of com ties being fixed at 50,000, and inasmuch as in the first para- graph of the memorial it was admitted that Warrington had not 50,000 inhabitants. He was bound to say that some little difficulty might have been created by that movement on the part of the Borough of Warrington, as in their memorial they say that a small portion of the county of Lancaster shown on a plan sent with the me-1 morial was absolutely severed from that county by the borough, and no administration could be eonducted from the county without crossing the borough. Assuming ' for a moment that the borough had been made into a county the difficulty would be that the matter referred to in the memorial would have applied to the county of Lancaster for the county of Warrington would have to be crossed to get to that portion of Lancashire which might have ,been taken from Cheshire. Whether that had any effect he could not say, but, whilst the borough of Warrington I:o,:tai honourably put their:case to the President of the Government Board in seeking to be made a county, it may have to some extent prejudiced the question of the extension of , Lancashire. Appended to the annual report of the War- rington borough treasurer was a very useful statement of , the rates within the borough. Before the passing of the ' Union Chargeability Act in 1865 there had been occa- sional rates as high as 2.3 6d in the £, but by that Act of 1865 the poor of Warrington were no longer exclusively chargeable to Warrington, but was spread over the whole of the Union. If Warrington had been made a county and if poor-law administration was not to over- lap counties, the poor of Warrington would have to be separately provided for in the county of Warrington, and the effect of that would have been to put the inhabitants of Warrington in the position they were before 1865 of having to bear the entire cost of the poor regarded as belonging to Warrington • in other words the effect would have been to transfer to the County of Warrington nearly the whole of the expenditure in connection with both in-deer and out-door relief. The Clerk next re- ferred to the inquiry which Mr. Pelham, the boundary commissioner, some months ago held in Warrington. The proposal of the Commissioners at that time was that the Cheshire townships should be attached to Lancashire, and from ail the inferences he could draw from Mr. Pel- ham's manner and observations, that gentleman seemed to adhere to the Commissioners' proposals. There was this peculiar circumstance at the time. Mr. Parr said hehad been in communication with Mr. Smith Barry re- questing his attention to the matter, but the letter he get from Mr. Barry in reply was that it was useless—it was simply flogging a dead horse. It did seem from that as if there had been some conclusion come to by somebody, but that was quite contrary to what was said at the preliminary inquiry. What he un- derstood Mr. Pelham and the Commissioners to say was that the parishes were of more importance to the Unions then to the counties, but the decision that had now been come to was contrary to that. (Hear, hear.) As had been said the matter was very serious. The con- tribution taken from them would exceed £BOO, and he repeated that their expenditure would be no less 'when that £BOO a year would be given to the Runcorn Union. It had even more serious aspects than that, for they had been constantly lifting up the rateable value of the rail- ways in the Union on the improved traffic. The railway companies had always told them that when the railway traffic was less than it now is, then dowemust come the assessment. The Ship Canal Company were hopeful that they would take a great deal of _the traffic at least between Liverpool and Manchester, and as this -.mold be largely taken from the railways the consequences would be that the rateable values of the railways would come down, while the rateable value of the new canal would now go almost entirely out of the Warrington Union.— Mr. W. Hots:anon said there would be a small length at Woolston.—Mr. JOLLEY : And the Warrington docks.— The CLERK, in conclusion, said he believed the recom- mendations of the Boundary Commissioners would be sent to the new County Councils for their consideration, and then they would be submitted for confirmation to Parliament. He was rather inclined to think, since the passing of that Boundaries Act, that the Government had some other intention to deal with poor-law unions than that which had before influericcd their minds and if that were so that Board did not need to mind, but as it was of the greatest possible importance that the par- ishes should remain with them, and in view of the fact that the proposals would come before the County Coun- cils, it would be necessary for the Board, both before the County Councils and before Parliament, to offer the most determined resistance to the exclusion of the Cheshire townships from the Union as an unjust interference with financial and administrative matters that concerned them. (Rev hear.)—The CHAIRMAN said the present proposals would scarcely fall in *.iith the original inten- tions to have the borders of Unions and counties simpli- fied if as extension of the borough of Warrington in Cheshire wa.s obtained. There would then be part of Cheshire in the borough of Warrington.—Mr. Tozzey thought the borough would not be permitted to extend further into Cheshire.--The CLERK assented to this opinion. From what he had read of the proceedings of the House of Lords, that House had attached a clause to the Local Government Bill to the effect that there should be no portion of a country district attached to a borough without notice having first been given to the County Council within whose district it came. There was great meaning in that. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It meant that the County Councils would object to any portion of their districts beingincluded in any other district. That would be a difficulty which towns had not hitherto en- countered in seeking extension.—Mr. DARRYSHIRE said he was sorry that the Boundary Commissioners had recommended that the Cheshire townships be put to the Runcorn Union, because it would place so many diffi- culties in the way of the administration of the poor-law. —The subject then dropped. The relief cases were next taken.

Tim public have now been put in possession of the final report of the Royal Commission on the Education Acts, and it is seen that, as was antici- pated from its complexion, it is distinctly reac- tionary in its tendency. It was not to be expected that a body so heterogenous in its composition would be able to agree at every point; there were some true friends of education on the Committee such as the Hon. E. L. STANLEY, Dr. DALE, and Mr. HENRY RICHARD, and they have been under the necessity of issuing a minority report. What the majority of the Commissioners hanker after is what they call putting board schools and volun- tary schools on a footing of equality. They desire that, as board schools are rate-aided, voluntary schools shall also be supported out of the rates. The demand appears on the face of it very reason- able; but when it is put to the test it is seen that there would be no real equality if the reactionists hatil their way. Board schools are ratepayers' • schools in the sense that they are aided by the rates and managed by the ratepayers. It is be- cause every ratepayer is taxed that every ratepayer has a voice in electing the committee of manage- ment. If that committee does its work badly, or shows itself to be extravagant, the ratepayers have a, remedy; they can insist on a fresh body of managers by altering the composition of the school board at the next election. But voluntary schools, because they are voluntary, are not subject to the control of the ratepayers. The managers do as they like, subject to the control of the Education Department; and if they ask for support from the rates they must be prepared to accept the control •of the-ratepayers., •But that they decidedly object to; they want equally with the managers of board schooli to make a call-on the rates, but they do not wish to be subject, equally with the managers of board whoa*•to the verdict of the ratepayers. Their cry for equality, is therefore an absurdity; they are anxious to dip into the ratepayers' "lucky bag," but they have no thought of paying the price. They are as oblivious of what is really re- quired as "Simple Simon " was when he asked for a pie without offering a penny; but we do think the reaetionizts are quite as simple as Simon. It is the ratepayer who is to be caughlt on the simple side"with the fine cry of equality when there is no equality. Then there is the proposal to examine Board schools in religious knowledge; that has an limo- oent air, too, but it will be seen when it comes to be considered that it re-opens the whole question of state-aid for sectarian 'teaching. At present, by what we regard as a wise provision of the law, the 'schoolmaster is not called upon by the State to give any distinctive religious teaching. He is not paid to do the work of the parent or the parson; it is not a subject for (which a grant is given. And very properly so. Society is agreed as to secular education; and the community as a whole is legiti- mately taxed for the teaching of that as to which all the members ot it are agreed. But introduce another factor—introduce sectarian teaching—and

tficee who have hitherto been in agreement are at • !oboe set by the ears. What one regards as vital truth presents itself to another as detestable error; and to tax a citizen for the teaching of that which is in his eyes untrue and therefore injurious, is • • amongst the worst forms of tyranny. By all means let children at our elementary schools be taught 'the principles of morality; Christian and Jew agree as to that; but when • sectarianism is added it is going beyond the province of the school-teacher; Whilst it opens the door to a thousand assaults

upon those who have tender consciences in matters 2 this kind. The State has meddled mischievously for many generations in matters of religion. It is recognised in these later days that the less the State has to do with religion the better it is for • religion and for the State. There should be no 'countenance given to the proposals of the reaction- aries in education; we must go forward, and not 'bdckward.

Now that the period is close at hand at which ''ltPplications are mane for licenses to sell intoxica- ting liquors, the inhabitants of the various dis- tricts likely to be affected would do well to bestir themselves in letting it be known whether they want any more plague spots in their midst. At 'Warrington, there is evidence' of a most persistent littenipt, especially on the part of Messrs. Gam:N- ALL, WHITLEYi mid CO., to secure the sanction of. Vie Licensing ommittee for two public-houses 'Which they propose to erect with a view to exten- ding their operations. It is in vain that the

'll*i-dents in the neighbourhood of Battersby- , lane and. of Bewsey-road have demonstrated, ' by numerously-signed petitions, that they do tot require additional facilities for obtaining intoxicating liquor. The drink-selling fraternity ^think they ought to be better supplied ;- and noe the determination, by hook or by crook, to l'DiSt new licenses on the community. Mr. Emus Z.Awrow has an off-license foT "The Grove," inßew- -4eY-road, and he seeks, a& before, to obtain a per- to sell either on or off the premises. Messrs. IMIRINALL, WHITLEY, and Co. also desire to °per- itte in Bewsey-road ; they propose to build a pub- Ic-linuse at the corner of Catherine-st. and Bew- -I.°a(l, as if it would not be quite sufficient to extend tile license for "The Grove," if further facilities "na needed, which we do not by any means admit. 'ford-lane and Battersby-lane are being patro- ' lii&ad in a similar way; the inhabitants—if the l'elvors are to have their own way—are to 4ve something thrust upon them which they 114! not desire. It is true that Messrs. GREEN- , 1.1.7 WiarLsr, and Co. offer to give up

certain licenses in quarters of the town that are admittedly overstocked with drink shops. But if these places are not doing a paying business they will close themselves in time. There is no merit, at any rate, in giving up an unprofitable license; and as to a license which is profitable we may be quite sure that Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. are not the people to suriender it. It is generally admitted that one license to every thousand inhabitants would be a fair supply; but at this rate the Licensing Committee ought to re- duce the number not by three or four but by 150; for the total number of licensed houses is 200 to a population of less than 50,000. It would be inter- esting to know whether the Chief Constable thinks it desirable to grant any of these new applications. Warrington is notorious for drunkenness, es- pecially drunkenness amongst females, and the right oourse to take is to lessen, not to increase, the facilities for obtaining intoxicants. The new Licensing Committee, appointed on Monday last, consists• of the MAYOS. (Alderman Surrox), and Aldermen PIGIEDIERE, HOLMES, Heintz - sox, and Councillors FRANOOMB, and GREEN: ING, and LITTON. There has been a change in• the composition of the Committee; but who will say that the change is an improve- ment, when it is noticed that Alderman DsviEs and Mr. Joinv FAIRCLOUGH have had to retire to make way for Alderman SUTTON and Councillor Llrrox ? Can it be that something is being " cooked " to serve private rather than pub- lic ends ? We trust to find that there is no foun- dation for the rumours that are abroad. In the present state of the law, the Licensing Committee I are an important, body of men. They are respon- sible to a large extent fort le morals of the com- munity ; and it is to be hoped they will do justice . to their own reputation, and to the reputation of the town, by . ref using, as heretofore, to grant a single new license.-

MR. PARNELL has played a trump card by tak- ing proceedings against the "Times" in the Scotch Court of Sessions. The claim is for £.50,000 dam- ages for the libels upon him in " Parnellism and Crime," and in leading articles in the leading jour- nal. His opponents have been asking all along why he did not ko before a jury, and now when he is putting himself in a position to appoal to a jury they are anything but happy. The "Times" tries to make a point by directing attention to "the ex- traordinary delay in Mr. Parnell's. resort to his legal remedy," but as to this it must not be fort gotten that the Irish loader has all along contended that the proper course to take in testing the charges against him as a member of Parliament was to appoint a Select Committee of the House of Commons. So much confidence had he that such a Committee would do him justice that he was willing that not a single member of the Irish party should sit upon it. He confessed that he had no hope of obtaining justice at the hands of an English jury—particularly as a single stupid or prejudiced juryman csuld stand in the way of a satisfactory verdict. As to the Commission of 'Judges, it has been apparent as the bill proceeded that its object was not, so far as the Government were concerned, to get at the truth of the Forged Letters; but to harrass the Parnel- lites by an expensive and interminable inves- tigation. Mr. PAermu., with the Liberal party at his back, did his best to confine ;the inquiry within reasonable limits; but when he finds that fair play is out of the question he is more than justified in resorting, as he is doing, to a Scotch Court to obtain that justice which is denied him in this country. It is significant that the " Times ". already sings small in the matter; " WALTBR " and " BUCKLE " do not enjoy the prospect of having to meet Mr. PAarrELL upon something like equal terms. The Scotch Court of Ses ion will not per- mit of time and money being wasted by inquiry into irrelevant matters. The judge will keep witnesses strictly to the issue before the court; and a majority of the jury will decide whether Mr. PenNuLT. ig or is not entitled to damages. It will thus be seen that the trial will be a fair one; and if the plaintiff should succeed in obtaining a verdict against the "Times," it is needless to say that the subsequent inquiry of the Commission of Judges will be as tedious as a thrice-told tale. Their occupation will, in truth, be that of whip- ping a dead horse.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GU:
div.p: "TOUCH AND GU:

Grouse shooting commenced as usual on "the twelfth". sport for the men but death for the birds. Will the time ever come when killing for sport will be generally and properly designated as brutal butchery?

The big gooseberry has turned up at Croft. It ;vas conveyed to Golborne the other day and won the first prize. Its weight is 18 ilwts. 19grs., and it is named "Hero of the Nile." Great Nelson! what it is to be a great gooseberry! This is indeed fame.

The card-room hands have "caved in" as to their demand for another five per cent advance in their wages and a strike in the cotton trade is a- voided. 'Discretion is the better part of valour." The operatives have got one advance, and " a bird ill the hand is worth two in the bush."

Mr. Chamberlain has failed to score in accepting Mr. Parnell's challenge. Ho is "as gentle as a sucking dove" in dealing with the Irish leader. It is something new to see the member for West Birmingham turn the left cheek when smitteh on the right. Not that he has ever been accounted short of cheek; by no means.

Widnes is a growing place, but it has not grown of late as rapidly as some people seem to have supposed. The population has been estimated for some time at• 33,000; but a cen- sus just taken gives the total of 29,006 in- habitants. The population at the census of 1881 was 24,935.

It is satisfactory to see that the heavy fine of £5 and costs has been imposed upon a Liverpool cheese factor for ,exposing unwholesome cheeses for sale in Warrington. He has suffered the loss, too, of his fifty cheeses. This should teach him a lesson; he should not come to Warrington to palm off his rubbish; " it's not the cheese.

Lymm is a sleepy hollow, but it " wakes " once a year. The Morris dancers and the rush bearers have not yet gone out; but they aro going out. On Saturday last, instead bf the orthodox rush cart, a coal waggon adorned with rushes was brought into use. Picture a coal waggon as the central feature of rural festivity 1 It is all over with Lymm wakes.

There are lawyers ill the land who are—shall we say ?—conscientious about earning their fees. At Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, some three hours were occupied in going through a case of assault which resulted in a fine of " lOs and costs." There must have been, at times, a good deal of spinning without tow. It is useless to toll law- yers that "speech is silvern and silence golden" ; their eyes are set on the silver.

' The police authorities of Runcorn are to be commended for doing their duty fearlessly. On Monday the landlord of a notorious inn was fined £l4 and costs for allowing his house to be "the resort of habitual prostitutes;" and another landlord was fined 20s and costs for supplying intoxicating liquor to drunken persons. The
, • law on this head is broken every night in War- rington; but asto getting a conviction;thatseeins ut of the question.

The Government have done one good thing; they have pensioned a St. Helens man who was really deserving of aid. Mr. W. Hopton, whp has been put on the Civil List for £lOO per year, is a retired colliery manager who has done good service by Writing standard works on how to prevent acci- dents in coal mines. Failing eyesight compelled him to retire from active management; and if ever a pension was deserved it is in this ease. "Peace hath her victories no less renowned than wsx."

Me recommendation of the Boundary Commis- sioners to transfer the townships of Latchford and Grappenhall from Warrington to Runcorn Union came up for consideration at the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, on Wednesday. As might be expected, a pretty general opinion was expressed that the alteration would be an in- justice to the Warrington Union. Mr. J. C. Sut- ton, clerk, made a lucid statement of what was involved in the recommendation. it is surely not yet too late to prevent this wrong being done.

There was a boat accident at Warrington on Sunday. Four "niggers" who had been perform- ing in the town took a boat towards the Weir, and then took it into their heads to bathe. This must have been because they wanted to be black all over ; they could not think of cleansing themselves in the waters of the Mersey. .The boat was up- set; but three of the " niggers" could swim, and they succeeded in saving themselves, and tho non- swimmer. "Niggers " should be more careful; it is one thing to perform on land, and quite another to perform in the water.

Last week we announced the resignation of the Rev. Priestley Prime as minister of Cairo-street Chapel, Warrington. On Sunday he preached 'his farewell sermon, and it is noteworthy that he spoke of the worshippers in Cairo-street as coming up to his ideal of "a perfect church." It is a pity that the reverend gentleman's health did not permit of his continuing in a ministry which promised so well; and it is impossible not to sym- pathise with the congregation in that they are without pastor for a second time within twelve mpnths.

Mr. Cecil F. Parr, writing from Hartford to the London Tinies," lets it be seen that there are two sides to the question of running express trains at very high speed from London to Edinburgh. Pas- sengers from smaller centres are proportionably delayed; the many are put to a disadvantage 7hilst the few are accommodated. Of "the shelv- ing of goods traffic and the increased danger to life and limb," he has not, he says. space to speak. But it is quite sufficient to mention these things to set railway travellers thinking; and it ought to set Railway Directors thinking.

The Bank Quay Horticultural Society are to be congratulated on their excellent show, opened yesterday by His Worship the Mayor. Love of flowers, as Alderman Sutton remarked, tends to love of home. The poets have delighted in des- cribing flowers. Milton seems to have anticipated an exhibition when he said :

Bring the rathe primrose that forsaken dies, The tufted crow-toe, and pale jessamine, 'The white pink, and the pansy freak'd with jet, The glowing violet, The musk-rose, and the well-attir'd wood-bine, With cowslips wan that hang the pensive head.

As six out of the seven of the new Licensing Committee were on the bench at the War- rington Police Court, ' on Monday, they were in a position to judge of the quality of some of the finished articles turned out by "the trade." It was " drink " and " drink "to it. One man had been taken to the police station be- cause he was "apparently of unsound miwl." Be had, the Chief Constable said, "been drinking heavily." Another was brought up for attempting to commit suicide. According to his wife's state- ment, he had "lost his senses through "excessive drinking." "Oh that men should put an enemy in their mouths to steal away their brains," and oh that there should be so many places licensed for the operations of the enemy.!

The man who attempted suicide was a Ship Canal labourer, and it was a clOse shave with him. Tho clothes line gave way, or he would, in another minute or so, have been a dead man. It would ap- pear that the first woman who saw him suspended went toitell another woman instead of cutting the man down.. Incredible as it may seem, there is an idiotic idea abroad in some districts that it is a dangerous interference with "the law" for an un- authorised person to meddle with a fellow creature who is hanging. There is reason to believe that many lives have been sacrificed through stupidity of this kind.

The Emperor of Germany sounded • a warlike note on Thursday, at Frankfort-on-the-Oder, at the unveiling of a monument to Prince Frederick Charles. He said—" There can be no question of surrendering what has been gained. Upon this i point there s only one mind—namely, that our eighteen army corps and our forty-two million in. habitants should rather be left on the field, than that we should permit even one stone of what we have gained to be taken from us." This is a liroad hint to a neighbour; but, although it was in the Emperor's mmd, would it not have been better, being likely to irritate France, if . it had been left unsaid?

LANCASHIIIE AND YORPHIEE RAILWAY.OO.—The , half-yearly meeting of the Lancashire and Yerk-. shire Railway was held iA Manchester on Wednes- day. Mr. G. J. Armytage, chairman of the com- pany, in moving the adoption of. the Directors' report, said there had been an increase in the receipts of £53,864. The increase was almost entirely in respect of goods and minerals. The working • expenses on the traffic Were 54.63 per cent., a small increase on the previous year, mainly due to the fact .that the increase in receipts came from goods and minerals and not from passengers. A number of questions were asked, but the shareholders in general seemed satisfied with the position of the company's affairs. The dividend is at the rate of ' per cent. per annum. 'GOOD TEMPLAIte CONVENTION.—A session of the South-West Lancashire No. I. Good Templar Con- vention was held in the Temperance Hall, George- at., St. Helens, on Saturday evening. The represen- tatives of the following lodges were present :—St. ' Helens, Haydock, Earlestown, and Golborne. The reports of the various lodge representatives showed the lodges to be in a fair condition. Golborne was reported to need help, and it was resolved fb assist that lodge. It was resolved to -hold the next ses- sion at Hay-dock on September Bth. The conven- tion was closed in the usual manner, after which the members adjourned for tea, which WHS provided by Sisters Lindon and Brockblink. After tea a pub- lic meeting was held; Brother Brockbank, who gave an address, occupying the chair. It. was re- solved to continue the Saturday night's me2tings during the winter, and the meeting cll/4ed in the , usual manner.

Fentiwownt CHURCH.—The Rev.W. Edwardson, curate in charge, has formed a bible class in connection with the church. The members meet each Wednesday even- ing, and the class is likely to prove very beneficial'. ACCIDENT TO A CHILD AT WIDNES.—TIIO young daugh- ter of Mrs. Partington. of Bridge-st., whilst out for a walk on Sunday, fell down and fractured her. forearm. Dr. Hutchinson's deputy set the bone, and the girl is doing well. ZION METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES,-Special sermons in aid of the funds of this church.were preached , on Sunday by the Rev. E. Hall. of Runcorn,,and there ' were good congregations. On'Monclay evening a social tea meeting was held under the' presidency of Mr. J. Brock, J.P. The Rev.- J. W. Chisholm, of Liverpool, delivered a lecture entitled " Take care of Number One." The usual votes of thanks were passed. HARTLAND CHAPEL BAND. Or HOPE, WIDNES.—The members of this society had their annual. trent on Satur- day afternoon, when they walked in processional order to a field at Ditton. The Oakland-st. brass band walked in front of the young people, who were in charge of Mr. John Harper, conductor of the choir, Mr-. James Harper, secretary, and Mr. Thomas Whitby. A, pleasant after- noon was spent, ample refreshments being provided, and home was reached at a reasonable hour. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH Scuoms.—The children attending the Parish Church day and Sunday schools had their annual treat on Saturdav afternoon.. Together with a large number of friends no less than about 1,500 assembled at the schools, and, headed by the Soap Works Brass Band, walked in processional order through the tawn to a field at Appleton, kindly lent by Mr. H. Wade Deacon, .T.P. The weather was all that could be desiied, and a most happy time was spent in running foot races and playing a variety of games. A substantial tea was provided. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY.—During the past month there had been borrowed or consulted in the reading room 4,696 volumes, being an increase of 423. The total daily attendance was 12,992, averaging 499 each day for the 26 days the library was open. This is an increase of 1688 on the corresponding period of last year. Mr. Henry A. Papps. secretary to the Gilchrist Education Trust, has notified to the committee that the trustees could not accede to their application for a course of lec- tures at Widnes next winter. A course of lectures will, however, be arranged by the committee at a cost not ex- ceeding £2O. WIDENS.—LOCAL WORKMEN% HANDICAP.—A 120 ynrds handicap was run on Saturday on the Millfield Ground. There were 14 heats marked, but owing to some being absent only 13 were run. The first was won by 0. Jones, with a start of 14 yards; the second by R. Parkinson; third, Morgan; fourth, H. Scuts; fifth, a walk over for W. Brandreth ; sixth was won by J. Banner; seventh, Mr. Davies eighth. P. Redman; ninth, F. Lahey ; tenth, a walk over for F. Murphy; eleventh, Tansey ; twelfth, Fagan; fourteenth, between T. Edwardson and J. Roscoe. was won by the latter, Edwardson having a start of 4-lt yards. The prizes amount to £8 Ns. The final will be next Saturday. W. B. Cross was the handi- capper, and J. Carey referee. , Fauwwoirrn TEMPERANCE PICEIC.—On Saturday after- noon, a picnic in connection vaith the Farnworth Church , of England Temperance Society went to Hale. A party ' of about 60 persons journeyed in three waggonettes sup- plied for the occasion by Mr. $. H. Lee. The company started about two o'clock to Hale Park. the seat of Co. Blackburn. having gained permission from his agent to inspect the grounds. The arrangements were carried out under the supervision of Miss ilibbert, who was the principal advocate in the affair: and after roaming about the beautiful village, the honieward journey was commenced, arriving at their destination about nine o'clock. The weather was most salubrious. • WESLEYANISM AT WIDNES.—In connection with the re- opening of Lacey-.st. Sunday School, special services were held in the Victoria-road Chapel, on Sunday. The school had been closed for several weeks, whilst Mr. Thomas Sadler, joiner and builder, and Mr.. C. J. Sutcliffe, pain- ter and decorator, were buisilv engaged in renovating and beautifying the interior. The furniture of the school has been increased by the addition of 30 new benches. The ground surrounding the school and chapel has also been tiled. The total cost of the work was about £l5O. It is row proposed to renovate the chapel and also to re-. pair and retune the organ, besides improving the venti- lation by the substitution of patent windows. On Sun- day the morning and evening services were conducted by the Rev. Thomas Waugh, the well known evangelist, and he preached two admirable sermons. In the after- noon the revd. gentleman delivered an address to the young people. There were good congregations at each service, and the collections were very satisfactory. LAWN TENNlS.—Widnes v. - GALLANT RESCUE FROM DROWNINE AT RUNCORN.— There have just come to light the details era gallant rescue from drowning at Runcorn. On Friday afternoon , last week, Mr. Fred Mack, a clerk in the telegraph de- partment of the Post Office, was on No Man's Land, , when a boy named Frank Bailey, aged 11 yeas.s. whose home iFt in Fryerst., fell into the gut while playing near , the wooden bridge. The tide was on the ebb, and there was a great quantity of water flowing through at a rapid rate, and the boy wa,52 being carried away with great rapidity. Throwing off his coat. Mr. Mack boldly sprang into the stream, and seized hold of the boy. - He swam to the side, but he ws.s unable to land because the wall was so steep. He, however, kept the boy's head well dear of the water, and a man coming along, both rescuer and rescued were quickly brought to terra firma. Happily the boy was very little the worse for his immersion. Mr. Mack's clothes were almost rendered worthless by the action of the filthy water, and, unfor- tunately, a silver watch he was wearing at the time is comnletely ruined. The gallant act ought to be brought , under the' notice of the Humane SOcinty, especially as he has previously risked his life in the endeavour to save that of another person. ~, ' -TRI O NITY RDWAY SCHOOL, RIINCORN.—About 300 chil- dren attending this school spent a pleasant day on Mr. Hayes farm, .at Daresbury, on rhursday. The large party were conveyed.to their destination in two boats along the 'Bridgewater Canal. Ample refreshments were provided. The Rev. W. and Mrs Preston were present. UNJUST SCALES AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Ses- sions on Thursday, John Rhodes, butcher, Mersey-road, was charged with having in his possession a pair of coun— ter scales which were unjust. On the 4th hist Superin- tendent Johnson visited the defendant's premises, and found the scales 3 drachms out of balance against the purchaser.. A fine of 5s and costs was imposed. HALTON WESLEY BAND OF HOFE.-012 Saturday hist the members of the aboveband of hope held their annual trip to Overton Hill. Upwards of 150 children were taken in lurries kindly lent by Messrs. John Baguley, Joseph Baguley, Richard Nixon. John Ackerley, John Booth. Upwards of 60 adult members and friends were taken in waggonettes supplied by Mr. Peck. of Runcorn. ,The children arrived home at 8-30, after spending a very enjoyable afternoon. TRINITY NATIONAL SCHOOLS, RoNCORN.—From the re- ports of the Government inspector, it appears that the , boys at the above-named school have earned £1 Os ed per head out of £1 Os 10d limit: the girls, 19s 9d out of £1 ls 10d ; and infants 16s 6d out of 17s. The total , grant is nearly £5OO, but there is a reduction of £5O 17s 2d owing to exr-em of grant over income. This is owing to the working of article 114 a. The Government awarded " excellent " to each of the departments' and, the last clause of the boys' report states " that the whole school is fairly entitled to place in the highest class."

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT Woes.—Mr. G. H. Denby. the Clerk, summoned the following parents to Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, for not sending their chil- dren regularly to school: —Patrick McMullan, 32, Bed- ford-st ; Thomas Drannore. 52, Elixabeth-st ; Michael hicPartland, 13, Pleasant-st t John Daley. 9, Pear-st ; Kenrick Hughes, 61, Dock-st ; Fanny Ashley, 41. James- st ; Hugh Jones, 7. Pitt-st ; James Bright, 49, Lacey-st ; Martin Paton, 13, Ellison-st ; John Yurns, 35, Pleasant- st ; Walter Allen, 31, Pleasant-st ; John Connolley, 9, ' Moon-st ; William Edwardson, 20. Grove-st. The usual penalty of 5s was imposed in each case. 1 VIOLENT ASSAULT ON A WIDNES CONSTAELE.—John Smith, a vagrant, was brought before the Widnes magis- trates, on Thursday, charged with having slept upon the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co.. on Tuesday morn- ing, and further with assaulting P.C. Dean. The pri- soner was one of a gang of four who were arrested on the works, but the prisoner acted in a very violent fashion, kicking the officer about the legs most ferociously, and some difficulty was experienced in getting him to the police station.. A black list was produced against the prisoner, who was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for sleeping out, and a month's hard, labour for assaulting the officer. CENSUS AT WIDNES —The census which has been taken of the inhabitants of Widnes in order to ascertain how many representatives Widnes would be entitled to in the new County Council, has resulted in considerable dis- appointment. For some time past the population has been estimated at 33.000 in making official calculations. but the census has shown that the town does not num- ber more than 2.0,006 inhabitants.. There are 4,990 in- habited houses, and the average is 5.8 persons per house. as compared with 57 in 1881. The clerk of the Local Board has checked the result, which has since been coin- ' pared with the School B.*rti returns, and the numbers may be considered fairly accurate.

.)lARRIAOR OF A RUNCORN GENTLEMAN.—At Southport, on Thursday. Mr. Frank Adains Lightburn, eldest son of Mr. J. W. Lightburn, of Heath House, Runcorn, was married to Miss Georgina Augusta Stnith, eldest daugh- ter of Mr. W. H. Smith, of Parr's Bank and Leyland- road, Southport. The marriage, which was carried out on a very quiet scale, took place by license at All Saints' Church, the officiating clergyman being the Rev. Dr. Porter. The bride, who was attired in atravelling dress, ' was attended by her sisters, Miss E. 0. Smith and Miss Kathleen Smith' as bridesmaids. Mr. J. H. Lightburn as the best man. Immediately after the cere- mony the happy couple departed by train for London, se route to Paris, where the honeymoon will be spent. The presents were numerous and costly. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL PICNIC, WIDNES.—A, pic- nic party, consisting of about 40 elder scholars and teachers of Lacey-st. Sunday Schools, journeyed to Prover Hall and Tabley Hall, in Cheshire, on Thursday. Fivg conveyances were required for the party, and Cie.:o were supplied by Mr. Lea, and a pleasant drive through a most picturesque portion of. Cheshire was much en- joyed. the route taken being through Arley. A pleasant time was spent in .viewing the novelties of the ancient halls ad the time worn fane of St. Peter also attracted the halls, of the party. In the course of the after- noon a capital tea was served on Mr. Dean's farm. The return journey was commenced at half-past seven, and Widnes was safely reached at half-past ten. The arrangements of the "out" were camel out by Messrs. B. Brown, T. S. Swale S. Read, Peate, Guy, A. Loines, J. Davies, and R. Webster. RohniNd A Dirrox ORCHARD.—On Thursday, at Wid- nes Petty Sessions, James Carney, William Feay, Martin Caine, Patrick Meale,agh, John Farley, boys, were charged with wilfully doing damage to fruit trees, flowers, Ex., to the extent of £l, the property of John , Thomas Parker, gardener, Ditton. The boys were fur- ther charged with intending to steal the fruit.. On the Bth inst. the prosecutor discovered that his garden had been entered by some persons, who had trampled down potatoes broken branches of fruit trees, and other serious damage had been done. Later in the afternoon the prisoners were given into the custody of P.C. Hudson by Henry Moss, a gamekeeper in the employ of Lord Sefton, who had seen them take the fruit. The constable found a considerable quantity of apples and pears in the possession of the boys. A fine of 5s and costs was im- yosed upon each defendant, or in default 14 day's hail 1 ibour.

_ THE RABIES ORDER AND CHESHIRE FOTHOIINDS.—At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Messrs. J. Handley and G. Lloyd Wigg, Mr. Thomas Thuifield, partner and manager of the BOto. Wo:ks, Frodsham I Bridge, appeared to answer a stimmons charging him 'with contravening the order which was issued in May last, by permitting two dogs to be at ls.rge unmuzzled at IHalton, on the 28th ult.—Mr. Hatifieldsaid the dogs were 'foxhounds belonging to the Cheshire Hunt, and they were exempt from the Act, he believed.—Joseph Wil- kinson, a groom, employed by Mr. Dixon, of Halton Hill, proved the ease.—Mr. Hadfield admitted that they. were at large. They are hounds that are put out all over the county, ana it is impossible to keep them muz- zled or fastened up. They are sent out for the purpose of running about the fields.—Superintenclent Hollins- worth said the dogs could not be allowed to go along the highway without someone in charge of them.—Mr. Hadfield :We cannot keep these hounds un. If you fine lin a case like this, all the hounds will have to go back to the kennels.—Superintendent Hollingworth referred to the Act, and showed that such dogs were not exempt from the order.—The magistrates were of opinion that the dogs were not exempt, and fined Mr. Hadfield Bd, and 13s costs.—Mr. Hadfield said he had no more to do with the dogs than any one else in court so far as owner- ship went. ALLF.OIeD CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. John Brock and Mr. H. Wade Deacon, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, John Astles, contractor, Albert-road, was summoned for having cruelly illtreated his horse. P.C. Richardson stated that on Wednesday afternoon, the Bth inst.. he went into the defendant's stables and found there a dead horse lying on the floor. The defendant told witness that he had hit the horse, but he did not intend to kill it. He'added that he was bet- ter without a brute like that. In cross-examination by Mr. Knowles (who defended) witness said the defendant told him that the horse had reared and struck its head against the top of the stable. James Catterall (14), 20, Cross-st. ; Agnes Howard, wife of William Howard, Albert-road ; and John Clegg gave evidence to the effect that the defendant had thrashed the horse with a very thick stick, and that the horse was kicking. For the de- fence Mr. Knowles contended that there never were any grounds for bringing the case. The horse was killed by its own vengeance and viciousness. When taken into the stable on the day in question the horse tried to squeeze the defendant's son against the corn bin. Thct animal then reared up and struck its head at the top of the stable, and by Born. means it got its leg over its neck and fell down, striking its head against a provender tub. The 'horse died a few minutes afterwards. A num- ber of witnesses were called who corroborated this state- ment. And who denied that the horse was cruelly thrashed. Mr. Brock said there was a doubt in the case and the defendant should have the benefit. The summons was dismissed. Mr. Brock added that the police were Justified in bringing the matter before the court. " "

RUNCORN FREE I.7IIR.ARY ComiirmE.—The monthly meeting was held in the Town Hall on Wednesday even- ing. Mr. W. Handley presided, and there were present Messrs. F. J. Norman, T. Riley, and J. D. Jones (librarian). The Librarian reported that there-was a balance in hand of La 4s 81. During the past month the issues in the lending department were as follows :-- Theology, 27 ; philosophy, 5 ; science, 38 : history, 4;c., 98; poetry, 18; fiction, 1,443; miscellaneous, 102; total, 1,729; showing' an increase on corresponding month of last year of 185: In the reference department there had only been two issues. The annual report of the committee called attention to the increased useful- ness of thQ institution. The library had been open for the issue of books 141 days, and the number of issues had been 21,758, being an increase of 1,087 over the previous year. The average daily issue was 154. The number of borrowers tickets which had been issued during-the year was 805, being an increase of .70 over last year. During the year 586 volumes had been added to the library-483 by purchase and 103 by gift. The total number of volumes on the shelves was 4,590. The reading room continued to be a source of intellectual pleasure and profit to increasing numbers, and the opinion expressed in the last report that the enlargement of the reading room would greatly add to its usefUln&ss and comfort' had-often been grate- fully acknowledged. The committee again tendered their thanks for the numerous gifts of money, papers, and periodicals. The receipts for the year amounted to £206 37d, including £lBO 16s front the rates- and £6 15s 2d fines: A balance of Vain hand'at the commence- ment or the year brought the total airtotint'up, tb+l2B9 ã:-7d: The report' was adopted..

NELSON-ST. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RIINCORN.—The anniversary was celebrated on Sunday, when three ser- vices were held in Camden Chapel. In the morning and evening the Rev. G. Young, of Warrington, occupied the pulpit, and in the afternoon the Rev. G. E. Finch, the newly-appointed Primitive Methodist minister, preached. There were good congregations at each service, and the scholars rendered specially selected music under the leadership of Mr. Bazley. The collections realised £lB 10s.

RUNCORN SALITLTIOX ARKTECITRSION - A trip to Winnington Park, the reaiden of Mr. J. T. Brunner, 11P:, organised by the Salvation. Anny, took place on Wednesday. Upwards of 150 adults and children em- barked on a barge at Weston, and were taken along the river Weaver by a steamer, kindly placed at the disposal of the Army by Captain Clarke. After a plea-1 sant sail Winnington was reached at twelve o'clock, and the band playeda selection in front of the Hall. Games, and other means of enjoyment were engaged in in the Park, and the physical wants of the party were well attended to. Captain and Mrs. Waldron had charge of the party, which arrived safely back at Weston Point at half-past eight. _ _ _

SALT IN WIDNES.—The following letter was ad- dressed to the editor of "The Chemical Trade Journal ":—Sir.—lt. may be interesting to some of your readers to know that in 1866, and for some years after (how many, or if up to the present time I do not know) there existed a drinking fountain set in the wall adjoining the road from Widnes to the old ferry. and close to the premises of Messrs. .T. Hutchinson and Co. I recollect the mingled feel.- ing of disappointment and loathing which followed my first and only attempt to quench my thirst at this fountain. The water was horribly saline in flavour. I remember taking a sample with me to Runcorn, where / was then resident, and analysing it, but I have lost the analytical data. Still there the fact that water of a vety saline nature was , rising far above the sealerel in Widnes. That water I came from somewhere below the earth, and when I tasted it it was more saline than sea water.—Yours, &C.. WATSON SMITIL If AYDOCK PARE PONY AND GALLOWAY RACES.— Every weather inducement was offered to the public to patronise the holiday gathering at Hay- I dock Park, on Saturday. In addition to a nice pro- gramme of half a dozen events, in which all the most famous ponies of the district were entered, the London and North-Western RailwayCompanyplaceol , a special train at excursion rates at the service of the sport-loving public of Liverpool, Manchester, Wigan, Warrington, Bolton, St. Helens, .t.c The admission to the ground was reduced to the popular i price of 6d, and, n addition to the excellent sport, a first-rate military band discoursed sweet strains , during the intervals of the racing. There is certain- ly nowhere in Lancashire a more prettily situated or a better laid out course, or one more suited to all the requirements of either flat or hurdle racing or steeplechasing, and it is to be hoped that in the in- terest of sport the directors will persevere in the endeavour to popularise the grounds, and in time, no doubt, a remunerative return will reward their energy. Tarcvciii RIDE FRO* LAND'S END TO JOIIN-d- GRoAr's.-Mr. J. B. Warren, a membelrof the St.llelens Cyclist's Club, started at twelve o'clock on Sunday night, on a tricycle ride from Land's End to John- o'-Groats, intending to reach the latter place in six days and beat all previous records. From telegrams received in St. Helens during the week it appears that he reached Bodmin at seven o'clock the same morning, and there he was joined by Mr. Fred Fothergill, a member of the club. Exeter was reached at four o'clock. At Bristol they proceeded through the Severn Tunnel by rail, and came via Hereford, Shrewsbury, Chester, and Warrington. Mr. Fothergill is taking various stages by rail,while Warren is, of course, " doing the road." Warring- ton was reached at 2-40 on Wednesday afternoon, the delay having been occasioned by Warren losing his way on the Welsh borders. A very short stay was made at Warrington, and Wigan was in view about four o'clock. Warren pressed forward. hoping to reach Penrith the same night, in order to accomplish a good half of the journey.

' EXPOSING BAD FISD POD SLIM AT RUNCORN.7- At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. before Messrs. J. Handley and G. Lloyd Wigg, Jane Connor, fish dealer, of 16 Court, Henry Rdwar d-et., Liver- pool, was summoned for exposing fish for sale in Runcorn market, on the 21st ult., which was unfit for the food of man.—Mr. W. El. Lin aker appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners.—James Percival, inspector of nuis- ances, deposed that on the 21st ult. he made an in- spection of the fish at defendant's stall, and found two pieces of ray, one mackerel, and one haddock, which were unlit for food. The fish was taken be- fore the magistrates, and it was ordered to be de- stroyed.—Dr. McDougall (medical officer of health) deposed that the fish was in a state of putrefaction. The pieces of fish were in a filthy condition, and were certainly unfit for Human food.—Defendant said it was a close, warm day, hut the fish was fit for food, and she could have eaten it.—The magis- trates tined defendant 20s, and 38s costs, or one month's imprisonment in default of payment. LANCASHIIIR COAL INDUSTRY.—A new com- pany lids just re-opened the Halsnead Colliery at Whiston, formerly worked by the late Thomas Lea and Sons, which had been closed for four .years. Negotiations have passed between the principal owner, Mr. H. R. D'a Willis, of Halsnead, and Mr. William Barton (late manager at the Carr's Colliery, Whiston), promoter of the new Halsnead Colliery Co. during the last six months, with the object of fully developing the coal industry, and opening up the rich seams in that district. A start has been made, and coal of fine quality and abundant in quantity has been reached by opening out pit No. 5 in the Halanead sevbn-foot seam, at a depth of 150 yards. Temporary gearing has been placed for the experiment. The pit in question had been closed for twenty years. Already sixty-five men are en- gaged in the new workings, and in a few days the pit will be connected by rail with the London and North-Western Railway system. The total area of the colliery consists at present of between 300 and 400 acres, and in about eighteen months it is com- puted that there will be an output of 2,000 tons per day, from six seams, when the two new shafts that are contemplated are sunk and the new plant is got into working order. WIGAN COA.T. AND IRON COMPANY, LIMITED.— The report of the directors of this company for the half-year ending 30th June last was issued to the shareholders on Monday. This states that the out- put of fuel had slightly increased, but the sales had been less than in the previous half-year. Prices bad remained about the same as during the previous half-year. No change had been made in the rate of wages. The furnaces in operation continued to , work well, but the iron trade remained in a de- pressed state. The now works for the production of steel have made good progress. The accounts for the half-year show a profit of £10,340 8s 84 on the ' whole operations of the company, and the sum of .£92 3s 5d was brought from last half-year. The directors propose to svitlid raw a sum of Tl,OOO from the reserve fund, which now consists of £6,296 Si 3d in Consols, and istaken in the balance-sheet as £2,300, being the balance now remaining of the cost of the original investment. The directors re- commend a dividend after the rate of 1* per cent/ per annum, free of income tax, which will absorb .£11,310 155; 74, leaving £l2l 16s 6d to be carried forward. The balance shows that the paid-up share capital of the company amounts to £1,809,725, and the mortgage debt to .£83,706. The mine rent suspense account now stands at £302,000 166 9d.

PENKETH WESLEYAN Scitoor..—On Monday even- ing a lecture was given in the Wesleyan School be- fore a crowded audience, by Mr. Gnanamuttbu I. Israel. He had a few ladies and gentlemen dressed up in Indian costumes, which presented a very striking appearance. The lecturer's object is to raise funds for the education of low-caste Hindu children in Madras. The address was listened to with great interest by the large audience. Mr. Dignum, Mr. Garnett, and the Rev. E. H. Jackson, Warrington, also addressed the meeting. A collec- tion was made at the close. A LANCASHIRE FOOTBALLER DROWNED IN Aus- =ALIA. A special cablegram from the correspon- dent of the " Sporting Li fe,"dated Newcastle, August 15, states: "R. L. Seddon, a member of the Eng- lish Football Team' was drowned to-day in the River Hunter, near Maitland, New South Wales He was sculling in an outrigger, which was capsized." Seddon was a particularly smart forward. He first distinguished himself in England in the ranks of the Swinton Club, and also rendered yeoman service for Lancashire. The last match of importance in which Seddon played in England was North v. South at Rectory Field, Blackheath, on February 4 of the present year. Seddon was 26 years of age, Mt. 11in. high, and weighed 12st. His untimely end will be greatly deplored by all Rugby football players, with whom he was exceedingly popular. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. _ _ _ _ _ . _

The fortnightly meeting of this Board N-s;as held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. Col. Ashton presided, and there were also present Messrs Grice, Wallington, BrandrEith, Jones, Taylor, Weir, Aaron, Lewis, J Hall, Campkin ; H. Linaker (clerk), Mr. Dansey (Local Government Board Inspector) was also present. AN ArrticarioN.—A letter was read from the school- master at the Workhouse asking for a testimonial from the Board in order that he might apply for another situa- tion.—lt waA decided to grant the application. THE CHAPIAIN Qursriarc—Mr. Grice moved that the question of the appointment of chaplain to the work- house be left over for a fortnight.—Mr. Aaron seconded this proposal.—Mr. Wallington thought if they could get a person to take the office as a labour of love it would be better for all sides. If they could not do that he should be inclined to suggest that the salary be £2O instead of £3O as heretofore, and that the other LIO be applied to , paying the expenses in coming of the minister of any other denomination whose services might be wanted at the workhouse.—The Clerk said he did not see how it could be done.—Mr. Wallington said he knew several cases in which the Roman Catholic priest had to pay for a car from Warrington at all times in the night. This was rather hard when they considered that the Catholics of both Weston and Runcorn paid a good deal of rates. They would be perfectly satisfied if they could get the car .fee.—The Chairman suggested that Mr. Wallington should be put upon the Committee which had to deal with the question and report to the Board.—Mr. Weir seconded this proposal, which was agreed to.—The matter of the chaplaincy was also left over to the next meeting. —Mr. Dansey said he did not think the Board could apply the £lO in the way suggested by Mr. Wallington without previously naming the person to whom money was to be paid. He did not think they could legally do it.—Mr. Wallington: What do you think would be the proper course ?—Mr. Dansey said that must be left to the Com- mittee. They could appoint a priest as well as a minister of the Church of England, but the name must be mentioned.—Mr. Grice: Could that be done with regard to any other denomination as well ?—The Clerk: I don't think so.—Mr. Dansey said be did not know of any ease in which it had been done.—The matter then dropped. Ties PROSECUTION OFPICER.—Mr. Dansey referred to the appointment of the collector as the person to prose- cute in certain cases, a fixed fee to be paid him in each case,and said this was a new appointment,at least he had never heard of such an appointment.—After the matter had been discussed and the reasons for the appointment explained, Mr. Dansey said he would report to the Local Government Board on the subject, and it would be for them to either approve or disapprove of the appointment. This was the principal business.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Hr. E. Carey occupied the chair, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. S. Sadler, J. Houghton, H. Gaskell, J. Taylor, R. Cook, W. W. Gossage, D. Wright, F. Heyes, F. C. Liddell, J. T. Allen (clerk), T. Higginson (surveyor), I. Carr (engineer), Dr. Cooper (medical officer).

TM FATALITIES IN BOWERS BROOK. A letter addressed from the Solicitors Department of the London and North-Western Railway Company, Lon- don, was read, and contained the following paragraph: —" With regard to the recent fatal accident at Bowers Brook, I cannot advise the company to continue clearing away the deposit formed by the chemicals which are allowed to run into the brook. The brook being used as a sewer by the Local Board is, I presume, vested in them under the Public Health Act, and as notwithstanding the efforts of the company for sometime past to make a pro- per arrangement for the diversion of the chemical matter, no successful result has been achieved. I am instructed to request the Local Board to take the matter up, and in the meantime the company disclaim any responsibility for whatever consequences may ensue from the blocking up of the culvert.—Yours truly, C. H. MASON."—The Chairman said a meeting of those inter. ested in this question had been called by Mr. Gossage and held. At that meeting a suggestion was made which had been reported to Mr. Mason, and they still a*aited his reply.—The letter was referred to the corn- mittee.

The Rev. G. A. Le Bert, incumbent of St. Ambrose Church, Warrington-road, wrote asking for the use of the Board-room and adjoining apartments for the purpose of holding a bazaar in aid of the organ fund of the Church. —Mr. Wright said if this request was granted it would be a very wide precedent.—The Chairman said whatever was done all religious bodies must be treated alike. It was the desire of the Board that this building should be made as useful, as it reasonably couid to the ratepayer at large, and that without regard to party or denetnlna- tion—of course always subject to the staff not being in- terfered with. If they had had the large rooms built they would be in a better position.—Mr. Keyes thought the rooms were too small for the purpose intended.—The Chairman; Then propose that in the opinion of the Board the building is not yet adapted for the purpose.— Mr. Keyes did so.—Mr. Taylor: Mr. Le Bert wants the rooms for nothing.—The Chairman: Oh, but we should have to make a charge.—Mr. Gaskell : I think it would be very unwise policy to let these rooms at all. Con- siderable damage was certain to be done.—Mr. Keyes contended that the staff would also be interfered with in their, work.—The Clerk concurred.—The Chairman: In other words it would hinder public business.—Mr. Heye.' motion was seconded by Mr. Wright, and carried with- out dissent.

ABUSING FATHER THOMPSON.—Mary Smith, a tramp, who said she came from Eccles, was brought up charged with begging in Knutsford-road, and with using abusive language to Father Thompson. It appeared that the woman asked the rev, gentleman for assistance, and he gave her some bread. She became very violent, and threw the bread at him. Defendant, who had two chil- dren expressed great penitence for the offence, and was discharged on promising to leave the town atonce,Father Thompson not wishing to press the CARP. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs P. Stubs and H. Stanton. CHARGE AGAINST A PUBLICAN. John Scattergood, landlord of the Green Dragon, Heatley, was charged with having permitted gaming, namely dorninoe playing, for beer, on his licensed premises, on the 7th July; he was also charged with permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises on the same date and place.—Mr. Jen- kins, of Warrington, appeared on behalf o 1 the defen- dant. Joseph Winstanley, a young man, who had been convicted at the previous court for having been drunk and disorderly in and refusing to quit, the Grego Dragon, gave evidence for the prosecution. .He stated that he had played at dominoes with some navvies for quarts of beer on the defendant's premises. He was in the house about two and a half hours, when, because he refused to quit and to give the dominoes up to the land- lord's son, a policeman was sent for and he was ejected. P.C. Total Total 99 WARRINGTON V., LIVERPOOL. —The return match

_ between these teams took place on the Arpley ground on Saturday, before a large number of spectators, and resulted in a win for the visitors by 101 runs. Liver- pool winning the toss elected to bat, and were repre- sented by A. T. Kemble and D. Q. Steel, to the deliveries of Fleetwood and Lawton. Runs were scored pretty , freely off the former until a good catch by Jolley dis- missed Steel. Kemble soon followed, being dismissed by a bailer from Lawton. A. Price next made his ap- pearance, but after scoring she was clean bowled by Lawton. Upon H. B. Steel coming in he showed some fine hitting and punished Fleetwood's bowling severely, and caused Jolley to go on in his place. The change somewhat checked the run-getting, and eventually Steel was caught at the boundary from a tremendous drive off Jolley's bowling. With H. B. Steel's departure Fleetwood resumed, and with his first ball bowled Nicholson. Melly was caught by Podmore, but upon Richardson and W. Price getting together a good stand was made, the former being eventually caught by Podmore, and Price bowled by Fleet- wood. Hood was easily caught and bowled by Jolley, and the innings closed for 128. As a bowler Jol- ley met with great success, and is to be congratulated upon his performance. In all he took five wickets at an average of five runs each. Lawton was evidently very difficult to play, as none of the batters were prepared to take any liberties with him, and he sent down maiden af- ter maiden. Fleetwood's wickets were rather expensive, 60 runs being scored off him. On Warrington going in to bat the resistance they made was feeble in the ex- treme, and no one was prepared for the collapse which followed. Tinsley and Crosfield went first to the wickets being opposed to the bowling of Richardson and W Price (two of the Nottingham County bowlers.) Tinsley had the first over, and drove Richardson to the boundary for

four, though the ball touched one of the fielders' hands. Crosfield was easily caught and bowled by Price in his first over, and made way for Lawton. Tinsley again got Richardson away to the boundary for four and also scored a two hit, but in the next over he Was bowled middle stump. Lawton was neatly stumped by Kern- ble, and Clarke bowled by Richardson, also middle stump. Dunn played very carefully for a few overs, but struck too late at one from Richardson, and Jolley was beaten by a good ball from Price. The bowlers were nil. playable, and one by one the players came out and re- ' turned to the pavilion, no one being able to relieve the monotony. Woodhead was caught in his first over, and Fleetwood bowled first ball. Fairclough scored It single and was then bowled, and Collin was also dismissed without scoring, the innings closing for the small total of 25. The Liverpool fielding was admirable, and Kern- ble kept wicket in grand style. W Price and Richardson showed grand form with the ball, the former taking 4 wickets for four rims, and the latter 6 for 19 runs. Score :

Several county matches were brought to a conclusion on Saturday. The Cheshire men were easily beaten at Stockport by Yorkshire, who had an innings and 40 runs to spare. It was a foregone conclusion that Surrey would beat Stissex at the Oval. Sussex had nine wickets to fall in their second innings, and in an hour and twenty minutes the innings was finished off for a total of 99. At Clifton Gloucestershire gained a brilliant victory over the Australians by 257 runs, the success of the home side being particularly popular from the fact that the wes- tern county had never previously defeated any Colonial team. The win was thoroughly well deserved, and formed a fitting climax to the recent improvement in Gloucester- shire cricket.

In the match with M.C.C. and Wiltshire, at Lords, on Tuesday, the overnight score of 514 for the loss of only two wickets was increased to 735 before Marylebone was disposed of. Mr. E. Sainsbury made 180, Flowers 88, Mr. H. Brougham 117, and there were 71 extras. Wilt- shire scored 130 and 60 for two wickets, so that the match was left drawn. Three first-class cricket matches were completed on Tuesday. At Kennington Oval an England eleven gained a mest decisive victory over the Australians by an innings and 137 runs. Sussex best Lancashire, at Brighton, by nine wickets; and, at Derby, Yorkshire were defeated by Derbyshire by seven wickets. Of the three, the first-named contest was, of course, the one in which most interest was centred, and the bowling feat of Briggs is now a matter of history. In the first innings of the Australians ho succeeded in taking five wickets for 25 runs.
