THE kA.NCEESTE It SHIP CANAL.

VISIT OF GEOLOGISTS. The members of the Manchester Geological Society visited the works ef the Manchester Ship Canal on Wednesday, in the neighbourhood of Warburton and Thelwall. Mr. Mark Stirrup, one of the secretaries of the society, accompanied the party, which was later on joined by Mr. Prowse, contractor's agent, and Mr. Brown' resident engineer. Mr. C. E. De Rance, of Her Majesty's Geological Survey, also made one of the visitors. Starting frcm Oxford- road station, the party, numbering fifty or sixty persons, proceeded by rail to Lymm. From thence a pleasant walk along green lanes brought them-to- Warburton. Ilere they viewed the clearing opera- tions With much interest. The works at this place have considerably advanced, and the visitors were able to see two of the steam nay,' vies briskly employed in excavating the md- terial, which in some places was so rough as to require loosening by blasting before these powerful instruments could work upon it with effect. As explained by Mr. Prowse, the canal will be about 120 feet at the bottom width. A little , way from that spot a swing...bridge will cross the , Warburton-road. There is a continuous line of work from Latchford up to Hollins Ferry. By the route the visitors were to follow they would cross seveial bridges, being sometimes in Lancashire and sometimes in Cheshire, and they would see where it was proposed to elivt•rt the river Mersey. • In answer to questions, Mr. Prowse said that where the ground of the canal was not sufficiently stable at the sides it would be pitched for seven feet above the water line. In many places it would be sodded.—Mr. De Rance made a few observations on the geological aspects of the ground at that part. He said that the sections they were about to visit, and those to the east, and the sections in the Run- corn district and at Birkenhead, all told the same story, that the Mersey had what had been termed a valley within a valley. They found the 11 curioue fact on examination that the old and original Mersey valley was not coin- cident in line with the track the River Mersey took at the present time. If they made borings at intermediate points between Birkenhead and Manchester they would find the Mersey actu- ally at points 150 feet below the sea level. At Pres- ton they had it about 150 feet above the sea, the Iwhole composed of glacial drift which had been piled up; but in the Mersey area instead of the bot- tom being of or about high water mark as at Pres- , I ton, it was about 150 feet below it. On the north*: east coast they found valleys within valleys—Val- leys cut in the rock and filled up with drift, and when they examined the bottom they found it at 100 or 150 feet. They found that before the glacial drift was deposited valleys were excavated not only as deep as now but (leerier. in other words, the re- lative levels of the land and tea were somewhat dif- rferent from what they *ere at the present time. Pointing to the sand in the neighbourhood and the 'boulder clay beneath, he said that underneath the latter were the marls which he took to be the lowest bed of the Tieuper marls resting immediately on the Keuper stones. There was no demarcation geo- logically between the Keuper marls and the Reaper waterstones. Considering that coal measures had been found in the neighbourhood of Warrington, and assuming what was true of Warrington was true of that neighbourhood, there was reason to be- lieve a profitable coalfield might be found along that valley, and if it should come alongside a mag- nificent piece of engineering like that before them they might all hope for commercial advantages and a time of plenty as regarded the district which could leave nothing to be desired. (Rear, hear.) Afterwards the party went on to Wildgrave and Thelwall, crossing the river by temporary bridges several times. They were able to inspect the places where many men are busy at the works for diver- ting the river, and they also witnessed the marvel- lous capabilities of the German steam navvy, which works on the principal of a dredger, and which was scooping up soft material at a marvellous rate. From Thelwall station the visitors returned to Lymm, where they separated after a most instruc- tive and interesting excursion.

CADISHEAD. Great progress is being made on the Cadishead sec- tion, a great number of men being at work on the east side of the railway from Stockport to Liverpool. A wooden trestle bridge has been thrown over the river at the Rooler or Idirdham point, and near here the canal crosses the old stream 3 times in a shorter distance than 400 yards. A steam navvy is fitted, and will be put to work shortly. An engine is busy at work, and a bridge is being built near Knowe Rock to facilitate the working of the railway that is being put down for the entire length of the section. At Irlam the same thing is being done, and two steam navvies are at work. BARTON.

Rapid progress is being made on the section between Warburton and Barton, and there are now upwards of 500 men at work. Many more will be required shortly, when the machinery now being erected is got to work. There are already four steam cranes and a couple of locomotives at work. Three steam navvies are being put together, and are ertected to be ready soon. A bridge is being built across the river at Sandy Island, near Partington, and is so far completed as to be ready for the laying of rails across it. The bridge at Irlam is finished. A horse road has been started at Sandy Island, near Partington, and it is said to be an improvement on either the horse and barrow or steam and barrow roads used in connection with the rail- way diversion at Thelwall. In place of an ordinary bar-

row an handcart is used, which is capable of holding up- wards of a ton of earth This is drawn up the incline by a horse with equal facility as it would draw up a bar- row. MANCHESTER. The starting point of section 8, extending from Barton to Manchester, is at the Warburton end of Stickens Is- land. In the first cutting a French steam navvy—the only one on the Canal works—is engaged taking out the earth, which is tough and full of stones, at the rate of upwards of 2,000 tons a day. I'n the next cutting, nearer Barton, a landslip has taken place. caused by the rains. but fortunately this has not caused any stoppage of the lines. Near where this landslip is a quantity of peat has been found, in which Oere sonte fossils of trees. A powerful pumping engine keeps the water down in this cutting, which not only receives a large quantity from the drains on the north bank, but being very near the river course, the water from thence percolates the bank on the south side. At the Bridges at Barton the Old Corn Mill has been demolished. A little further on is a cutting on the Eccles sub-section, where stone is being got for building the boundary wall of Trafford Park. In this cutting there is a steam navvy taking off the earth for five or six feet deep, a steam crane excavator at the other end of the cutting working in a similar manner, and an ordinary steam travelling crane taking away the i stone to the wagons. The Trafford Estate s already fenced off with temporary wooden fence, and prepara- tions are being made to build the permanent wall. Op- posite Salford Cemetery a large tract of land has been taken for the purpose of a spoil ground, and three or four engines arecontinually running backwards and forwards, with a dozen wagons or so each, from the cutting at the Docks. An immense quantity of material has recently arrived here, and is still coming in from the Preston Docks, which have been abandoned for a time, and many of the employees from those works have been started here. The North Dock is almost entirely cut out; the required depth and concreting for it has begun. They are also widening out the branch dock in accordance with the revised scheme recently passed by Parliament. On the site of the Docks alone there are 550 men at work, on the Eccles and Barton sub-sectioits 460 and 850 men, respectively, making a total of 1,660 men on this section.

div.head: OPENING OF MISSION BOOMS.
div.p: OPENING OF MISSION BOOMS.

On Sunday, the Salford Mission Hall in Trafford-road I was opened, when there was a special service in the evening. Tho following meetings have been arranged for in connection with the Mission Hall :—Sundays, morning Sunday school; 10-45, morning service; 2-0, I afternoon Sunday school; 3-0, men's Bible class; 6-30, evening service. Monday, 7.30, temperance meeting (every fortnight) ; Tuesday, 7-30, prayer meeting; Wed- nesday. 7-30, night school (free to men and boys on the works) ; Thursday, 2-30, mothers' meeting; Friday, 7-30, choir practice. The iron .Mission Hall at Cawdor- st, Patricroft, was also opened on Sunday. There will be the following services in connection with this hall : Sunday school, 9-30; Morning service, 11-0: Sunday school, 2-0; Bible class, 3-15; Evening service, 6-30; Prayer meeting, Monday, 7-30 : Evangelistic service, !Wednesday, 7-30.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

Students and lovers of literature generally will welcome the issue by Messrs. Cassell and Co., of the third volume of English Writers, which is modestly described by the author, Professor Henry Morley, as "An attempt towards a history of English litera- ture." The volume to hand covers the period from the Conquest to Chaucer, and there is evidence on every page of the erudition and painstaking which have distinguished the first parts of this magnifi- cent work. It is particularly interesting to people' in this part, of the country to note that 'Chester is, the first city of England that had a book written about it. Lucian, the monk of St. Werbergh's wrote the book about the year 1,100, and entitled it De Laudibus Cestrias—or the praises of Chester. The great feature of Chester in this writer's eyes was the monastery of St. Werbergh. The city was its ad- mirable outhouse." This account of the work is perhaps a trifle hard upon the monk, who has at any rate achieved immortality—of a kind—for himself and his book. In order that the reader may learn something of the contents of this third volume of Professor Morley'a history, we give the headings Of the various chapters, which are as, follows :-1, Light from the South—close of the eleventh cen- tury; 2, Ordericus Viialis and William of Malmes- bury—Gesti Stephani ; 3, Geoffrey of Monmouth ; 4, Church Militant—Thomas Becket—Giraldus Cam- brensis ; 5, Retrospect Chroniclers —Henry of Huntington—Miracle Plays of 'Marius; 6, Wal- ter Map; 7, Nigel Wireker--more Chroniclers— Neckham and Gervase of Tilbury; 8, Layamon ; 9, The Ormulum and the Ancren Riwle ; 10, English Songs and Ballads—the Bards in Wales; 11, Eng- lish Metrical Romance; 12, Foundations of the Do- minicians and Franciscans -- Gosseteste Roger Bacon; 13, Songs, Satires, Fables; 14, Chronicles, Sermons, Proverbs • 15, .Robert of Brunne—Gesta Romanorum—Alleory and Romance 16, The Italian Revival. It will be gathered from the above that the period is exhaustively treated. It is announced that the fourth volume will be issued early in December. It will de- scribe the literature of the fourteenth cen- tury; and " will include results' of a new study of vexed questions upon the life and works of Chaucer." In the Magazine of Art for August, Mr. Walter Crane continues his instructiye papers on "The Language of Lino." Hadrian aS an art patron is very readable, and there is an article on "Art in the Theatre," with, aniongst either illustrations,, a fine portrait of Miss Mary Anderson as " Hermione." A paper on "The Salon" is adorned with several strik- ing illustrations, the most notable of which is that of "The Watling of Summer," from the painting by Raphael Collier. "Mr. Ruskin's Museum at Shef- field" furnishes some curious information. The frontispiece is a beautiful photogravure of a paint- mg by Gustave Courtois—" A sword shall pierce through thy own soul also." The current issue of "The Woman's World" is more than usually strong. A portrait of Josephine, the wife of the first Napoleon, makes an, attractive frontispiece. She was indeed an attractive woman, and, as the accompanying text shows,Napoleon owed more to her than is generally acknowledged. Amongst other illustrated articles are "An old fashioned Irish town,' "Marie Bashkertseff, the Russian painter" Vasser," and "August Fashions." "The Mer-haby'/ should be mentioned as a pretty story in Verse by Violet Pane. Cassell's Magazine is" always good alike," though the phrase may be varied by saying the illustrations improve every year. Mr. Harry Furniss illustrates in his own humorous way a capital ipaper by Mr. H. Frith on "how I tried to write a story;" Mr. George Howell, M.P., answers the question—" What is a Royal Commission-?" and Mr. S. P. Hall gives it, by illustrations, a formidable air, The "Family Doc- tor" reveals his wisdom on "Ventilation and Health," there is a spirited poem on "King Philip's Invincible Fleet," and the usual supply of continued and complete stories, Rm. "The Quiver" opens ap- propriately with "The story of the Spanish Armada," by the Rev. T. F. Thistleton. It is illus- trated, as are several other admirable paper and stories. "Little Folks" for August is just the thing for brightening a wet day at the seaside when the youngsters are kept indoors. It is full of "tit- bits" in prose and verse, all illustrated in first-class style. We have also received from Messrs. Cassell and Co. the current parts of "Milton's Paradise Lost," illustrated by Gustave Dore, the Illustrated Shake- speare, Encyclopedic Dictionary, Familiar Wild Flowers, Dictionary of Histery. and "The Sea; its tirring story of Adventure, Peril, and Heroism." The English Illustrated Magazine has for frontis- lece a One engraving—the Parish Clerk, by Gains- Jorough. "A Rugby Ramble," by Mr. H. A. New- ton, is illustrated by Mr. W. H. Oakley; and there is another illustrated article on "Post-office Parcels and Telegraphs," which is 'us ell worth careful read- ing. Mr. H. D. Train's "Et Ctetera" preserves its interest, and there is a fair supply of story and verse.

div.head: FROM LONDON LETTERS, &c.
div.p: FROM LONDON LETTERS, &c.

Now that the grave has closed over Dean Burgon, and his many quaintnesses must soon pass into oblivion, it may be permissable to record a favourite story of Mr. Gladstone's about the excellent Dean. His devotion to the Anglican via media of theology as distinguished on the one hand from Romanism and on the other from Puritanism is well known, and once, in the pulpit of St. Mary's, after expatia- ting on his favourite theme with passionate vehem- ence, he concluded with the fervent aspiration "Be mine the blessed lot to live the life of a Taylor and die the death of a Bull." Mr. Henry Cunynghame, who has been appointed secretary to the Parnellite Commission, is a kind of Admiral Crichton on a small scale. He is a very short man, but extremely active and energetic. He was a distinguished officer in the Engineers, but quitted the service early for the law. He is now a barrister, an Assistant Charity Commissioner, a great mechanician and mathematician, and a most vigorous and vivacious speaker. He is a son of General Sir Arthur Cunynghame, and grandson, ma- ternally, of Field Marshal Viscount Hardinge, of In- dian fame. Mr. Cunynghame is a staunch Liberal, a member of the Eighty Club, and a pillar of Liberal- ism in Fulham, where he resides. The price of gas in London has for some years been getting lower, and at present the price per thousand cubic feet is as low as 2s 5d under one company and 2s 10d under another. Remembering the comparatively high price of coal in the metro- polis this must be regarded as a satisfactory low price. Notwithstanding this the dividends of the companies are increasing. The directors of one company declare that they have two years divi- dends in hand, and that there is a prospect of an early reduction in the price of gas again. The fear originally was that the reduction would be followed by a loss of dividend, but the cheapening ot gas is apparently followed by a considerable increase in consumption. The electric light competition no longer frightens gas companies. The fact is that there is a growing demand for gas in London for cooking purposes. The gas companies themselves lend out gas cooking stoves, which are found to be very suitable to the housekeeper. They are cleanly, they save fire in summer, and properly used there is no fear of the food being tainted with gas vapars. In small busi- nesses also there is a free use of gas for motive power. The gas engine is very useful for wolk of a certain class. Then the income of the gas com- panies from the sale of their residual products is large. Those who hastily parted with their gas shares a few years ago when the electric light scare was upon us must now be consumed with vain regrets. The American papers to hand by the last mail contain circumstantial reports of the wedding of Mrs. Langtry and Mr. Frederick Gebhardt. The divorce was obtained in June, and almost immedi- ately afterwards, according to these veracious chroniclers, the arrangements for the marriage with her manager were made. They are residing in a villa at Long Branen, and Mrs. Langtry's mother-- the widow of the late Dean of Jersey—and two nieces are under the same roof. It is said that they have no present intention of ;entering upon a theatrical tour. As far as money is concerned, the "Jersey Lily' is now comfortably off, and unless she indulges in extravagance—of which there is no sign—she may not again be under the n6cessity of treading the stage. An amusing incident is said to have occurred dur- ing the rehearsal of "The Golden , Legend" at the recent Chester Musical Festival. In a particular passage of the legend the maiden who offers her life for Prince Henry, in response to the question, "Have you thought well of this?" replies, "1 come not to argue but to die." Here Sir Arthur Sullivan, who was conducting the rehearsal, turned back to the page of his score and said " letter D." This sounded like "let her dee " (Yorkshire dialect for die), nude loud roar of laughter went up from the chorus. Sir Arthur was puzzled to know the reason of the hila- rity, and when it was explained to him he joined heartily in the laughter. The King and Queen of the Belgians have been spending some weeks at the Royal. Pavillion on the Digue. The King is a tall, good-lotkinq man of i fifty-five, wears pince-nez, for which his Majesty has ample " accommodati-n," and walks with a de- cided limp. He evidently delights to throw off the formalities of State and Court etiquette. and may be seen any morning on the sands during the bath- ing time, most sensibly arrayed in white ducks and straw hat, chatting with his friends and enjoying the humours of the scene. The Queen, who is still handsome, frequently patronises the theatre, especi- ally when opera-bouffe is performed, but she is sel- dom seen on the " plage," though she generally ac- companies the King on any grand occasion, such as a State visit to the races, when the strictest cere- mony is de rigueur, and the Royal turn-out is quite imposing. It is astonishing to learn that many of the hard- est-headed men of business are also the slaves of superstition. There is Mr. Jay Gould, for ex- ample, one of the richest men in America. When he begins to walk he always puts his left foot first, and, if through absent mindedness, he should omit to do so, he invariably returns and starts afresh. It is also reported of him that he objects to enter into business relations with fair people. All his clerks are dark, and the darker they are the more he confides in them, but he is not singujar in his prejudices. Napoleon 1., it is said, never trusted a general who had light air or moustaches. On the other hand, a well-known newspaper editor in Lotr don will never, if he can help it, employ a dark man on any important affair. Now that Londoners have saved Richmond Park from the ravages of the National Rifle Association they do not very much concern themselves about the choice of another site. Those who regard the annual meeting as a mere form of social entertain- ment favour the claims of Patcham, near Brighton, as affording the prospect of pleasant picnic parties from London; and it has an enthusiastic advocate in Sir Henry Fletcher. M.P. for Mid-Sussex, who is a prominent member of the Association, and whose property would be generally hoproved by the selec- tion of the Patcham site. But those who regard the matter seriously, as a question affecting our military training, are strongly in favour of Cannock Chase, on account of the facility of access to it from all parts of the northern and midland counties as well as from London. Should Cannock Chase be chosen, Lord Lichfield and Lord Anglesey are among the proprietors who would derive direct or indirect advantage.
WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB ROAD RACE.

On Saturday afternoon a fifty mile road race in connection with the Warrington Cycling Club was brought off, the prizes being two gold and four silver medals. The starcinc, place was near the Mulberry Tree Inn, Stockton death, and the course lay along the Chester-road to the Dog and Dart and then off to the right through high Leigh, Kuntsford, Holmes Chapel, to Church Lawton and back again over the same route. There were fifteen entries for ' the race, and twelve starters, who were handicaaped as follows :—Richard Bennett, 35 minutes start ; 'J. Barton, 30 minutes; W. Brown, •20 minutes; W. Jenkinson, 16 minutes ; R. Bennett, 15 minutes ; C. H. Wood, 10 minutes; T. C. Hollingsworth, 10 lminutes ; W. 11. Bellian, S. Newall, P. W. Fair, and T. Waywell, five minutes each ; F. Sutton, scratch. R. Bennett was started about 20 minutes past two and the others followed in due course. Mr. Fair. Turnerofficiated as starter. From beginning to end the limit man, R. Bennett, maintained the lead and came in a somewhat easy wirner. P. W. Fair won the secona gold medal, covering the fitty miles in the very good time of 3 hours 38 minutes and 5 see,s. The silver medals were won as follows :—William Bellian, 3; Thomas Waywell, 4 • W. Jenkinson, 5; and C. 11. Wood, 6. Two or three of the riders had "spills" on the road, but only one, J. Barton, was anything like seriously hurt. He fell a little beyond Knutsford, and having injured his shoulder, he had to be taken to the nearest inn, at which he stayed till the next day, when he rode home again.
ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT NVARRIGITON.

At the Borough Police Couh, at Warrington, on Monday, a man named John Vickers's (33), a Ship Canal navvy, who is a native of Winsford, but who for two or three months past has been living in Smith-st., off Mersey-st., was brought up in custody on a charge of having attempted suicide at 12-20 o'clock on Sunday morning. It appeared from a statement made by Mr. Hunt (the chief constable) that on Saturday night the prisoner went home the worse for drink, and asked. his wife for some sup- per. She was at the time cooking some herrings for him, and he asked for some vinegar. She told him to fetch it himself, and he went out for that purpose. He left some money on the table, which the wife saw, and thinking she would also like something tasty for her supper, she went out to purchase something. The prisoner soon returned to the house with the vinegar, but his wife had not got back. A neighbour named Mrs Kirk at this time had occasion to go to Vickers' door, when she saw the prisoner suspended by a rope, with a run- ning noose, to the clothes line, which stretched from side to side of the house. Mrs Kirk screamed, and meeting Mrs Vickers said to her, "Go t.) your house, and you will see what you will see." Mrs Vickers at once went into the house, followed by another neighbour named Joseph Urey, who was just in time to see the prisoner drop into a chair in a sit- ting position, owing to the clothes line having slipped. P.C. Caldwell also went into the house and saw the prisoner. He was exceedingly white, and he was gasping for breath. Urey remained with the prisoner about half-an hour, and when Inspec- tor Spinks arrived that officer felt it his duty to lock Vickers up on the charge of having attempted to commit suicide. When the prisoner was sober, his wife said lie was a very good husband, but he oc- casionally gave way to excessive drinking, and lost his senses. She had never had any idea that he would attempt to take his life. When asked by Urey what induced him to attempt to commit suicide, prisoner said--" I cannot tell you. Something came over me and told me to do it." When before the magistrates prisoner said that he had been drink- ing different sorts of "stuff" on Saturday, and it had got over him. Ile promised not to attempt such a thing again, and the magistrates allowed him to go on his entering into his own recognisances to appear if called upon within a month's time.

THE ALLEGED ADVERTISING FRAUD. POLICE PROCEEDINGS AT WARRINGTON. Mr. Robert Garnett, one of the Borough magis- trates, sat at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednesday morning, to hear a case in which Rose Williams, aliaa Clarke, of SO. Windermere-st., Liverpool. was charged with having, on Tuesday, the 17th of July last, in the borough of Warrington, unlawfully attempted to obtain money by false pre- tences from George,Millman, a clothier and outfit- ter, who lives in Gladstone-st. Mr. Collingwood , Hone, barrister, (Liverpnol), instructed by the Town ' Clerk of Warrington, appeared for the prosecution, I and Ur. Tnomas Swift, barrister, (Liverpool), in- structed by Mr. A. Browne. solicitor, Warrington, was for the defence.—Mr. Hope said that the cir- .cumstances that surrounded the case were peculiar, and were very suspicious. On the 16th of July, and for some time previous to that date, notices had ap- peared in the Liverpool papers from a person asking for a temporary loan of money, and offering a very • tempting security, and also a very high rate of interest. The charge in question was one based upon an advertisemelnt , that appeared on the 16th July, which read as fol- lows :—" lOs interest given by a lady for imme- diate advance of £7 until the 25th inst. Good I security. Urgent.—Mrs Clarke, 45, Coniston-st." Seeing that advertisement Mr. George Millman ' Caused a letter to be written and sent to the address given. Thereupon Mrs Clarke, or Williams, called upon the prosecutor at his address in Gladstone-st., Warrington, and brought prosecutor's letter with her. She saw the prosecutor and asked if he was the per- San who had written the letter. He replied that he was. Defendant practically repeated the request contained in the newspapers, and asked for a loan. Pro- secutor asked what security she had and she handed him a bundle of pawntickets. Mr. Millman, however, WAS not satisfied, and asked for something more tangible. Defendant then said that she had house pro- perty in London, and expected her rents on the 25th of that month. Mr. Millman remarked that probably shb would have a trustee and solicitors, and she replied that her trustees were Mr. Hubbard and Mr. Rendle, of 120, Strand, London. This, Mr. Hope said, was a material part of the case, because it was on this statement of the defendant that the charge of false pre- tences was based. Prosecutor, being suspicious, did not advance the money, but at once sent for the police, and gave the defendant in charge. It had since been ascer- tained that there was no Mr. Hubbard, and that there ' was no Mr. Rendle, at the address given-120, Strand, London. As a matter of fact, there was no such num- ber in the Strand.—The prosecutor was then called, and detailed at length how he caused the advertisement to be answered, and what subsequently transpired in connection with the visit to him of the defendant. Having corroborated thestaternent of counsel for the prosecution, he in addition said that he had been twice before swin- dled by the defendant, although he had I not had any transactions with her personally. In March last he saw an advertisement offering £3 for a temporary loan of £6, with good security. He answered the adver- tisement, and received a bundle of pawntivkets and a promissory note. He then sent the £6, the receipt of which was acknowledged. He afterwards lent another £5, the sum of £2 being offered as interest. Witness had not advanced any additional loans. None of the men( y had been repaid. In answer to Mr. Swift, witness said that he did not answer the advertisement in July for the purpose of catching some one, but he admitted having said something to that effect at a previous hearing of the case.—lnspector Spinks said that on the 7th of July lie was called to 15, Gladstone-st. the residence of the last witness, where he received defendant into custody, and took her to the police station. He charged her with having attempted to obtain £7 by false pretences from George Millman the same day, and she made the reply, "I drd'ut intend to defraud.' She had a bag, which witness opened and examined. He found a large num- ber of communications and letters (produced.) Under- neath the papers he found a purse containing £4 17s 6d in money. On the 17th and 19th July witness went to Liverpool and visited certain pawnshops. He took with him tickets received from the prosecutor. Articles were shown him as being those referred to in the tic- kets. Ile believed that the full value of the ar- ticles had been lent on them, but he would not have paid the advances required to redeem them.—Wil- Ham Hilton, assistant overseer of the three parishes com- prised in the Strand, London, said the defendant was not rated in respect of any property in the Strand or near it. There was no such number as 120, Strand. The numbers ran 115 to 125, there being a street intervening —Savov-st.—For the defence, Mr. Swift submitted that a prima facie case had not been made out against the defen- dant. Before a case could be made out it must be satis- factorily clear that the defendant, by means of some false pretence of some existing fact, had endeavoured to obtain mariey from the prosecutor with intent to defraud. The only security- offered in this case were the pawn- tickets, and defendant did not mention the property in London as an inducement to lend the money, but merely to satisfy inquiry. The pawn-tickets were the only security offered, and it was admitted that they were genuine. Mr. Swift also commented on the actions of persons who advanced money at such a high rate of in- terest. The sum of £3 10s for a loan of £7 for eight days was at the rate of £5O per cent., and at the rate of £2,281 per cent, per annum.—Mr. Garnett, after con- sulting with the magistrates' clerk (Mr. H. B. White), said that although the case was surrounded by a large amount of suspicion, he did not think there was any- thing in it to justify the Court in committing the defen- dant for trial. He felt compelled, though with some reluctance, tO (rasa:Liss the cam

GOVERNMENT PENSION FOR A ST. HELENS MAN. Mr. William Hopton, certificated colliery rallnai ger, St. Helens, has during the past week receive the gratifying intelligence that his name had beeo. added to the Civil List for a pension of £lOO I,e' annum, in consideration of his services in writing books on how best accidents could be Prevented ill coal mines. Mr. Hopton, by his works, has made himself well known throughout the mining world. The son of a Yorkshire miner, he went to work it the pit when he was only seven years of age, an about thirty years since he came to St. Helens tv take charge of the mines at Cropper's Hill C,ollierf for the late Alderman James Radley. In 1886 be went to Messrs. Pilkington's, and on his leaving there in 1870 he was presented with a gold wate bearing the following inscription ;—" Presented bi the miners of the St. Helens Colliery to Mr. Wm. MP: ton, manager, as a mark of esteem and appreciatim of his services, 29th October, 1870." Mr. Ropy); returned to the service of Mr. Hadley, and to° charge of Sutton Heath Collieries, where he re' mained until failing eyesight compelled him tore". linquish active duties. For many years Mr. Hoptoi has devoted himself to the study of preventing cidents in mines, and on this subject he has =WI several valuable works. He is the author of "T.b9o Lundhill Mode of Ventilation." " APractical on Gases, Explosions, Ventilation, and the Working' of Mines," and "Conversations on Mines. Bzc., tween a Father and Son." This last work has through eight editions, the sale having now reache, 28,000 copies. The late Mr. Hermon, M.P. for? ton,gave £275 for the best suggestions for the don of catastrophes in mines, and 300 competed. Mr. Hopt on was awarded the prize. At At the beginning of this year several Helens gentlemen advised the author to ask Treasury to place his name on the Civil List for_ pension, because of the good he had done to mining public, and a petition was signed by Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P., the Mayor (Alderman MK-eel' several ex-Mayors, magistrates, solicitors, minist%, and other gentlemen. Both Mr. B. Pickard, and Mr. H. Hall, her Majesty's Inspector of Mini spoke highly of Mr. Hopton's book. The petit was sent to the First Lord of the Treasury, with result that Mr. Hopton will now receive a pei of £lOO per annum. The miners of South-West cashire especially, and, indeed, the miners of cashire and Yorkshire generally; will be gratia this recognition of the merit-, of one of their in her. Mr. Ifopton, on Monday night, gave a lecture, "God's great, grand universal empire of worlds, the Salvation Army Barracks, Lowe-st. There a crowded attendance, and Mr. llopton's - was greatly appreciated.

TFIE CORPORATION AccouNrs. Sir,—So it appears Councillor Dixon was quite right when he said the annual accounts of the Corporation, in- cluding those of the Gas Committee, were not presented to the Town Council for consideration and discussion, and those other gentlemen who, boiling with virtuous in- dignation, all but gave Councillor Dixon the lie, are quite wr.ng. Isee from what took place at the last meeting of the Town Covncil, that we have nothing less than this on the authority of the Mayor himself. Councillor W. Pierpoint askea a question about some item in the an- nual statement of accounts—which had apparently been sent to him within a few days previously—and he was told by the Mayor that it was not in order to discuss those accounts. I have no doubt whatever that the -Mayor's action was perfectly in accordance with the orders which regulate the Council's proceedings, but what are we to think of those who all but accuse others of telling an untruth when they said nothing more than what the Mayor, in his official capacity, has now corro- borated?
A BURGESS.

div.head: Warrington, August 13th, 1888.
div.p: Warrington, August 13th, 1888.

THE LICENSING QUESTION. Sir,—Notice having been given of application for new licenses, and the constitution of the present licensing committee being such that there is a probability of these applications being granted, I think it tight that the voice of the people should be heard on this question. As a householder in one of the districts where a license is sought to be obtained, I must enter my most emphatic protest against any further extension of facilities for • drinking in this neighbourhood. We have sufficient facilities at present, Mall conscience , to satisfy any reason- able person, and to attempt to force anymore housesupon us will be a public outrage that will meet with the re- sentment of all the respectable people in the district. - What are the benefits conferred upon the people by these licensed houses that the magistrates should still further increase them? The manner in which very many of them are conducted is a disgrace to the town. Very few of them exist to supply the legitimate wants of the inhabitants, but are the means of degrading and de- moralizing the people. Many of them are of such a character that no respectable man would dream of enter-

jug them. If the Licensing Committee recommend the granting of these licenses, I would suggest the calling of a public meeting to indignantly protest against such a measure, and to pass censure upon the committee. Let us not be trifled with in this matter. If our magistrates were more manly and independent, they would refuse to play into the hands of the church-building brewer of Walton Hall. ORFORD LANE.

THE MUSIC IN THE PARK. Sir,—l quite agree with "Spectator," who throws him.self about, as it were, in a letter in your last issue anent the music in the Park, that there is great room for improvement as regards that matter. A new band stand is wanted, but lam afraid the Town Council will be a long time before providing it. The first part of your correspondent's letter is all serene, but as his pen slips forward it runs away with him entirely, and leads him into the broad path of mistakes. He says—" If my esti- mate of the character of Warrington people is correct they will make themselves hard in the matter, and will, through the Town Council, pay for their luxuries them- selves." Yes; that's good. It has a pretty sound. But still it's a fallacy. The "people" may make themselves heard, even to the extent of the Salvation Army drum, but the Council, sir, is deaf. Deaf as a post and blind as a bat in so far as the wishes of the ratepayers are con- cerned. What are a few score ratepayers compared to a portly aldervian ? They are but as trifles. What are a few common councillors compared to the aldermen? They, too, are but as trifles, and verily, they are led by the nose. The people can make themselves heard as much as they like, but unless they can " get over " the aldermen it will be no good. Those personages rule the roast, and one bright particular star among them evidently feels annoyed that brainless persons of an impudent turn of mind are able to " write to the papers." These elderly municipal jossers, " Spectator," would boss creation if they could, and you have done the worst thing you could to suggest in print that the public should force their at- tention to a particular thing. It's just the way to set them againk it. If you had delicately intimated that the public hated music, and that they would kick down any ugly new band stand, we should have had a beauti- ful one next season; but r.ow all hope is gone. "Spec- tator," you have, with the best intention in the world, defeated your own laudable desire. Alas! The next time you wish that the Corporate body should be moved, remember that the wish of the public is just the thing that has not to be considered.—Yours, &c., KO-KO. Warrington, August 16, 1888.

GOVERNMENT TORTURE OF IRISH POLITICAL PRISONERS. Sir,—The distressinkdetails of prison torture, brought out in evidence at the inquest tm the body of Dr. Ridley, the late medical attendant at Tullamore gaol, Ireland, are enough to make a man's blood boil with indignation, and wonder why the people have not arisen before now and once for all abolished the tyrannous system which prevails under the sanction and with the apparent sup- port of the present Coercion Government. It almost seems as if the Government, knowing their inability to convince the people of the justice of their proceedings in Ireland on its merits, were determined to force the peo- ple into a sham belief in their liberty and equality witlf the rest of the fellow-subjects of Her Majesty. In the case of the late Mr. John Mandeville, the jury declared that he died from inflammation, brought about by the brutal and unjustifiable treatment in Tullamore gaol; and they protested against the system of treating politi- cal pr senses, and the cruel methods by which the prison rules were enforced. " Protested " indeed What effect will that have on Messrs. Balfour and Co.? rust about as much as a drop of water on the back of a duck. But while Mr. Mandeville's cruel death is bad enough, what I'.as to be said on the suicide of Dr. Ridley? At the time of writing the jury have not come to their decision, but the evidence has revealed a state of things which it is almost impossible to believe could have existed. Evidence given by several members of Parliament and other witnesses shows that Dr. Ridley was never known of himself to be cruel to the prisoners. On the contrary, his acts of kindness to those who suffered from the effects of Government persecution were many. Every- thing he did to lessen their hardships seemed to be over- shadowed by fear of the authorities—his employers. He complained of being watched from Dublin Castle, and actually on one occasion, two days after ordering a mat- trais for one of the prisoners, he received a communica- tion from Dublin "calling him over the coals" for it. Does not this seem a determined and persistent effort on the part of the authorities to administer punishment of the bitterest, if not revengeful character, on those of their political opponents who may happen to fall within their clutches? It almost ceases to be a wonder to me that Dr. Ridley took his own life after Mr. Mandeville bad been "done to death," and after the abominable manner in which Dr. Ridley was compelled to treat pri- soners who were unfit and unable to bear the inflictions put upon them. It need cause no surprise- therefore to learn from thc evidence of Mr. William O'Brien, 'M.P., that he never saw a more wretched look upon a man's face than that upon Dr. Ridley's, and well might the lat- ter say that an uneasy feeling "haunted" him. Dr. Ridley admitted to Mr. O'Brien t,,at their treatment was unnatural, but he asked what could he do? His own words were that he had a wife and family, and he had to earn a few half-pence. These revelations, sir, make me wonder if the Government have not so goaded on Dr. Ridley to "unnatural treatment" of prisoners to such an extent that he has found relief only in taking his own life. If this is so, surely the Government, or the authori- ties under them, will be brought to account for the death of one who was said at the inquest to have been a con- scientious and skilful man!' I wender how much longer the people will permit this tyranny to continue ; pro- bably until the next general election, when I hope a great and radical change will be wrought.—Yeurs &c., JUSTICE TO IRELAND. August 14th, 1883.

LETTER FROAt MR. GLADSTONE.—A letter WU read from Mr. Gladstone at a meeting held at Dalkeith on Tuesday evening to protest against the imprisonment of Mr. Dillon. The right hon. gentleman says the Govern- ment forced the Plan of Campaign into operation by not taking cognisance in 1887 of the inability of many of the Irish tenantry to meet their obligations, and then they took advantage of "the Plan" in order to bring Ireland under the present cruel system of coercion. If Mr. Dillon broke the law he was driven to do so by this gross misconduct. -- - _

ROYAL IRISH CONSTABULARY.—The Lord Lieutenant of Ireland and the Chief Secretary visited the Royal Irish Constabulary depot in F'hcenix Park on Wednesday, and witnessed a parade of the men. Lord Londonderry, addressing the force, expressed his high admiration of the loyalty and devotion to duty which they had always displayed. Mr. Balfour also addressed the men. In the name of the Government, he expressed his great sense of the service which they had performed for their Queen and country. In no country, he said, had the duties of the police been performed under greater difficulty. NAVAL MANCEllVll.F.S.—lntelligence received on Wed- nesday from the respective fleets engaged in the naval rnanceuvres shows that the " belligerents" are still taking matters easily. Admiral Tryon, whose squadron remains at anchor in Lough Swilly, was doing nothing more startling than putting the crew of the Severn through a stiff inspection, and Admiral Baird's defend- ing fleet, after a night's uneventful cruise in the Chan- nel, returned on Wednesday afternoon to the Downs, anchoring off Deal. The cruiser Sandfly was again busy among the Atlantic liners in the neighbourhood of Queenstown.

div.head: GOOD WORD FOR BRIGGS.
div.p: A GOOD WORD FOR BRIGGS.

Briggs was (says a London correspondent) the hero at Kennington Oval on Monday. Mr. Glad- stone may be a great man, and so may Lord Salis- bury, but the greatest of living personages for that day amongst the vast concourse of people who wit- nessed the match of England against Australia was Briggs of Lancashire. Briggs, paysically, is not a big man—in fact, he is a small man, but the mind 'is the standard of the man. and Briggs as a bowler was simply a giant. Ile sent down 14 maiden overs in succession ; he took five wickets for 25 runs, and he threw a sixth Australian out. It was owing to his splen- did cricketing skill that the Australians' first inn- ings reached only 80 runs, on a good dry wicket. When the Englishmen started it looked as if they Would never reach even 80. Grace went out when the score stood at two, and Illyett out when it had reached six. W. W. Read and A. Shuter raised the hopes of the multitude who were watching the game as if the fate of the English nation de- pended on the result. The Surrey captain and crack did very well, and averted any disaster, but it was not until Barnes and Abel got , together that the enthusiasm of the crowd rose to the appropriate pitch. The Surrey and Nottingham professionals simply collared the bowling, and the Australian total was doubled before Barnes was, caught for a splendid 62. Abel was not out at the drawing of the stumps, Sugg being his partner. Abel, next to Briggs, was the greatest hero of the day, and was the recipient of an ovation of which an Emperor might be proud. Yet he stands only a I little over five feet, and it looks as if the two small- est cricketers in England, so far as height is con- cerned, will prove themselves the best men in this great cricketing encounter.

div.head: MANCHESTER MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from pcule 6.)
div.p: THE MANCHESTER MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from pcule 6.)
A CONSUL'S VIEW OF _THE SIIIP CANAL.

We take the follqwing from an article in the "Liverpool Journal of Commerce" for yesterday : Major E. J. Hale, United States Consul for the Manchester district in England, has drawn up a re- port, addressed to the American Department of State, on the Manchester Ship Canal, which has been published as a "special issue." Manchester, according to Major Hale, ranks next in precedence to London, and far excels the other cities in the magnitude of its interests, lie tells the Govern- ment he represents that the densely popu- lated manufacturing districts of which Man- chester is the metropolis is on the eve of undergoing a great change, the importance of which it is impossible to estimate. The Ship Canal, concerning which the department has been infoimed, is now in course of construction; and four years hence a population of more than 7,000,000, one-fifth of the whole population of the ' United Kingdom, will have a nearer ocean steamer port than they now possess. The district affected, he remarks, embraces more than 150 industrial towns, one hundred of which have a population ex- ceeding ten thousand, the population of eleven of them exceeding one hundred thousand. Major Hale gives a list of names of cities and towns, with the number of inhabitants, and their characteristic industries, lie supplies an outline chart to show the lttanchester Ship Canal district and the nearest ocean steamer ports. Newcastle. Middlesbor- ough. Hull, Harwich, London, Southampton, Holyhead, Liverpool. Fleetwood, the Ribble and Dee ports are to cease supplying the district of Manchester. Major Hale draws a triangle with its base on a line from Blackpool through Padham, Colne, Keighley, Kirkstall, and Leeds to represent the distribution of population , rround Manchester. One side of the triangle runs h.= Leeds to Chapel-en-le-Frith, and from that apex to parts beyond Preston. The inl- abitants to be furnished with sea imports from Mar chester ex- tends considerably beyond the area enclosed within the triangle. The area of the triangle will enclose a population of about 5,414 per square mile. Major Hale speaks of the cotton manufacturing trades, the great bulk of which are located in the Slanches- ter district, and the mechanical industries, 7-rhich are unpaialleled in the world, embracing b.mo- tives, steam boilers, and railway plant of every de- scriptiom, and every variety of machinery. Manchester is forcibly exemplified by its numerous exchanges and markets, including the stock, corn, provisions, coal, and cotton-waste ex- changes. The Royal Exchange has about seven thousand subscribers, which far exceeds the num- ber of subscribers to any other Exchange outside of London, and three thousand of the members attend from places beyond Manchester. At present the port of Manchester for Customs purposes ranks ninth on the list of one hundred and thirty-five ports in the amount of duties collected, and comes after Hull. before Southampton, Plymouth, Dover, Sunderland, Grimsby, Cardiff, Swansea, Greenock, Dundee, Middlesbrough, and other well-known sea- ports. Manchester is also the focus of a complete system of railways and canals, so that the changes which must follow from the constitution of a ship- ping Dort of the first class will be enormous. RUN CORN.

There is not much-lialviti-alsplayed on this sec- tion at present, but there arena wanting Signs that engineering operations of great danger and magni- tude will shortly be commenced. For a considerable time past there has only been one steam navvy at work, and this monstre machine having made the cutting as far as Norman's Pottery,which is doomed to demolition, has been stopped. During the pre- sent week, therefore, digging operations have been at a standstill, but yesterday the navvy was taken back nearer Norton, and was set to work upon another heading, or in other words, in widening the cutting. In a short time it is expected that the three navvies that are on the scene will be in full operation. This view is borne out by the fact that traffic has been stopped on the Old Quay Canal, and we hear that the water is to be im- mediately drained off. Having this waterway of a past generation effaced, Mr. Gregson will be better,. enabled to commence the work in the bed of the i river Mersey, and in a brief space that engineer may be engaged in the task of overcoming the for- ces of nature in the way of tides, &c. Day after day vast loads of material are being shipped at the Old Quay Dock, where there are now stacked some hundreds of piles, and enormous quantities of other timber. The railway line has not yet been,taken beyond the Old Quay Dock the permission of the Board of Commissioners to traverse certain streets on the river side being evidently waited for. WESTON.

On this section digging operations are being car- ried on on a fairly extensive scale, and the line of the proposed canal along Frodsham Marish can now be plainly discerned from Weston Hill. Mr. Kirk- ham has nearly completed the village of huts on the marsh, and as soon as a propert water supply can be obtained several of the huts will be occupied. THELWALL AND LYMM.

Great progress is still being made on this section, but there is little further to add. On Monday last the Lymm fustian cutters who have been offered " jobs" on the canal began work on a part of the section lying to the Thelwall side of what was formerly Lymm sewage farm. Work has been provided for about forty "cutters," but as the local festival of Rushbearing fell on Monday, only about twelve started that day. On Tuesday, however, forty-two " hands " turned up, and these have worked in seven gangs. The gangs work on commumistic lines, each man working according to his strength and all drawing equal pay for the work done. At the Statham brick-works it is said that about 100.000 bricks are be- ing produced weekly. Over the river, on Rixton Leys, the German navvy is still kept steadily to work, and is doing great execution. SALFORD.

The work on this secasn7l--cOn-ii—nues to be pushed for- ward with all speed. The three bays forming the Sal- ford dock have been almost cut out, and present to the visitor a good idea of what it will be like when it is finished. The total number of men employed in the docks is 500, while two of Rushton and Proctor's and two of Whittaker's steam excavators are continu- ously at work in tearing up the earth in the middle and south bays. In the north bay a number of men are employed night and day in laying concrete for the dock wall, which will be faced with stone masonry, and will be Bft. above the water level. The coping of the wall will be of granite, a cargo of which has already arrived. Owing to the Ship Canal Company not having gained possession of the land, the work for the Manchester dock has not yet commenced. On the Trafford section 370 men and six locomotives are employed, and at Barton there are 700 men and six loco- motives, making a total of 1,620 men on the Salford sec- tion.

OVERCROWDING MANX STEAMERS—At the Liverpool Police Court, on Thursday, the captain of the Manx line steamer Prince of Wales was, for having permitted his ship to be overcrowded on the passage from Douglas to Liverpool on Bank Holiday, fined £5 and costs, and 6d. for each of 480 passengers carried in excess of the licence. The defence was that the officers and crew of the steamer were powerless against the horde of return- ing pleasure-seekers who invaded the vessel on the evening of the great festival, and the Bench expressed the opinion that the managers of the line had "taken almost every precaution to prevent overcrowding."

div.head: ,e "•"- • THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 18, 1888.
div.p: ,e "•"- • THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 18, 1888.
WARRINGTONIANS IN AMERICA.

Mr. John Gandy, grocer, Church-st., has recently received I.tters from three well-known Warring- tonians, who have sought a home in the ne w world, namely, Mr. H. Whitham, Mr. W. Porter, and Mr. James Winstanley. Mr. Winstanley, who departed from Warrington only a short time ago, dates his letter 20th July, from on board the Parisian, which at that time had reached the river St. Lawrence. As might be expected the emigrants suffered from sea sickness during the first day or two of the voy- age, but this malady having rim its course the rest of the voyage was uneventful and fairly comfor- table. Mr. Winstanley says :—" After a long and cold but very fine passage we are steaming ahead up the beautiful river St. Lawrence. We expect to land at Quebec on Saturday morning early. lam sorry to tell you Nellie has been very ill all the way out ; after two days she did not leave her berth until this, Friday morning, when I got her on deck for a short while. She has had , the doctor twice a day attending her, and the stewardess is very kind and attentive to her. I am thankful she is so much better, and I hope we shall be able to leave Quebec on the Satur- day night special, as I dread the French hotels. We had a fine sail out to Loch Foyle, and we waited three Iniurs for the mails, and then for the long rolling sea of the Atlantic, which soon began to make us all sick. It is a dreadful sensation, and I think it is contagious--one helping on the other until all become almost helpless. But by the next day we get about all right again, and begin to want some food. We sighted only one ship, shortly after leaving Ireland. and no more until we came in sight of lonely Labrador, with its snow-covered hills and ravines. It became very cold on the second day out, and it took all the coats and wraps you could muster to make the sheltered side of the deck tolerable. We first saw a large shoal of fish swim- ming on the top of the sea, some very large ones; and then we had a few sharks playing about for a short time, but tbe good ship soon left them behind. After this the voyage became monotonous. Now and again huge waves would come sweeping along the deck and half-drowning some poor passenger or other. We have a nice musical lot of twelve in my room, a Canadian or two -going home, and taken on the whole a good lot. Just before reaching the strai's of Belle Isle we passed some very beautiful icebergs of all sizes and shapes. It then became very cold indeed, and we had to retreat to our cabins, which soon became very stuffy. The food on board is very good, but very roughly served; it is a case of taking it or leaving it—there is no choice about it at all. flie sail up the St. Lawrence is indeed very beauti- ful; it is a magnificent stream of water, and along its banks there are very many wooden houses, some very pretty villages and churches—some in course of erection—and nearly all are French." Mr. Porter, who dates the 31st July, from Vancouver, states that Mr. Winstanley and his family had arrived there, after their overland jour- ney, and after staying a few days had gone on to Portland. Mr. Winstanley had been well pleased with what he saw at Vancouver, and work had been offered him at three dollars twenty-five cents per day, but he decided to go on to Portland or San Francisco. Of himself and family Mr. Porter says— " We are all first-class, and hope soon to take a trip to old Warrington." Mr. Whitham's is also an in- teracting but more private letter, and contains many remembrances te old friends in this district.

div.head: RUNCORN NIGHTSOIL CONTRACTOR
div.p: THE RUNCORN NIGHTSOIL CONTRACTOR

IN COURT. At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday. before Mr. games Ilandley and Mr. 0. Lloyd Wigg. Edwin Field. nightsoil contractor to the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, was brought up under a warrant charged with using threats to James Percival, the nuisance inspector, from which the latter was afraid that the defendant would do him some bodily in- jury. The defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. W. 11. Linaker, law clerk, prosecuted.—The posecutor said it was part of his duty to superintend the re- moval of nightsoil. The defendant had been em- ployed by the Commissioners for three years, and for the past 21 years he had discharged his duties very irregularly, and was behind in his work. At the end of last month he was 113 ashpits behind, and he reported to the committee that Field was neglecting to empty them. The fol- lowing dav the Chairman of the Health Com- mittee and the surveyor made an arrangement With Edwin Tuckey to do part of the work. Field had only one gang of men and one cart at work ; in his (witness's) opinion it would take three horses and carts and three gangs of men to keep the nightsoil of Runcorn under proper control. On Friday night, the 9th instant, about half-past eleven, he was in Wellington-st. watch- ing the men remove nightsoil, when the defendant came up and blamed him for the extra men being put on. He replied that he had nothing to do with it, and the defendant said, "You are robbing me—both you and the Commissioners." He walked down the street, and the defendant followed him and said "I don't care a if I am in Jackson's place, one of you two men will be scarce before long." He did not know whether defen- dant meant Tuckev or Tuckey's foreman. Defendant had ' said some very bad things about him that he would have to prove in another court. The defendant had never threatened him before. He was drunk; he was right enough when he was sober. In consequence of what the &fendant said, and his manner, he was afraid he would lo him some bodily injury. He did not go out after Friday night because he "did not want to be ill-used by having him planted in a dark entry waiting for him."— By Mr. Handley: The contract had a year and seven months to run.—Thomas Caldwell, foreman to Mr. Tuckey, corroborated, and said the defendant interrupted the work on the night in question.--Field was about to enter into all the details of the contract, but Mr. Hand- ley said the Bench had nothing whatever to do with that.—The defendant denied that he had used the words attributed to him, and said that he used to give Percival something every time he got his money—he had brought him boots and other sorts of things—and because he had stopped the practise Perci- val had been ten times worse, When he lived at Zion- place he killed a pig and Percival came to the house, and he had nearly half of the pig. He said he liked good • bacon.—Mr. Handley said the Bench believed that the • threat had been used, and the defendant was ordered to • be bound over to keep the peace for three month in his , own recognisance of £2O, and pay the costs, £1 143 10d. In default, a month's hard labour.—The defendant: I must not have a month. I can do without that.—Mr. Johnson: Have you got the money to pay P—The defen- • dant : Yes, I have.—The defendant then sat down at the solicitor's table, and made out a cheque, which his wife took, and shortly afterwards returned with the money.
TERRIBLE DISASTER IN THE NORTH ATLANTIC. PASSENGER STEAMERS IN COLLISION. 119 LIVES LOST.

NEW onx, THURSDAY.—The steamship Geiser bound from New York for Stettin, was sunk, in• consequence of collision with tlae Danish steamer Thingvalla, off Cape Race, on Tuesday. It is be- lieved that at least seventy-two passengers and thirty-three of the crew were drowned. The re- mainder were saved by the Thingvalla and the Hamburg steamer Wieland, the latter of which ar- rived here to-day, and gave scanty information. So far as is known, the Thingvalla, although much damaged, was able to proceed to Halifax. Captain Mueilor, of the Geiser, was amongst the saved. NEW YORK, THURSDAY EVENlNG.—Further in- quiries among the officers and crew of the Wieland elicit the fact that one side of the Geiser was stove in, and so completely that the vessel sank within five minutes. There were only fourteen ot the passengers and seventeen of the crew saved. The captain of the Wieland has good reason for be- lieving that none save those mentioned were res- cued. The Wieland also brought 455 passengersfrom the Thingvalla, in case that vessel should not reach Halifax in safety.

[REUTER'S TELEGRAM.] NEW lona, THURSDA.Y.—The Hamburg-American Company's steamer Wieland, which has arrived here, brings intelligence of a collision between the steamers Thingvalla and Geiser at four o'clock on the morning of the 14th instant, when off Sable Island. The Geiser sank five minutes after the collision, and of ker passengers and crew only four- teen of the former and seventeen of the latter, in- cluding Captain Moller, were saved, the remainder, comprising seventy-two passengers and thirty-three of the crew, being drowned. The Thingvalla sus- tained serious damage, and transferred her passen- gers, who number 455 persons, to the Wieland. They were brought here by that vessel, together with the survivors of the Geiser. The Thingvalla Will endeavour to reach nalifax. OFFICIAL REPORT.
of I

[CENTRAL NEWS TELEGRAM.] NEW YOUR. FRIDAY MORNING..2-The official re- vised report of the collision which took place off Sable Island on the 14th inst. between the steam- ship Geiser, bound from New York to Stettin, and the steamer Thingvalla shows that 119 lives have been lost, including eighty passengers, thirty-three of the crew, and six officers. Those saved include fourteen passengers, seventeen of the crew, and four officers, the latter consisting of the captain of the Geiser, the second and third mates; named Gorgen- sen and Petersen respectively, and the doctor Dierks. All these belonged to the Geiser, no lives being lost of those belonging to the Thingvalla. There were only seven cabin passengers in the Geiser, and all of these, who were in bed at the time, were drowned. Captain Moller, of the Geiser, states that when he retired on the night of the collision, at eleven o'clock, , 'he night was clear and the sea quite calm, 'no mist whatever being perceptible at that hour. About half-past three in the morning, as they were off Cape Sable, he was suddenly aroused by the man on watch, and rushing on to the bridge of his vessel he saw indistinctly through the cloudy and rainy atmosphere the starboard side of a vessel, which afterwards turned out to be the Thingvalla. In the stillness of the night he distinctly heard three loud whistles warning him of the imminent , danger the two vessels were in. Ile 'immediately reversed the engines, and he could see that the Thingvalla did likewise, but they were going at too great a speed to stop all at once, and with a fearful crash they struck 6ne another, creating wild confusion and panic among their respective passengers. A glance sufficed to sholvth at the Geiser had suffered irreparable damage, one .'of her sides be- ing completely stoved in by the shock. The passen- gers and crew,with frantic cries and terror-stricken countenances, being awakened by the crash, rushed on deck, knocking one another over in the wild attempt to reach a place of temporary safety. The boats were quickly lowered, but so great was the panic that they were all capsized in no time, or overweighted by the poor wretches who sought to stet into them, so that few escaped by the boats. The vessel sank within five minutes of the time of the collision. Captain Moller was very nearly drowned, he being picked up in a very exhausted condition by a boat from the Thingvalla, which rescued several others. Most of the passengers on board the Geiser were North-Western farmers in well-to-do circumstances, who, having emigrated from Germany to America, were returning to visit their native land, some, it is said, intending to pay a visit to the Copenhagen Exhibition. The Thing- calla will endeavour to reach llalifax, notwith- standing the serious damage she sustained, but 455 of her passengers went back to New York with the Wieland, in case the vessel should not reach her destination in safety. [CENTRAL NEWS TELEGRAM.] NEW Yomx. FRIDAY MORNING.--The Thingvalla will come to New York instead of going to Halifax, as first intended. The Geiser was an iron screw steamer of 2,831 gross tons, built at Copenhagen in 1881, and the Thingvalla an iron screw steamer of 2,524 gross tons, built at Copenhagen in 1874. Both steamers belong to the Thingvalla Line, are owned in Copenhagen, and run between that port and New York.
A Reuter's New York telegram says: Many of the Geiser's passengers were excursionists from Min- nesota. Very few succeeded in reaching the deck, most of them being drowned in their berths. _
Lloyd's agent at Halifax telegraphs that the Thingvalla, which was in collision with the Geiser, had put into Halfax with her bows stove in.

The well-known Highland mail steamer Clansman, one of Messrs. Maebray-ne's fleet, has gone ashore while on her passage to Stornoway at a desolate spot on the coast of Skye. Throe steamers have left Glasgow to take off her passengers—most of whom are tourists—and to ren- der other assistance.

div.head: BANK QUAY HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: BANK QUAY HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.

The . annual exhibition a flowers, fruits, and vegetables, in connection with this society, was opened in Trinity Schoolroom, Museum-st., War- rington, yesterday afternoon, and will be continued to-day (Saturday). The society, it may be men- tioned, is under distinguished patronage, and has , for its president the Mayor (Mr. T. H. Sutton). The vice-presidents are Mr. H. B. White, Aldermen Pickmere and Davies, Councillors Monks, Percival, Taylor, and Ashton; and Messrs. T. Morris, F. W. Monks, W. Milner, T. Hall, J. Kneen, R, Mellor, and S. J. Barlow. The committee is composed as fol- lows: -Messrs. W. Lawless (chairman), W. Holmes (vice-chairman), W. Bellian, J, Gleave, jun., G. Bax- ter, J. Webb, D. Ferguson, G. Bailey, G. Parry, G. Wilcox, Thomas Roughley, and William Gleave. Mr. J. Massey is honorary treasurer, and Mr. 1 Lish- man makes an indefatigable honorary secretary. The show was opened soon after three o'oclock yes- terday afternoon by the MAYOR, who said that the object of the society was •to cultivate a taste amongst the working people for the growing of flowers, plants, and fruits. He thought that it was a very good object indeed, for with the cultivation of a taste for growing flowers and plants there came to the mind of the working-man a love for home end a love for those home comforts which must be a very great advantage to him and his family. He was very pleased to see so many excellent exhibits there that day: These exhibits were a credit to those who bad sent them. He hoped that exhibi- tions of that kind would be encouraged by the people of Warrington, because he was sure that they were calculated to:do a creat amount, of good. -Mr. R. DASIES, in the course of a few remarks, said that he had often wondered why Warrington could not regularly have one flower show in the year. The present exhibition might be taken as a scat of beginning. He himself felt a peculiar plea- sure in horticulture, for he had made it his hobby- together with a little botany-and he was delighted to see the exhibits that had that day been brought together. He congratulated the committee on the I success of their efforts, and trusted that the exhibi- tion would be the precursor of an annual flower show for Warrington.. He read of other places producing monstre gooseberries, but they did not hear of anything of the sort in Warrington. He had great pleasure indieed in helping in a humble way to promote the success of the affair.-Mr. LAWLESS, as chairman of the committee, expressed his thanks to the ladies and gentlemen who had by their subscriptions conduced to the success of the exhibition. He also thanked Mr. Carleton for kindly allowing the use of the room. He hoped that the cottagers in the neighbourhood of Bank Quay would endeavour to further the object of the society, and that the society would be successful.- The exhibits were staged round the large school- room, in the middle of which were a number of splendid plants that had been sent for exhibition, and not for competition. In another part of the building were a number of wild flower bouquets that had been submitted for competition by the children attending Holy Trinity Schools. Mr. John Crosfield, of Wal- ton Lea (gardener Mr. Kipps) lent a magnifi- cent collection of stove and greenhouse plants, ferns, and palms, which were placed in a prominent position in the middle of the large room, and made a veg pretty effect. Mr. Crosfield also lent for view a splendid Stage Horn fern, and collections of fruit and cut flowers. Mr. Fletcher, of Museum- st., lent a collection of palms, and there was a col- lection of plants from Bank Park Gardens (gardener Mr. Green). Councillor Bolton, who has gained dis- tinction as a rose-glowur, added to the attractive- ness of the exhibition by lending a collection of cut flowers, including some fine specimens of roses. On the whole the display was an excellent one, and one that reflects credit on the coutmittee, and all con- cerned. The judges were Messrs. John Holmes (Liscard), Edward Green (gardener, Bank Park Gardens). and W. Kipps (gardener at Walton Lea.) Appended is a list of the 'prize-takers:- VARIOUS.-SiX stoves greenhouse plants, 1, George Ambrose, Vyne Nursery ; 2, W. H. Holmes, Lovely-lane Nursery. Six ferns (exotics), 1, W. H. Holmes. Six gloxinias, 1, W. H. Holmes. Six colenses, 2, W. H. Holmes. One fern, any variety, 1, W. H. Holmes. One palm, any variety, 1, W. H. Holmes; 2, S. Frodoux.
