div.head: PROSECUTIONS AGAINST, -RUNCORN PUBLICANS. "THE MAN AT THE WHEEL."
div.p: PROSECUTIONS AGAINST, -RUNCORN PUBLICANS. "THE MAN AT THE WHEEL."

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. James Handley and Mr. G. Lloyd Wigg, Alfred Ellison, landlord of "The Man at the Wheel" public-house. Church-st., was summoned for having on the 28th July sold intoxicating liquor to two drunken persons named John Garner and Thomas Brockley and also with permit- ting drunkenness to take place on the same day. Mr. Thompson of Birkenhead was for the defence.—lnspector O'Donnell stated that on Saturday night, the 28th ult., he was on daty in Church-st., at 10 minutes to eleven o'clock, and heard a disturbance in the ."Man at the Wheel." He and P.C. Mansell entered the house and found inside a number of drunken people amongst whom were several women. Two men were ' visibly supplied" one of them having in his han i a glass half filled with beer. Witness afterwards ascertained that the man's name was Gardner. There was another man, named Brockley, staggering about the vaults, and another man pulled him down on to a seat. Witness' asked Brockley where his beer was and he walked up to the counter and took up a glass which he said was his. There was some fighting taking place, and the attention of the defendant was called to the disorder,and the men were ejected with the assis- tance of the police. Witness asked the landlord to look round as the house was very badly conducted, and there was a lot of drunkenness. He then asked the defendant to point-out a single man in the house who was sober, but he could not.—P.C.'s Mansell and Gosling gave cor- roborative evidence.—P.C. Dale also stated that he visi- ted the house, and could not see a sober man amongst the dozen men present.—Mr. Thompson having addressed the Bench, called the defendant, who was sworn, and stated that at the time the constables entered he was ejecting a woman. The Inspector said—" Don't you think that all the people in the house are drunk 2" Wit- ness replied—" Certainly not." Inspector O'Donneil then said—" We will see," and went up to Brockley and asked him if he was drunk. BrOckley replied that he was not. The Inspector then went to an old man, a navvy, who was cutting tobacco, and asked him his name, and the man replied, " r will not tell you; I shall not give you my name," and the Inspector -struck him on the chest; The inspector ha 4 in cross-examination, denied these allegations. The constables rendered no assistance 'in ejecting the men who were fighting. John Gardner was not in the house after eight o'clock that night. Brockley had only been in the house about five minutes, and had only one glass of bees there.—Thomas Brockley, John Barratt, and William Sheen also gave evidence of a corroborative character.—Mr. Handley said the Bench were fully satisfied that drunkenness was permitted, and adked was there any conviction against 'the house.— Superintendent Hollingworth said there had been no conviction against the house since it came into the pos- session of Sir A. B. Walker and Co.—A fine of 20s and costs was imposed. THE CUSTOMERS OF THE GOLDEN LION.

David Snell, landlord of the Golden Lion or Blue Ball Inn, in Fryer-st., was charged with having, on the 4th August, and on divers other days, allowed his house to be the resort of habitual prostitutes, who were allowed to remain a longer time than was necessary for reasonable refreshment.—Defendant pleaded not guilty, and was defended by Mr. Calvert (of the firm of Marsh, Son, and Calvert, of Bedford Leigh). Evidence was given by Constables Ratcliffe, Breeze, Dale, Sergeants Gosling, and Woolley, showing that women of ill-fame frequented the house and stayed there for some time, varying from a quarter of an hour to an horir. Frequently it was stated dancing was carried on to the music of a tin whistle or a fiddle, and the women took part. Sergeant Woolley said during the 18 months he had been in Run- torn he had only visited the Blue Ball Inn on one occasion when there had not been a prostitute there. Inspector O'Donnell gave evidence that since he had come to Runcorn he had found that the inn was a regular meeting place for women of bad repute. He had visited the house weekly and bi-weekly, and had always found such women there with one exception. He had pointed out the character of the women to the landlord, who said he should serve them so long as they had three halfpence. Otherwise the house was as well conducted as could, be expected considerin,-, its situation. The defendant was sworn, and alleged' that the women never remained more than ten minutes at a time. He had not known that the women were prostitutes, and had seen nothing wrong with them.—Mr. Handley: Do you mean to tell us seriously that you did not know the girls were prostitutes ?—Witness : No, sir; I have never seen anything wrong with them in my house.— Evidence was given by a number of witnesses, proving that the police had exaggerated the number of women in the house on one occasion.—ln reply to the Bench, Superintendent Hollingworth stated that the defendant had not been convicted previously; but the previous tenant had been fined three times, and his license had been endorsed.—Mr. Handley said the magistrates were convinced this case had been clearly proved, and the defendant was fined £4 and costs, the license not to be endorsed. A

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday morning. Col. Ashton presided, and there were also present Messrs. Wallington, Aaron, Brandreth, P. Hall, J. Hall, Lewis; H. Linaker (clerk), and Farrington (nuisance inspector.) NAVVIES' HUTS o FRODSHAM MARSH—An application was made for a certificate of tenancy for six navvies' huts on Frodsham Marsh. It was stated that every- thing had been carried out according to the plans except the water supply, which was in the hands of Mr. Tim- mins, of Runcorn. In the meantime if the certificate was granted a guarantee would be given that a sufficient supply of water would be carted from Frodsham, until water had been found on the spot .—The Clerk said a well had been sunk but the water did not pa is the analyst. Mr. Timmins was now boring down to the same level at which the Gas and . Water Company's water was got from.—lt was agreed to allow the huts to be inhabited on the guarantee above mentioned being given, a certifi- cate to be granted when an independent supply of water had been secured. _

NEW HOUSES AT NETHERTON.—A certificate of occupa- tion was granted to Mr. R. Bate for four new houses. erected by him, at Netherton, Frodsham Lordship, the water supply thereto being satisfactory. POLLUTED WATER, &C AT ,KEICEWICH.—The Inspector reported that the public well situatg at Kekewich was highly polluted with sewage which emanates from some cottages, and instructions were given to the inspector to require the owner of the cottages to prevest such pollu- tion by diversion or otherwise of the ,sewage.—lt was also reported that certain cottages at Kekewich were without sufficient drainage and the necessary notice was ordered to be served.

'WATER SUPPLY TO COTTAGES AT ROCK SAVAGE,—Mr. Farrington reported that some cottages situate at Rock Savage were without any available supply of water, and also that the privies needed attending to. He had called the owners attention to the matter, and no doubt both matters would be looked after forthwith.

DEFECTIVE SEWER AT MOOR.—The Inspector reported that the Sewdr at Moore had,become defective owing to the outfall being silted up, and directions were given for the inspector to confer with the clerk in reference o the matter. This was all the business.

• PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present Mr. J Kenwright (chairman), the Rev. Dean Finegan Messrs. J. W. Wareing, E. Syder, W. Middlehurst, J. Janson, J. Lowe, J. Buckley, J. Burchall, J. Birchall, T. F. Hill, R. Tuson, J. Ellison, C. B. Johpson, H. Hulme, W. Tyrer, J. Whalley, W. Swift,.and S. H. Hartley (clerk). GOVERNMENT. REPAYMENT. The Local Government Board wrote that they had paid to the Board's treasurer £338 lOs Bd, the amount repayable to the Guardians in respect of the salaries of medical officers and teachers of workhouse and district schools for the year ended 25th March last. A SINGULAR APPLICATION.—The Rev. E. W. Watson, curate-in-charge of St. Paul's Mission Church, St.Helens, wrote asking the Guardians to secure the admission of an orphan girl, named Ruth Glover, into some home for girls where she would be trained for service.—The Clerk said the girl had been on the boarding-out system, and if the Guardians began to give relief after the periods , had expired, they would have other applications.—On the motion of Mr. Wareing, seconded by Mr. Hill, the ap- plication was refused. •

THE ESTIMATE.—The Clerk submitted the estimate of the probable expenditure for the half-year ending 25th March last, which amounted to £22,527, witht,en per cent. added for contingencies, making a total of £24;779. The estimate was slightly in excess of the corresponding period last year.—The estimate was adopted. ILLNESS OF' AN OFFICIAL. The School Attendance Committee recommended the appointment of Mr. R. G. Waterman, as temporary ' substitute for Mr. Henry Kay, school attendance officer, who was incapacitated from performing his duties through illness.—Mr. Hill gave notice that he would move a motion to that effect at the next meeting. MILIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 505 inmates this week, 499 last week, and 462 in the cor- responding week last year; 71 vagrants had been re- lieved against 60 last year. This was all the business.
Mr. Blaine. in a speech delivered at Portland, "de- nounced" the Fisheries Treaty. A Washington telegram says that the Republican Senators will press the Fisheries Bill to a division.
... . A strike in which three hundred men are concerned has occurred among the boiler • makers, platers, and rivetters of the Aberdeen shipbuilding yards, who are agitating for .an advance of wages.
LATEST NEWS.

Lord Salisbury leaves tO-day (Saturday) for Royat. Mr. Parnell telegraphs that there is no foundation for the rumour that he intends to vacate his seat. A" Sporting Life" New York telegram on Thurs- day sap that Sullivan Wks been fined for drunkenness. A serious Are has broken out at the Farnborough Sta- tion on the South-Eastern Railway. It is still burning. Alfred William Oakley, aged seventeen, fell 100 feet from St. John's Church steeple, Brighton, yesterday, and was killed.

Mr. Balfour is still busy in Dublin with official work. The Attorney-General for Ireland left Kingstown for En- gland on Friday morning. The tenants on the Taafe estate, Ballvhaunis, have come to terms with the 'agent, who has accepted one year's rent, remitting all arrears. Evictions are thus , averted.

THE PARNELL CommissioN.--Sir James Haimen, presi- dent of the Parnell Commission, is visiting Mr. Justice Smith, and will shortly visit Lord Coleridge. Mr. Cunyn- hame, secretary to the Commission, is engaged daily ar- ranging preliminaries. The" Daily News "says the special express trains to Edinburgh which were put on at the beginning of the month by the London and North-Western and Great Northern Companies are to to discontinued on the 31st inst.

Timm. OF CsunisEs, &c.—While the cmstabulary were attending a proclaimed meeting at Ballinasloe, on Thursday, the police barracks at Cummer, near Tuam, were entered, and several carbines taken. It is also asserted that £2O was stolen.

OKTRAGE BY MOONLIGHTERS.—TiMOdIy Sullivan, a l labour& was fired at on Thursday night while sitting at his fireside at Killeen, near Gortatlea Kerry. The bul- let'Passed through his whiskers and lodged in the wall. He had been cautioned not to work for a widow in the TICE SHOEBURYNESS ARTILLERY MEETING.—The compe- titions of the Southern detachments having concluded on Thursday at the Volunteers Artillery meeting; the men on. Friday left by train on the London; Tilbury, and Southend. Railway for London, whence they proceeded to their respective 'destinations, The Devon, Cornwall, and North Yorkshire detachments departed the first at 745, and, the Dorset, Cheshire, and Carnarvon and other de- tachn3ents left by subsequent trains. ALLEGED SHOCKING POLICE BRIITALITY.—Jas. Maher, policeman, was charged at Manchester on Friday, with the manbaughter of William Swan. A long inquiry irtto the cause of deceased's death by the coroner resulted in a verdict of " Manslaughter,".against the accused. It was asserted that he took deceased out of his own house to the lock-up, struck and truncheoned him' and used such brutal violence that death resulted therefrom. Maher, who denied the imputations, was remanded till Tuesday week.

ANOTHER DEATH FROM CARBOLIC POISONING.—Another death (the third within ten days) occurred in Liverpool on Friday from carbolic acid poisoning,. Fanny Short- man, widow, was found insensible in her house on Fri- day morning, and, the doctor being called, she was dis- covered to have taken carbolic acid. She was removed to the Infirmary, where she died without recovering consciousness. It is not known how she came to- take the poison, but, as the woman was of drunken habits, it is believed she swallowed it in mistake.

INQUEST ON Du. RIDLEY.—The inqt;e-si. on Dr. Ridley Was resumed at Fermoy en Friday morning. Mr. Moor- head, 8.L., addressed the jury on behalf of Dr: Moor- head. • He stated that it was owing to the inability of Dr. Ridley to do anything that the Mitchelstown and this inquest resulted. There were extraordinary facts in connection with Dr. Barr. He was first in the room that morning, subsequently took away a bag, and aftefwards felt his position keenly, and also the comments made by the coroner. He asked the jury to completely exonerate Dr. Moorhead.

EXTRAORDINARY FLOOD IN IRELAND. Particulars of an extraordinary flood this week, in the isolated district of Cross-roads, Killygordon; are reported from Londonderry. The river Finn overflowed its banks swept everything before it, tearing up trees, and carry- ing away the crops. The police barracks were flooded, the water being several feet in depth inside. The force had great difficulty in removing the furniture, tsgether with constable's boxes, rifles, bayonets, Ike., to a place of safety. Owing to the efforts by one constable, some im- portant papers were saved. Two other constables re- turning from duty, w...re suddenly surrounded by the flood, and had to seek refuge in trees, where they were kept prisoners for a considerable time. A farmer, dri- ving some cows, was obliged to abandon the cattle and climb atree. The flood was rising, and as the farmer could not swim, he was eventually rescued by another man swimming to the tree and tying a cord round his body. A stone bridge was completely swept away.

div.head: STRIKE OF FRENCH NAVVIES.
div.p: THE STRIKE OF FRENCH NAVVIES.

Rims, FRIDAY.—At a general meeting to-day, the nav- vies decided to return to work, owing to the great misery which had been caused to them by the strike. GERMAN ANNEXATION IN ZANZIBAR. A " Times " Zanzibar telegram says the German com- pany on Thursday received officially charge of the ad- ministration of the coastline from the Sultan, hoisting their flags at fourteen ports, in conjunction with the Sultan's flags. THE HEALTH QF THE POPE. - A "Daily News" Rome telegram says :—Yesterday the Pope did not receive several persons who were to have had an audience. Besides this, he has not for three days taken his favourite drive. These circumstances lead to the supposition that his Holiness is still unwell. Such is the opinion at the Vatican. The utmost secrecy is, how- ever, maintained there on the subject.
MARKETS.
The body of George Davy, of Sale, one of the three young men drowned at Douglas on the eveninz of the 27th July, was found on Thursday close to the scene of the lamentable accident.

The first through train to Constantinople seoms to have caused some excitement during its journey. It reached Adrianople at midnight. An immense crowd, estimated at 10,000 persons, assembled at the station. The New Church Conference was resumed on Thurs- day, at Accrington, when an eight hours' discussion took place as to whether fermented or unfermented wine should be used at the Sacrament. Eventually it was de- cided to hold two Communion Services during conference week.

div.head: BIRTHS.
div.p: BIRTHS.

CONSHRVATIVE PICNIC.—On Thursday the Garstonef servative Club paid their annual picnic to Lymm. tak up their headquarters at the Plough Hotel. The paw numbered about 100. They came by rail at 10 a.f and proceeded to a field belonging to Mr. L. Warbur ..t0"....; where athletic sports took place till two o'clOCk. the company adjourned to dinner in the pavilion dr, hotel. Mr. W. J. Stewart, the president of the c presided as host, and after dinner the usual loyal patriotic toasts were duly honoured, after which, on motion of the chairman, a resolution of confidence ill , Majesty's Government was carried with acclamatioa, After dinner the party again adjourned to the field a° completed the sports. LYME SUNDAY SCHOOLe ANNUAL EXCURSION.— annual trip in connection with the above schools place, to Blackpool, on Monday, where a most enk. day was spent. Art early start was made, the train parting from Lymm at six o'clock. On arriving at ' destination the visitors formed into small parties search of the various amusements. Many indulged a refreshing bathe, while others preferred rowing sailing, for which there were ample facilities. Si arrangements had been made to admit the excursioi into the Winter Gardens and Aquarium. During whole day the weather was fine at Blackpool, though Lymm it rained very heavily at times. The rc journey was commenced from Blackpool at 7-40, 1,3 'being reached about midnight. It is estimated t about 800 persons accompanied the trip, which was every way a thorough success, much credit beiug Mr, E. Brown, jun , the hon. secretary, for the sat" tory manner in which the arrangements were r out.

"ROSE OF TRB VALLEY" DIVIDEND SOCIETY'S PICNIC' —The annual picnic of this society took place on Moir day to Liverpool, and was much enjoyed. The train left Lyznm at 9 a.m., returning at 8 p.m., ail being thoroughly satisfied with the day's outing. H COMPANY (LYNN) 3RD V.B.C.R. : CHURCH PARADO' —This company assembled at head-quarters on Sunda's' morning, and marched, under the' command of Lieut., L. T. Cookson, to Oughtrington Church for Divine ser- , vice. The route taken was by way of Eagle Brow, Pass , the Cross, and along the Higher-lane. After service the Journey home was through Oughtrington, and along ' Sandy-lane and Rush Green, back to headquarters* , where the men were dismissed. RUSH-BEARING MONDAY AT LYSIM.—TiIiS day at LyTTIT, i has vastly dwindled in importance from the great loo''' holiday it used to be. The days of cheap trips to the seaside, and other pleasure resorts are not the most aol-,. vantageous to keeping up the old festivals of May, 'Lli I roses, and of rush-bearing. This year the only rehe 0 , the great rush-bearing procession was a coal waggon' adorned with a few rushes, which was dragged about by", some boys. On Saturday morning the two usual trooP° of "Morris Dancers" danced gaily through the village: and the fair with hobby-horses and sweet stalls, an'' , " Aunt Sallies "was held, but otherwise, except as farnitY A re-unions, the rush-bearing festival has died out j° Lymm.

EXTRACTS FROM THE DIRECTORS' REPORT for the year ending April 30th, 1888.. Notwithstanding the liberal terms and conditions of the Company's Policies, and the heavy amount paid in claims, and for extension expenses (resulting in the 'largest increase of new business the Company has ever made in any one year), .Die Directors are pleased to state that after meeting all pay- ments and expenses, they have been able to mrry forward a !balance exceeding £15,000. Mr. James Sketchley, one of your Directors, retired in De- cember last for the purpose of travelling, ,when Mr. J. C. Fowke, who for upwards of twenty years' had been Solicitor to the'Company, was requested by the Board to fill up the vacancy, which we are pleased to say he consented to do, and he has proved to be a very important addition to the director- ate. Mr. Fowke is not a shareholder, but holds a Policy in the Company upon his own life for £l,OOO, and therefore may be looked upon as a more direct representative of the Policy holders. Thetotal income of the Company for the year :was £178,310 Ifis Bd, being an increase of £21,928 lls 9d.. Thetotal amount of payments was £163,018 14s ld, leaving a balance upon the year's.accounts of £15,292 4s 7d, making the total funds at the close of the year £96,302 19s Oil. The amount paid in Claims during the year was £77,479, including £4,411 66 Surrender Claims. The total sum paid up tO the 30th April, 1888, was £469,261 Is 10d. The number of A.ssurants upon the Company's books on the 30th April, 1888, was 374,098, and their annual premium would be £198,420 18s 10d, showing a net increase of 3%070 Assurants, and £27,820 lie 9d in Premium Income. lIENRY PORT, Managing Director.
